The Benedict Ong saga: Dunedin councillor’s complaints, expulsions and University of Otago allegations

New Zealand Herald September 07, 2026

Benedict Ong, 43, regularly posted photographs of himself with students at bars, parties and other social events.

He arrived on Dunedin’s political scene promising financial innovation and a decade without rates rises. Less than a year later, Benedict Ong has been stripped of roles, restricted from parts of the Civic Centre, suspended from committees and breached the city council’s code of conduct twice. Now the University of Otago is considering trespassing him from its entire campus after allegations about his student interactions. Ben Tomsett traces how it got here.

Benedict Ong appeared out of the ether as an unknown quantity in Dunedin politics when he launched bids for mayor and council last year.

Since being elected, his tenure has become one of the most turbulent in the council’s recent history – a rolling saga of complaints, investigations, confrontations and expulsions that has increasingly spilt beyond the council chamber.

The latest escalation involves allegations of unwanted physical proximity or contact with students and interactions that students reported made them feel uncomfortable or unsafe. Ong strongly denies the claims.

An unusually verbose interview subject, Ong rarely offers a straight answer when a winding one will do, and frequently returns to a repertoire of well-worn phrases (Dunedin is invariably “our most special city”).

He has offered little public reflection on his role in the controversies surrounding him.

Contact our South Island newsroom

Instead, controversies are often reframed as arising from his efforts to serve the city, or as political retaliation and “false attacks” against him – while few of his signature proposals have so far translated into council decisions.

Here is how his saga has unfolded.

August 29, 2025 – Ong enters the race

Ong emerged as a candidate for mayor and council after returning to his birthplace of Dunedin following much of his working life overseas.

His campaign material presented him as a former international banker and investor whose career had spanned corporate finance and investment across five continents.

His pitch was economic: “No Rate Rises”, more jobs and investment, and what he repeatedly described as “first-of-its-kind financial innovation”, drawing on his global debt expertise.

He told the Herald: “I am very proud to be able to come back to my hometown. I believe I have a lot of things to contribute to our community”.

October 11, 2025 – Elected to council

Ong failed in his bid for the mayoralty, won by Sophie Barker, but secured one of 14 seats at the Dunedin City Council table.

His high-profile grassroots campaign focused heavily on economic development, debt reform and restraining rates.

It was also the second-most expensive mayoral campaign of the 2025 election, with Ong declaring $44,098.72 in expenses – just behind Andrew Simms.

October 18 – Workplace concerns emerge within a week

Just a week after the election, the ODT reported council chief executive Sandy Graham had asked Ong to meet after receiving feedback from several people who had felt uncomfortable during recent interactions with him.

Graham said she did not believe any discomfort had been intentional, but wanted to discuss supporting Ong while maintaining a safe and professional workplace.

The ODT also reported returning councillor Lee Vandervis had blocked Ong’s number after a series of phone calls.

Ong disputed Vandervis’ description of those interactions.

No code of conduct process was underway at that stage.

December 2025-January 2026 – Ong makes his own code complaint

Days before Christmas, Ong lodged a code of conduct complaint against fellow first-term councillor John Chambers, alleging Chambers had made discriminatory remarks about Dunedin’s South Asian community.

Graham had asked Ong not to litigate the matter publicly or in the media while it was being assessed.

Ong nevertheless circulated correspondence about the complaint to media and, on January 13, published a lengthy social media post about it.

February 5, 2026 – The first complaint against Ong

Graham lodged a code of conduct complaint against Ong after he sent her an email on February 4 raising concerns about a council staff member while simultaneously copying media into the correspondence.

The staff member had been a witness in Ong’s complaint against Chambers.

February 11 – Ong’s complaint against Chambers dismissed

Independent investigator Steph Dyhrberg dismissed Ong’s complaint against Chambers, finding insufficient basis for a full investigation and the remark at the centre of the complaint had been misinterpreted.

Ong refused calls to apologise.

February 17 – Civic Centre access restricted

Ong’s access to parts of the Civic Centre was temporarily restricted while Graham undertook a health and safety assessment.

Correspondence leaked to media by Ong said concerns had been raised about Ong “floor walking/accosting staff” in staff areas, while preliminary findings from the separate code of conduct investigation had also prompted temporary measures.

Ong said the measures were retaliatory and linked them to his efforts to push his debt-financing proposals.

Graham rejected that.

February 20 – Tape over the mouth

Days later came one of the most memorable images of Ong’s term.

Ong arrived at an informal meeting with MPs with tape across his mouth.

Barker handed him a letter withdrawing his access to informal council meetings and stripping him of his deputy technology portfolio role after what she described as disrespectful behaviour and his refusal to remove disparaging online comments about Graham.

He was then asked to leave and escorted out by fellow councillors.

March 10 – Investigator finds a ‘very serious’ breach

Dyhrberg concluded Ong had materially breached the council’s code.

In her report, Dyhrberg wrote she found it was more likely than not Ong had acted in retaliation against the council staff member whose account had not supported his complaint against Chambers.

His attempt to discredit the staff member was described as particularly serious.

March 25 – Council asks Ong to resign

Ong was given up to 30 minutes to address councillors before they decided whether to accept the investigation.

Instead, he used much of the opportunity to read from Franz Kafka’s The Trial.

Councillors voted 10-2 to find he had materially breached the code and invite him to consider resigning.

Ong was also removed from his Otago Settlers Association and Toitū Otago Settlers Museum representative roles, on top of the technology role Barker had already removed.

The lost responsibilities reduced his annual remuneration from $100,577 to $84,496.

Asked by the Herald whether he would quit, Ong said: “Very simply, I have been elected”.

April 8 – Another council walkout

The ODT reported Ong walked out of a Te Pae Māori committee meeting after being told that, as he was not a member of the committee, he could observe but not speak or vote.

Ong complained he was being censored.

April 23 – A brief attempt at the NZME board

Away from the council chamber, Ong also nominated himself for a place on the board of NZME, which owns the New Zealand Herald.

His appointment received 1.85% support from shareholders, with 98.15% opposed.

April 29 – Another confidentiality complaint and another email to media

Graham lodged a second code of conduct complaint over emails Ong sent on April 20 and 21.

The complaint concerned the disclosure of confidential information relating to a potential developer for a hotel beside Forsyth Barr Stadium.

At 4.27pm, Graham emailed Ong telling him the new complaint was confidential and warning that publicising it could constitute a further breach.

Six minutes later, Ong replied while copying journalists into the email.

Ong told the Herald: “This code of conduct complaint is a continuation of the false attacks against me at every opportunity”.

May 7-8 – Further restrictions

Ong provided media with a draft preliminary assessment concerning his alleged leaking of confidential information.

The following day Graham imposed further restrictions: Ong would no longer be permitted to attend non-public workshops, and access to some confidential material would be supervised.

Ong forwarded that email to media as well.

May 18 – Second breach; nine-month suspension

Councillors accepted Dyhrberg’s findings that Ong had again breached the code, this time by disclosing commercially sensitive information about the potential stadium hotel development.

The council suspended him from all committees and subcommittees for nine months, through to February 18, 2027.

Crucially, the suspension did not remove him from the council itself. Barker stressed he remained entitled to attend and participate in full council meetings, including meetings held with the public excluded.

June 9 – A third complaint

Deputy Mayor Cherry Lucas then lodged a third code of conduct complaint, alleging Ong had again posted confidential information publicly and criticised Graham on social media.

It took Ong 18 minutes to forward the confidential complaint to media after receiving it.

The ODT reported Ong-related investigations had cost the council more than $17,000, with almost another $10,000 spent on legal advice.

July – Conflict spreads beyond the Civic Centre

The ODT reported Ong had been asked to leave two public events during July, including a student protest.

August 3 – Ejected from full council

Ong was again ejected from the meeting after causing disorder.

August 13 – Ejected again

Ten days later, Ong was escorted out of another council meeting.

The ODT reported Barker raised a point of order over a Facebook post she considered disrespectful.

Ong was asked to delete the post and apologise.

He edited it and offered an apology conditional on being “wrongfully” removed, before security escorted him out.

August 18 – A bid for the Fortune Theatre

Ong unveiled plans to buy the council-owned former Fortune Theatre for $88,888.88 and spend about $8m transforming it into the “Benedict Centre”, featuring luxury accommodation, dining, education and wellness facilities.

September 2 – OUSA moves to trespass Ong

Then, on Wednesday, the controversy moved decisively outside local government.

OUSA announced it planned to trespass Ong from its premises after receiving reports from students alleging “inappropriate and unwanted behaviours”.

OUSA president Daniel Leamy said the association’s priority was preventing harm and ensuring students felt safe, and urged the University of Otago to also prevent Ong from accessing the wider campus.

The university said it was discussing the matter with OUSA and could not comment further.

Ong strongly denied the allegations when interviewed by the Herald, describing them as malicious falsehoods and another politically motivated attack.

He said he intended to seek correspondence about the matter under official information legislation and raised the prospect of legal action.

“Maybe I literally need to find the time to get a good lawyer,” he said.

September 3 – University considers campus-wide trespass

The University of Otago formally told Ong it was considering trespassing him from its grounds after OUSA reported two incidents of alleged unwanted physical contact or proximity with students, as well as concerns about his late-night interactions with students around campus, Ubar and flat parties.

The university said students had reported feeling uncomfortable and unsafe and that Vice-Chancellor Grant Robertson had viewed video of a protest incident and spoken to two students involved.

Ong denied the allegations.

So, can the council actually get rid of him?

Not really.

The council can censure Ong, strip him of roles, restrict his access and suspend him from committees, but it cannot vote him out of office.

Unless Ong resigns or one of the limited statutory grounds for removing an elected councillor applies, his seat remains his.

For his part, Ong has shown no intention of going anywhere – in May he told The Platform he hoped to serve on the council for decades to come.

Ben Tomsett is a multimedia journalist based in Dunedin. He joined the Herald in 2023.

The man denies the offending. Photo / Thinkstock

A former Auckland teacher on trial for allegedly sexually abusing two boys says he shared a bed with one of the boys “simply because it was a place to sleep”.

The elderly man, who has interim name suppression, is facing eight historic abuse charges in relation to two boys, including several counts of indecency with a child and threatening to kill. Two of the initial 10 charges were dismissed in court yesterday.

Defence lawyer Nicholas Mani told the Auckland District Court jury his client denied the allegations.

While an accused person did not have to give evidence, the defendant opted to take the witness stand in his own defence.

Several of his family members were also scheduled to give evidence, including about one of the complainants allegedly “stealing and lying”.

“They will tell you they never saw anything inappropriate” between the defendant and the complainants at his house, he said.

The ex-teacher said one of the boys stayed in his home about eight to 10 times, later saying he stayed in his bed five or six times.

“I had a large bed and he would sleep on the side of the windows and I would sleep on ... the side of the door.”

The defendant said his mother used to say men should sleep by the door “because the man should be the protector so he would be awake first”.

Asked why he had shared the bed with the complainant, the defendant said: “Simply because it was a place to sleep.

“Sometimes, if they were available, I’d put pillows down the centre of the bed but not always. It was just a matter of what was available.”

He claimed one of the boys only stayed in his bed once and only due to an issue with his spare bed.

The ex-teacher told the court that the other complainant slept in his bedroom because he couldn’t be “trusted” not to steal things from other rooms in the home.

Prosecutor Clare Antenen said the man had indicated in his evidence that the boys had slept in his room as there was nowhere else to sleep.

He responded by saying he could not trust one of the boys not to steal and it would have been too cold in his downstairs room for the boy.

However, she then reminded him that he had earlier said in evidence that other people had sometimes slept in the downstairs room.

She then asked whether the two boys he acknowledged sleeping in a room with could have slept elsewhere in the home.

“They were quite happy,” the man said of the boys’ sleeping arrangements in his room.

He told the prosecutor he had shared a bed with one of the boys five or six times: “It wasn’t all that many.”

Referring to his earlier account that they had shared a bed only once, she responded: “There’s a big difference in what you said in your interview with police and what you’ve said today.”

He told her it had been “34 years” since the alleged offending.

“If he did [sleep in the bed] he was quite happy to, it was never compulsory.”

She also referenced a comment he had previously given to police about whether he found children sexually interesting.

“In a vague area, possibly yes, but it’s something I would never act on … A bit titillating, I suppose," he earlier told police.

In regard to one of the complainants, the defendant agreed he had taken images of him, some posed, some shirtless.

“I posed the top half of him in certain positions.”

However, and “mainly” because of where he got the photos developed, he said none of the images were “salacious”.

Middlemore Hospital nurses reportedly asked to work despite calling in sick

New Zealand Herald September 07, 2026

Staff shortages are putting pressure on Middlemore’s Emergency Department.

By Blessen Tom of RNZ

Some nurses working in the Emergency Department at Auckland’s Middlemore Hospital say they have been asked to come to work despite calling in sick.

They say they have repeatedly raised concerns with management about the pressure on staff over the past two months, but little has changed.

One of the country’s busiest hospitals, Middlemore has been under significant pressure in recent weeks as ED presentations and staff sickness increase.

Last week, an Emergency Department doctor at the hospital told RNZ that more than 100 people were waiting to be seen late on Wednesday night.

They described the situation as “appalling” for both patients and staff.

The doctor said the department reached 103 patients waiting in the queue at 11.15pm, with seven doctors rostered overnight.

Those patients were in addition to people already receiving treatment and waiting for hospital beds.

Last month, Health New Zealand chief executive Dale Bramley told RNZ’s Nine to Noon that the health system was under significant pressure from the country’s biggest flu outbreak in years.

Flu-related hospitalisations in Auckland are at a 10-year high, while national infection rates have reached a four-year high and are continuing to rise.

One nurse, who has worked at Middlemore for more than three years and who RNZ has decided to grant anonymity to protect her identity, said overcrowding was a regular occurrence.

“Even in summer, Middlemore has patients in the corridor,” she said.

“When this happened in North Shore it was picked up by everyone, but this is our daily life at Middlemore.”

She said she was used to dealing with high patient numbers but was concerned about the pressure being placed on staff who were unwell.

“When I called the [hospital] sick line, they told me to take paracetamol and come to work,” she said.

“That’s not acceptable and it’s very unusual. It wasn’t like that before.”

The nurse said there had been a lot of discussion among ED staff about the issue, and she believed it was more widespread than a few isolated incidents.

“I like working in Middlemore and we have incredible colleagues who are taking on more than they should with a lot of integrity,” she said.

“It’s not an easy place to work, so telling us to come in for a shift when we’re sick is not great.”

Another nurse said he had been asked to come to work while unwell.

“They told me to wear an N95 [mask] and come to work,” he said.

He said asking nurses to work while sick was unfair for both staff and patients.

“Coming to work while sick also compromises patient safety,” he said.

A third ED nurse described a similar experience.

He called in sick recently after developing a fever, sore throat and runny nose, but said he was told the department was experiencing a serious staff shortage and was asked to come in.

“I understood that the staff shortage was putting pressure on the department, but I genuinely felt very uncomfortable being encouraged to work when I was genuinely sick,” he said.

Vanessa Thornton, group director of operations for Counties Manukau, said Middlemore, like many hospitals across the country, was continuing to experience increased Emergency Department presentations and high demand for care.

“Health New Zealand supports our staff to stay home when they are sick and unable to work,” she said.

“High demand combined with staff sickness does create pressure in our EDs. However, we always have contingency planning in place to ensure care continues to be delivered safely.”

Thornton said anyone with concerns about the advice they had received about coming to work while sick could raise them through the appropriate Health New Zealand channels.

She said the concerns could then be addressed.

Health Minister Simeon Brown said the issue was an operational matter for Health New Zealand.

“The minister has respect and gratitude for frontline health staff looking after New Zealanders every day, and especially during this worst-in-a-decade flu season,” a spokesperson said.

The nurses who spoke to RNZ said they had raised their concerns with their superiors multiple times but had seen no change.

They also said they had raised concerns with the New Zealand Nurses Organisation.

The organisation’s president Anne Daniels said asking sick nurses to come to work was a “sign of desperation” from Health New Zealand.

She said nurses experiencing vomiting, diarrhoea or flu-like symptoms should not be expected to work.

“We should not be putting our patients at risk,” she said.

Daniels said nurses should strongly push back if they were being pressured to come to work while unwell.

She said nurses were already dealing with heavy workloads, and many were experiencing burnout.

- RNZ

A bus and truck-and-trailer have crashed on Auckland’s Northern Motorway, blocking all northbound lanes close to the Oteha Valley Rd offramp.

Motorists are being warned of delays on the motorway heading out of Auckland following the accident that happened just after 6am.

The truck is currently straddling the motorway, with its trailer tipped on its side and its load of gravel spread across the motorway. Video from the scene shows a back corner of the bus has caved in.

Witness Lizelle Erasmus was getting out of her car at the Albany bus station when the crash happened.

She believed the back corner of the bus had taken a “nasty hit” from the truck, which then swerved and came to rest against the motorway barrier, with the trailer jack-knifing and tipping over.

“I saw smoke starting to come from the bus and could see the bus driver opening both doors of the bus. The truck driver also got out of the truck,” she told the Herald.

“The whole corner of the bus is pushed in, so I am just really glad that the bus was empty. If someone was in the back, they would’ve been seriously injured or dead.”

A Fire and Emergency New Zealand spokesman confirmed the truck’s trailer had tipped over, spilling gravel across the motorway.

Police said one person has received minor injuries.

The crash has closed all three lanes heading north after the Greville Rd onramp, according to the NZ Transport Agency Waka Kotahi.

“Consider getting off the motorway at Greville Road and detour via Albany Expressway to get back on SH1 at Oteha Valley on-ramp,” the agency said.

A police spokesperson said motorists should seek an alternative route while the scene is cleared.

Havelock North: Arvida announces new $230 million retirement village

New Zealand Herald September 07, 2026

An artist's impression of villas at a separate Arvida development, similar to what could be built at its new Havelock North village. Photo / Arvida

Another large retirement village has been announced for Havelock North as part of a $230 million project.

Arvida has plans to build its second retirement village in Hawke’s Bay, less than 2km from its existing Mary Doyle retirement village in Havelock North, which celebrated its 30th anniversary last week.

The new village will feature 187 independent villas, 40 care suites and a “clubhouse” when built at 28 Thompson Rd and 176 Napier Rd.

The Overseas Investment Office (OIO) recently granted consent for Arvida to purchase that land, which covers about 10ha.

The property is being sold by a list of landowners, including developer Landsdale.

Landsdale previously had plans to subdivide the land into residential lots.

Landsdale declined to comment about the sale.

“The land is currently used ... as a mixture of commercial land, a residential home and bare undeveloped land,” the OIO decision read.

An Arvida spokesman said the project was in its early stages.

“Subject to approvals, our current expectation is to commence earthworks in 2027,” he said.

“Havelock North is a wonderful place to live and retire, offering a strong sense of community, convenient access to services, and a fantastic lifestyle.

“Hawke’s Bay also has a growing ageing population, and our Arvida Mary Doyle community has continued to see strong demand for high-quality retirement living options.

“The new village will bring significant economic and social benefits through investment, employment, and community infrastructure.”

The spokesman said Arvida had no plans to close its Mary Doyle retirement village.

“Arvida Mary Doyle remains Arvida’s flagship Hawke’s Bay community, and we are proud of its history and contribution to the region.

“We recently announced a $35 million investment that includes 18 new care suites and a refreshed cafe area.”

The land being developed for Arvida’s new village is zoned residential, meaning it is deemed suitable for housing.

Havelock North is attracting plenty of interest from retirement village providers, despite only having a population of about 15,000 people (according to Stats NZ).

Large retirement villages in Havelock North (of over 100 homes or suites) include Mary Doyle village, Ryman Healthcare’s new James Wattie village, and Summerset in the Vines.

Metlifecare is also planning a new retirement village with 144 villas and a 20-bed care home off Brookvale Rd.

That means Havelock North could boast five large retirement villages in the coming years.

Retirement Villages Association executive director Michelle Palmer said Hawke’s Bay, including Havelock North, was an attractive location.

She said many people first choose to retire in the region, before moving into village living later in life.

She said demand was growing for retirement villages.

“Independent [research] indicates New Zealand is likely to face a substantial shortage of retirement village homes as the number of people aged 75 and over grows.

“While the sector has expanded steadily over the past decade, new supply is still not keeping up with the projected need.

“Developments such as the proposed Arvida village in Havelock North will be an important part of the solution, helping ensure older people can remain in their communities while having access to modern housing, services and care as their needs change.”

Nineteen registered retirement villages operate in Hawke’s Bay, spanning a range of sizes and care options, with 11 of those having more than 100 independent living units, the association confirmed.

Boxing: Asma Nabizadeh builds 20-1 record with Youth Olympics in sight

New Zealand Herald September 07, 2026

Hamilton boxer Asma Nabizadeh, 15, with her coach, Dion McNabney, at Nabby’s Boxing Gym in Hamilton. Photo / Tom Eley

A 20-1 record and a place in the New Zealand Junior Development Squad are the latest milestones in 15-year-old Hamilton boxer Asma Nabizadeh’s rapid rise.

Three years ago, she walked through the Nabbys Boxing Gym’s doors expecting to stay for a week.

Her brother had started boxing at the Hamilton gym, and her dad wanted to give it a try, so Nabizadeh decided to join them.

“It was kind of fun getting to learn new things,” she said.

Three years later, Nabizadeh has built a 20-1 record, competed in New Zealand and Australia and earned a place in the New Zealand Junior Development Squad.

But her journey has had setbacks.

Earlier this year, Nabizadeh lost to an opponent she would meet again at the Australian Golden Gloves in Brisbane.

This time, she won.

Coach Dion McNabney said the rematch showed how much Nabizadeh had developed.

“She managed to turn it around and beat her,” he said.

For Nabizadeh, the loss became another lesson in a sport where composure can matter as much as strength.

She admits she had developed “a little ego” and was not taking her training as seriously as she should have.

“I feel like that going into the fight, the fitness going between, and I just lost my composure,” she said.

It was a lesson she did not want to repeat.

Boxing has taught her that aggression has its place – but only inside the ring.

“You can’t use a boxing feeling outside of the ring because that can get you in a lot of trouble,” she said.

Inside the ropes, however, Nabizadeh is comfortable embracing a different side of herself.

“I think I’m different, but it’s just more aggressive when you get there,” she said.

Before a fight, she researches her opponent through Instagram, YouTube and boxing records, looking for clues about how they fight.

If an opponent likes to keep their distance, Nabizadeh knows she may need to close the gap.

“Then I’m like, ‘Oh, they’re good at long distance, so I gotta go short’,” she said.

That preparation shows the growing maturity of a fighter who is still only 15.

McNabney said much of Nabizadeh’s progress came down to something less glamorous than a knockout or championship medal: turning up.

“She just turns up, trains, just consistently turns up,” he said.

“If you love it, it’ll love you back.”

Nabby’s Boxing Gym has become an important part of Nabizadeh’s development, giving her opportunities to train and compete.

McNabney said the focus was on teaching fundamentals, finding appropriate opponents and gradually building fighters rather than rushing them.

He said the gym had produced 59 New Zealand champions and sent fighters overseas to compete at major events.

Nabizadeh is beginning to follow that path.

She wanted to make the New Zealand Junior Development Squad last year but was not selected because she lacked international experience.

This year, she made it.

“I wanted to be in it last year, but they didn’t accept me because I didn’t have international fights,” she said.

Now she is gaining the experience she had been missing.

At the Australian Golden Gloves in Brisbane, one of the biggest tournaments in the Southern Hemisphere, she avenged her earlier loss.

McNabney took five boxers to the tournament and said the gym returned with four gold medals.

For Nabizadeh, the next challenge is closer to home.

She will compete in the two-day Victoria versus New Zealand tournament in Tauranga, where she will face the same opponent again.

Then comes the New Zealand nationals in Whanganui at the end of September.

McNabney’s long-term goal is to steadily build Nabizadeh’s international experience, with the Youth Olympics an eventual target.

As she progresses through the age groups, the Commonwealth Games and Olympics could follow.

But for now, Nabizadeh is still learning.

She trains alongside boys because there are fewer girls at the gym and she has learned to deal with the nerves that once threatened to overwhelm her before fights.

“When you’re nervous and you get up in the ring, you just don’t want to punch,” she said.

She is getting better at controlling those nerves.

She is also learning that being a serious athlete at 15 means making choices other teenagers might not.

“I do feel like I’m missing out,” she said.

But she is not convinced the alternative would take her where she wants to go.

For Nabizadeh, there is somewhere else she would rather be.

“In the gym grinding.”

Tom Eley is a multimedia journalist at the Waikato Herald. Before he joined the Hamilton-based team, he worked for the Weekend Sun and Sunlive. He worked as a journalist at Black Press Media in Canada and won a fellowship with the Vancouver Sun.

Colin from Accounts final season review – farewell to a blinding ray of TV sunshine

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 21:30:18 GMT

After season two’s mortifying ending, the charming hit comedy is back for the last time … with sex parties, extreme cringe and a final answer to the central will-they-won’t-they

There are cliffhangers, and then there’s whatever happened at the end of Colin from Accounts’ second season. We had, by that point, witnessed protagonists Ashley and Gordon’s unconventional love story evolve from bizarre meet-cute – key stages: boob-flashing, car accident, injured dog – to soulmate-level relationship. But what starts with an exposed nipple can abruptly go tits up. On a heaving dancefloor at Ash’s best friend’s wedding, Gordon – drunk and buoyed up by the DJ dropping Slice of Heaven by Dave Dobbyn (the Oceanian equivalent of Come on Eileen, judging by the euphoric reaction) – decides to ask his girlfriend to marry him. Ash, humiliated by the circumstances, doesn’t respond. Everyone else films it and laughs. Gordon insists the whole thing was a joke and awkwardly boogies on. Then the credits roll.

If you had somehow managed to wipe this eye-watering faux pas from your mind’s eye, fear not: the Aussie rom-sitcom returns for its third and final series by replaying the agonising proposal in full. It gets worse. We discover the pair split soon after and haven’t seen each other for three years. In fact, they’ve both since found other (extremely attractive) partners: the kind but dim David and the hyper-capable and efficient Chelsea. As Ash later observes, they’ve “upgraded” – but you know their respective hearts don’t really belong to their nice new beaux.

Colin from Accounts – which is also the name of the dog the pair maim then adopt at the start of the show – is the sort of sitcom that runs almost entirely on charm. After all, there is no other way to convince an audience to watch two people fall in love, split up, get back together, split up again, then (I assume – the final two episodes weren’t available for review) reunite once more aside from cultivating a deep and lasting affection for them. This, however, is a mysterious art. The fact the pair are played by real-life couple and show co-creators Patrick Brammall and Harriet Dyer provides a frisson of autobiographical intrigue and obviously helps with the chemistry, but it’s hard to pin down what exactly it is about these characters that is so appealing: they’re both annoying, immature and petty, and far from morally upstanding (once they bump into each other again, it’s not long before they’ve betrayed David and Chelsea). Still, we desperately want them to find love, ideally with each other.

Think of it like Friends if it had just been about Ross and Rachel, with the other characters consigned to supporting eccentrics. Among the roster of weirdos here is Ash’s stunningly awful mother Lynelle and her alarmingly creepy husband Lee, who are now deeply entrenched in the men’s rights movement. Then there’s Gordon’s thoroughly unreconstructed brother Heavy (catnip for Lynelle, then), plus his brewery colleagues – the furious yet resoundingly cool Chiara and hulking sweetheart Brett – alongside Ash’s bestie Megan and her wife Rumi. The fact that three of the last four turn out to be sex party people does later serve to make Ash and Gordon seem like relatable nerds in comparison.

You probably wouldn’t describe Colin from Accounts as a hard comedy: its primary objective is to make us invest in its central will-they-won’t-they, and therefore prioritises well-drawn friendships, realistic romantic messiness and amusingly sour banter over non-stop jokes. That said, it can be laugh-out-loud funny when it wants to be. This series seems to have saved all its best material for its third episode, which involves a particularly grim morning for Ashley, now a qualified GP, thanks to an old man who has brought in his stool diary and samples. Blessedly, she is forced to cut his appointment short when she discovers Lynelle has posted a video about her own murder on Facebook (“take your shit! Get up – go, mate!”). Later, when Ash and Gordon meet at a fancy restaurant to discuss their adulterous kiss at the latter’s birthday party, a smug waiter pours wine in excessively long, urine-like streams from a traditional Spanish pitcher in what feels like a reprise of classic 1990s sitcom silliness.

Ultimately, though, this is an immensely comforting show: very sweet, very gentle, yet prevented from tipping into saccharine territory by a bass note of blokey and invariably profane Australian humour. The insults are particularly impressive – it’s difficult to choose a favourite from this series but I think I’ll go with the simple but effective “fucking cockhead” (credit: Lynelle’s ex Bernie discussing her current husband Lee). Cringe comedy – and what feels like a slightly misjudged subplot about child abduction – aside, Colin from Accounts has been like a ray of sunshine in the schedules. It’s been a huge hit across the world, and many will mourn its ending. I hope it turns out to be a happy one at least.

Colin from Accounts aired on BBC One and is on iPlayer now in the UK. In Australia, it is on Binge.

Emery ready to ignite Aston Villa’s season at Club Brugge after familiar slow start

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 20:35:03 GMT

Manager remains calm despite his side taking one point and scoring no goals in opening three Premier League games

Unai Emery is not panicking. He may kick every ball on the touchline but, behind closed doors, Aston Villa’s players are used to him being the calmest person in the room, routinely more demanding after victory than defeat. John McGinn tells a story in which the Villa manager, early in his now almost four-year tenure, broke character and lost his cool during a half-time interval not owing to a lukewarm performance but because he witnessed his captain tearing into teammates. In Emery’s eyes, it was McGinn expending unnecessary energy rather than seeking solutions.

Emery, McGinn and Villa have been here before. Just last season, in fact; at this point, they were pointless in the Premier Leagueand still another 157 minutes from registering their first goal. So in one sense Villa, who shook off a slow start to qualify for the Champions League for the second time in three seasons, are ahead of schedule. Villa’s goalless draw at Hull on Saturday was not the most absorbing display but there were enough green shoots to trust Emery when he says he is confident they can again exceed expectations.

It is hard to disbelieve a man with Emery’s record, having overseen the most successful era in the club’s recent history. “When we started the project here, the ambition we had, it was [not even] in our highest expectations to be in Europe four years in a row,” the Villa manager says. “It was very difficult when we started working together but it was the ambition of the owner. We set our standards high with the players to be there and we are. Now is the moment to remember how we got here and the way we did. Now it is a different moment and chapter.”

In these moments, Emery tends to double down on his methods. Last season they did not taste victory until their seventh game of the season in all competitions, McGinn scoring the only goal in a Europa League win against Bologna. Before that game, players assembled around 11.30am for the kind of opposition analysis meeting to which they have grown accustomed, so much so McGinn says they now walk in like robots.

Emery lasers in on players’ positioning and tactical details. Jhon Durán, now on loan at Benfica from Al-Nassr after spells at Fenerbahce and Zenit St Petersburg, is famously the only player to have requested to leave mid-meeting.

Villa face Club Brugge on Tuesday for the fourth time in the past two years, hoping Europe will again ignite their season.

After that victory against Bologna last September, Villa embarked on an extraordinary run of 17 wins in 19 matches. Half of the 14 players involved in that game have departed but one of those who did feature, Emiliano Buendía, is hopeful that Emery’s new-look squad can put together a similar run. “It has not been the start we wanted, but we are trying to take the positive things from every match,” said the Argentinian, who has started all four Villa games this season. “We will try to change this momentum in terms of results and try to get our confidence back to perform well and [achieve] the results we want.”

Another Champions League campaign should not be taken for granted and returning to this stage, after winning the Europa League last season, is arguably Emery’s greatest feat. The strides made under Emery will surely occupy the minds of supporters as they wander the cobbled streets of Bruges and when they explore Barcelona in November, too.

Crucially, Emery is energised by the challenge, helped by the odd siesta at Villa’s Bodymoor Heath base. “Sometimes I need a good nap, after intensive work in the morning,” he said with a smile last week.

For now, George Hemmings’s 13th‑minute shot against Hull represents Villa’s sole effort on target this campaign. In the same game it was the 19-year-old, who joined from Nottingham Forest aged 16, who supplied Buendía for a golden chance. It is easy to focus on the shortcomings but it would also be remiss to overlook Villa’s encouraging performance in the Super Cup against, in Emery’s view, the best team on the planet; defeat against Paris Saint-Germain was less than a month ago and Villa have only strengthened since.

Giuliani says Mamdani should skip 9/11 ceremony during rant against Islam

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 20:25:33 GMT

New York City mayor confirms he will attend memorial service but declines to respond to Giuliani’s remarks

New York mayor Zohran Mamdani is set to come face-to-face with Rudy Giuliani at the main September 11 memorial service, just days after the former mayor – who led the city at the time of the 2001 terrorist attacks – disparaged his Muslim religion and said he should skip the ceremony.

In an interview with right-leaning Newsmax at the weekend, Giuliani said: “Having lost friends there and being very close to many of the families, it offends me that he’s coming.”

Mamdani confirmed on Monday, while attending a breakfast celebrating New York’s J’ouvert and West Indian Day Parade celebrations in Brooklyn, that he will attend the main ceremony and multiple 9/11 events on Friday, to stand with the families of those who died and first responders – as he did last year before taking office.

“I’m proud to be the mayor of this city. I love this city. I love this country,” he said. “What I want this week to be a focus on is on the families whose loved ones were stolen from them 25 years ago in the horrific act of terror of September 11th, and a focus also on the first responders who did everything they could.”

The mayor and his office have declined to respond to Giuliani’s remarks.

The former mayor and close ally of Donald Trump has said he will also attend this year’s ceremony to mark the attacks by Islamist terrorists representing al-Qaida, who flew hijacked passenger planes into the twin towers of the World Trade Center in lower Manhattan on September 11, 2001.

Reflecting pools with waterfalls constructed on the footprints of the towers and a 9/11 museum now mark the site that was dubbed Ground Zero in the aftermath of the attacks, and where each year the names of the almost 3,000 people who died are read out by survivors and loved ones, in a solemn ceremony attended by national and local leaders.

In the interview with Newsmax, Giuliani was asked if Mamdani should skip the ceremony. “Well, there’s no question he should,” he said. Giuliani was mayor of New York City from 1994 to 2001. He ran unsuccessfully for president and, more recently, has been an attorney to and a staunch ally of Donald Trump.

In the convoluted tirade on air on Saturday, Giuliani threw insults and baseless comparisons. He appeared to draw parallels between Mamdani’s faith and the 9/11 hijackers acting on the extremist orders of Osama bin Laden, the jihadist militant and terrorist leader killed by US forces during the Obama administration.

He remarked that the terrorists brought their ideological opposition to the United States “in the name of the Muslim religion” and “weren’t hiding it like Mamdani is trying to hide it”. He also declared the opinion that the mayor supports a notion that Islam should be the dominant religion.

Mamdani has previously spoken about how an Islamophobic backlash built after the 2001 attacks and had made anti-Muslim prejudice “a fact of life” for Muslim Americans. “It was this horrific day that was also, for many New Yorkers, the moment at which they were marked an ‘other’,” he told the New York Times last year.

Last week, Mamdani issued an executive order designating 9/11 an annual official “Day of Remembrance and Service” that requires the city administration to designate a moment of silence to mourn those who were killed and affected by the attacks. A second order established a new taskforce to help the city’s emergency preparedness.

Several high-profile figures, including Giuliani and former New York governor George Pataki have voiced opposition to Mamdani’s attendance at the ceremony, and an online petition arguing the same has gathered close to 100,000 signatures.

Dignitaries expected to attend Friday’s commemorations include former US presidents Bill Clinton, George W Bush and Barack Obama, and some other former mayors of New York. The White House has said Donald Trump is not attending but is expected to commemorate the 9/11 attack on the Pentagon at that site close to Washington DC, a decision that also has also drawn criticism. US vice-president JD Vance is expected to represent the White House in New York.

Zheng Qinwen erases another 5-0 deficit to stun Swiatek and reach US Open quarter-finals

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 20:10:27 GMT

Zheng makes astonishing recovery to win 7-5, 6-3

French Open champion Andreeva beats Potapova

The most important takeaway from the US Open is simple: do not, by any means, lead 5-0 against Zheng Qinwen. No scoreline is as hazardous. On Friday, the former ­Australian Open champion Madison Keys learned this lesson the hard way as she led Zheng 5-0 in the final set of an intense tussle before Zheng, the Olympic gold medallist, rolled through seven consecutive games to win the match.

Somehow, two days later, Zheng repeated the trick in her very next set against a greater opponent. Down 5-0 in the opening set of her fourth-round match against the six-time grand slam champion Iga Swiatek, Zheng again locked down her game and reeled off seven games in a row to take the set. Zheng refused to let it go as she pulled off one of the best wins of her career, reaching the quarter‑finals of the US Open with a 7-5, 6-3 victory.

This was a remarkable turn of events for a wide variety of reasons. A player winning seven games in a row from 0-5 down in consecutive sets against two different opponents is almost unheard of at the highest level; doing so against two grand slam champions has never happened before.

“In one moment, I even forgot the score in the first set at 4-5,” Zheng said. “That shows how I am focused. I guess, to come back 0-5 [again] is not lucky, that’s [what] I can say.”

Swiatek was one of the tournament favourites after winning her first title of the year at the Canadian Open and she seemed to be on the way to rediscovering the confidence that has marked her as the greatest player of her generation.

However, as soon as she lost control in the first set, Swiatek’s game unravelled in a stream of erratic unforced errors. While the Pole cited difficulties with anxiety and stress as reasons for her recent troubles, here she just could not feel the ball well enough.

“I wouldn’t say it had anything to do with mentality. It was more that I started making mistakes from easy balls and Qinwen stopped doing mistakes,” she said.

Most importantly, this is a transformative result for one of the biggest talents on the tour. Coming into this match, Zheng had defeated Swiatek just once in their eight meetings, but that was a devastating loss for the Pole as it came in the semi‑finals of the 2024 Paris Olympics at Roland Garros, where Swiatek had won her third consecutive French Open title just months earlier.

Things have been incredibly difficult since. Zheng fell as low as No 160 in June and has struggled to find rhythm. Coming here, her 2026 record was 11-13. Her US Open is testament to how quickly things can come together in tennis, and after starting off this tournament having to park her ego and drop down to compete in the qualifying draw, seven wins in New York have allowed Zheng to re-establish herself as a genuine contender.

Batons and synthetic pepper spray were used to repel hundreds of masked, black-clad vigilantes in Portsmouth on Sunday, it has emerged, as the policing minister said officers had been injured as they repelled organised “aggression”.

After police contained the weekend’s second disruptive demonstration against asylum seekers travelling to the UK in small boats, it was claimed that officers in Hampshire were pushed off their motorbikes and pelted with bricks. Sarah Jones, the Home Office minister, condemned groups behind the disorder for promoting “racism and thuggery”.

Activists wearing balaclavas clashed with police in Portsmouth on Sunday evening after a dinghy reached the UK from Normandy. Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary have launched an investigation into potential assaults and criminal damage.

Daniel Thomas, a far-right agitator closely linked to Tommy Robinson, the longtime anti-Islam figure whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, claimed to have arranged the protest.

Thomas was also behind disruption in Dover on Saturday, when crowds of people dressed in black and wearing balaclavas blocked the road around the port for several hours.

In a statement to MPs, Jones said: “Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary, with the support of other neighbouring forces, used a dispersal notice to ensure public safety and officers were forced to use batons and Pava spray to maintain order in the face of some aggression.”

Spencer Wragg, the chair of the Hampshire police federation, said one of the officers injured was a rookie who had only finished training school three days earlier. “Those scenes in that area of Portsmouth weren’t protests, they weren’t protests at all, it was clear that some people were intent on disorder and venting their frustrations,” he said.

About 120 people seeking asylum were brought to shore in Hampshire after travelling to the UK on a “mega-dinghy” which had departed from the Normandy coast and was at sea for roughly 10 hours.

The landing point of the dinghy was farther west than most small boat arrivals. Officials are concerned that people smugglers are starting to target new routes across England’s south coast, with craft launched from a wider stretch of the French shoreline.

An estimated 200 protesters gathered and clashed with riot police on Sunday night, vowing to prevent migrants leaving the port. Footage showed some chanting “send them back” as police officers with shields raised tried to maintain order.

Amid concerns that police were caught unawares by the unrest in Dover on Saturday, Jones said: “Work is ongoing to establish any lessons and ensure that relevant intelligence is shared at pace across our law enforcement system.”

Speaking to MPs and peers at a closed-door meeting on Monday, the prime minister Andy Burnham said Labour’s mission must be to counter “fear with positivity and hope”.

Burnham is understood to have told the parliamentary Labour party (PLP) that Britain would never accept any form of racism in its communities and stood for a sense of fairness and justice.

“We’ve got a fantastic opportunity in our hands to change this country for the better. We go into the autumn, in really good heart, with a spring in our step,” the prime minister said.

“There’s a lot at stake and it requires us to counter fear with positivity and hope. We have a responsibility in the times that we’re living in. It’s a solemn responsibility to prevent the politics of poison seeping into our streets.

“We are here to speak to the politics of hope and of positivity.”

Labour and Lib Dem MPs called on the government to explain why police appeared to have been caught off-guard by the events in Dover and Portsmouth.

Mike Tapp, the Labour MP for Dover and a former Home Office minister, questioned why the police were not aware of plans to block the local port. “Please ensure that the intelligence picture is strong enough so that the police can respond accordingly to future incidents,” he told MPs.

The Liberal Democrat Home Office spokesperson, Max Wilkinson, asked: “How is it that far-right thugs in balaclavas were able to close Britain’s busiest port without the police receiving any prior intelligence? And how is it that then an apparently separate group with some commonalities were then able to blockade another site the next evening?”

Jones said there was “a crossover in terms of online activity” and the government would learn lessons from the disorder.

In an on-camera confrontation on Monday, Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, told the Reform UK home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, that the Patriot Platform group he led would deliver working-class votes to Reform – but expressed anger at Nigel Farage’s criticisms of Dover demonstrators for wearing balaclavas.

Thomas said: “I understand Nigel is going to be prime minister one day and I understand he has to set a standard, which will basically be that you know he can’t just come out and say, everything’s great and these guys are fantastic, but Nigel needs to be very careful with his words.”

Yusuf said he would “take that message back” and added that Thomas had articulated why he and his group had organised demonstrations. “I think it’s important we listen to people. He was making his points respectfully,” he said.

Police could impose a balaclava ban on future anti-migrant demonstrations after officers were injured, Whitehall sources said.

Under the Crime and Policing Act, Hampshire police could apply for a ban to ensure that protesters cannot cover their faces. Facebook posts claim that a demonstration is planned for Saturday by a group called Portsmouth Patriots. Hampshire police has been approached for comment.

Ministers have been criticised for failing to condemn far-right groups behind the disorder. Nick Lowles, the chief executive of Hope Not Hate, which charts far-right activity, told the BBC: “To have 300, 400 people with balaclavas marching down the streets, stopping traffic. You know, it’s not just good enough. We need to call these people out for their politics and for the type of Britain that they want to see.

“We’ve got different ways to register our protest. We do not go on the street. We do not burn people out of their houses. We do not cause trouble and threaten to fight the police.”

The Hampshire and Isle of Wight police and crime commissioner, Donna Jones, said England’s south coast was not prepared for the arrival of migrants, and ministers would have a “significant issue” if people traffickers shifted their routes farther west. She warned that places such as Portsmouth were “not set up” for the arrival of migrants.

Kent police defended the force’s action after it described the highly organised protest action in Dover as “spontaneous”. Assistant chief constable Nigel Brookes said the term was used in line with national guidance and that the action had “developed rapidly”.

Eight boats carrying 625 people arrived in the UK on Sunday after crossing the English Channel, Home Office data shows.

From a paediatric doctor to a podium dancer: meet the 2026 stars of The Great British Bake Off

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 19:00:15 GMT

Yes it’s going to be the Nigella Show – but we need to make sure the bakers get a look-in too. Here are this year’s cohort, ranked from worst to best

The new contestants of this year’s Great British Bake Off don’t know how lucky they are. Usually when a new intake arrives, all eyes are on them. After all, this is a show with such a long and storied history that its audience is primed for the slightest culinary mistake.

But this time around the contestants will enjoy a temporary reprieve, because this is the year when Bake Off becomes The Nigella Show, and everyone will be so busy going moon-eyed over its glamorous new judge that they’ll barely even give the bakers a second look.

Nevertheless, as is tradition, Channel 4 has just sent out its contestant biographies. Using them, and no other quantifiable data, let’s rank their chances of success from worst to best, just for the hell of it.

Things aren’t looking great for Clara. A Portuguese “fantasy girlie”, it is said that her signature style is “chaotically beautiful”. As everybody knows, this is code for “Clara is not detail oriented”. What’s more, her official show biography states that she believes “the first bite of a bake is always with the eyes”. However, the first bite of anything is with the mouth. Eyes, by their very nature, cannot bite things. This failure to understand basic anatomy will almost certainly be her undoing.

Again, everything about Mo sounds like a whopping great red flag. In his contestant questionnaire he professes to not owning any cookbooks, calls himself “chaotic and random”, declares that he enjoys “winging it” and admits that he has never really watched The Great British Bake Off before. Worst of all, though, his description of Lawson is: “I remember my mum loved watching her growing up.” Being disorganised is one thing. Not watching Bake Off is one thing. But referring to Nigella Lawson in the past tense, as something only enjoyed by elderly people? This will not do.

Danni sounds great, but I fear they are not long for the world. Describing their baking style as “Chaos, chaos, chaos!” (there’s that red flag again), they also describe their superpower as never giving up. “Even if I fail and fail and fail and fail, I just get back up and keep going and try again in a different way.” I don’t want to appear psychic here, guys, but I’m pretty sure Danni failed.

Bake Off has been on the air for so long now that all its contestants tend to lapse into type. As such, Gary is this year’s “nice older man”. He’s pleasingly brief with his answers in the questionnaire, and appears to live very happily with his wife and all their animals. This is all good, of course, but expect him to be quickly outflanked by all the hungry youngsters who primarily see Bake off as a way to grow their Instagram followers.

Shannon is the exact opposite of Gary. By a wide margin, her questionnaire is the longest of the year, running to almost 2,000 words (for reference, Gary’s was about 500 words long). But what a wealth of information it is. For instance, we now know that she was a back-up baker on the show last year, that baking for the judges turned her stomach into “a swarm of butterflies” and that “Nigella brought this sensational presence into the tent, a kind of calm elegance that made the whole space feel homely and safe.” She seems lovely and earnest but – and I’m aware this is rich coming from me – the woman badly needs an editor.

The “daddy of Birmingham drag”, Gabe describes themself as a “professional nuisance”. This may bear out. In their questionnaire, Gabe reveals that they did shots with Nigella, previously had their bum smacked by Alison Hammond and was ready to cream pie themselves in front of Noel Fielding. Every year I do these, without fail, I end up being followed on Instagram by one Bake Off contestant. I have a feeling that this year it’s going to be Gabe.

From what I can tell, Moyin likes to present as the high achiever of the group. He was an under-20 100m champion, could make macarons by the age of 14 and makes a point of noting that he often attends seminars on global political thought. Alas, his questionnaire has given him away, in that he gives a full-blown spoiler in it. I won’t repeat it, but it does involve Danni and genitalia. In other words, Moyin is a huge gossip and cannot be trusted.

Yannis seems like a very composed, very thoughtful man. He is a Bangladeshi, born in Vienna but raised in London. He claims that Bake Off is the show that helped him learn to speak English. He puts great emphasis on caring for people. He is, as you will have seen, a paediatric doctor. So in that regard, I hope he does horribly here. The world needs more paediatric doctors and fewer people determined to leverage their stint on a cookery competition into semi-regular appearances on Sunday Brunch. Only instant failure can correct this cosmic unbalance.

Now we get to the bakers I think will actually do well. Based on his bio, Tom has the makings of a potential winner. He seems deeply unfazed by the prospect of appearing on Bake Off, not only because he describes himself as “super chill” but also because he seems to believe that it was his divine right to end up on the show. Also he claims to be obsessed by Nigella, which is the correct answer.

The primary thing to remember about Nikki is that she was once a podium dancer at Ziggy’s nightclub in Basingstoke in the 1990s. In truth, I am a little worried about Nikki, because in the questionnaire she described her baking style as “flavours, combinations and colours”, which is such a weirdly rudimentary statement that I’m worried she also describes her favourite film as “noises and shapes”. But, hey, anyone who danced on podiums in Basingstoke can almost certainly push through.

Connie loves baking cakes so much that people literally call her “the Cake Lady”, and she isn’t upset by it. Plenty of the other bakers go out of their way to name Connie in their bios, too, which has to be a good sign of how well-liked she is. She also keeps a jar of fruit permanently soaking in rum, which is what poachers did in Danny the Champion of the World. What I’m trying to say is that Connie sounds like someone who could poach animals for a living, and I’m too terrified to put her lower on the list.

Molly has been baking since she was six. However, that isn’t why I think she will win Bake Off this year. No, I think she will win Bake Off because her bio states that she is 25% of the way through a 350,000-stitch cross-stitch landscape of Rivendell. Can you imagine the patience, the attention to detail, the sheer bloody-minded obsessiveness required to do such a thing? Clearly this is the woman to beat.

Kevin Pietersen must tread carefully as England mentor after life as an outspoken pundit

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 19:00:15 GMT

The former player’s credentials speak for themselves but the ECB has also taken a risk in employing him until the end of next year

For most of the time since his retirement as a player Kevin Pietersen has worked as a pundit and commentator, encouraged to be outspoken, hold strong opinions and state them powerfully. After his surprise appointment as a specialist mentor to the England men’s white-ball teams he will have to tread a bit more carefully.

He will bring positivity, as all great players initially do because of their stature within the game, but the fact that he was a great player lasts only so long, and then it’s about the words he uses and his ability to tailor his messaging.

He has not done a lot of coaching, but I have seen masterclasses on Sky that demonstrate how much hard work he put in across his career to reach the heights he did, showing strong technical understanding, and excellent communication. His credentials speak for themselves, as a world-class player with huge reserves of experience to draw on, and someone who has stayed in touch with the game. He’s got this chance on merit.

But as a personality he can divide opinion: some have always sung his praises, while others might not enjoy his company so much. Normally when a consultant is brought in it’s for one tour, to see how things go. Pietersen is due to be involved with England until the end of next year. It is a big commitment, both from the England and Wales Cricket Board and from Pietersen, and also a bit of a risk.

He has been quite outspoken in his criticism of Brendon McCullum’s approach to Test cricket in particular, and it might be a clever move to take a critic out of the commentary box and turn him into an ally, but I’m sure his message as a dominant player will be to encourage the batters to take a similar approach, which would probably echo McCullum’s advice. The challenge of coaching as a former player is to adapt your message to each individual. You’ve had your career, now your job is to help people to make the most of theirs, not to tell them what you would have done. Language is so powerful to players, and Pietersen will need to show a mastery of nuance that he might be unused to.

Pakistan’s latest coaching appointments are, I think it’s fair to say, less encouraging. In fact if you want a demonstration of how not to manage an international cricket team, or for that matter any sports team, just take a look at this Pakistan set-up. In their latest brainwave they sacked their head coach and sent seven players home while calling up largely inexperienced replacements before the final Test this week. To me it smacks of administrators wanting to be seen to be proactive. Is it going to help? I can’t see it. But I’m not convinced that’s even their intention.

Sarfaraz Ahmed, the outgoing head coach, and the bowling coach Umar Gul, who was also sacked, are two former cricketers with a lot of experience – 469 international appearances between them across the three formats – who know what the players are going through. They did not have a lot of coaching experience – Sarfaraz was appointed in April, a month after he announced the end of his international playing career – but they were appointed for a reason, and they have not suddenly lost the ability to support players.

Mike Hesson, who has been Pakistan’s white-ball coach since last year and someone I’ve heard good things about, has come in and perhaps he should have been given the job in the first place, with the others working around him and learning off him, creating a unit that combined the calmness and experience of Hesson with the knowledge and respect of Sarfaraz and Gul.

I can only imagine what the experience of being sent home mid-tour does to a player’s confidence. Irrespective of their performances, and I’m sure they will be bitterly disappointed with their lack of success, I’m sad for those players as individuals. This has been a very public humiliation for them. I wonder how this will affect the psyche of all Pakistani players who dream of representing their country. If this is the way national teams treat their best players, it will only accelerate the exodus of talent to franchise tournaments. Their replacements face a real challenge: the forecast for Birmingham this week is excellent but it’ll be cloudy and against a very good bowling attack. On potentially another juicy pitch this will not be an easy task. The Pakistan Cricket Board does not deserve its gamble to succeed.

Subscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s action

after newsletter promotion

It was refreshing after the second Test to hear talk from the England camp of ruthlessness, a word Ben Stokes famously hated. They are facing weak opponents who appear to have made themselves weaker, and they should be determined to make it 3-0, smelling blood. There are runs and wickets to be had. For all that Pakistan are in disarray, England have played good, sensible, grown‑up cricket and it has been a pleasure to see it.

I was at Lord’s for every day of the second Test and England’s use of the conditions was outstanding. Ollie Robinson was almost unplayable, and the four seamers complement each other really well: the skill and accuracy of Robinson, the pace of Jofra Archer, the angle of Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson’s ability to swing the ball and make things happen is a thrilling combination.

We have to keep a sense of proportion, because this is not the strongest batting lineup in world cricket, but I am excited for the future and intrigued to find out how they fare over the winter on the slower surfaces of Bangladesh, and with a Kookaburra ball in South Africa that can do a bit early on but after that tends to favour the batter. It’s one thing rolling through Pakistan at an overcast Lord’s and another to toil all day in the heat. But there is every reason to confidently believe that this quartet would be a handful in English conditions against any opponents, hopefully including in the Ashes next summer.

And if any of the players want to know how winning the Ashes at home might feel, well, they can ask Kevin Pietersen.

UK to adopt tougher stance on Israel with illegal settlements trade ban

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 18:34:37 GMT

Ed Miliband to reassert support for Palestinian rights and a two-state solution in move likely to draw fierce criticism from US and Israel

Ed Miliband will announce what he has described as a broad reset of the UK’s relations with Israel on Tuesday, promising the government will take a more active approach in supporting the Palestinian cause.

In an intervention that is expected to draw fierce criticism from the US and Israel, the foreign secretary will impose a UK ban on the trade in goods and some services from illegal Israeli settlements.

He has also told civil society groups he is determined to reassert support for a two-state solution to the conflict with an appeal for the protection of Palestinian rights and respect for international law.

In his statement to MPs, Miliband is expected to use firmer language than his recent predecessors in calling out the humanitarian injustices suffered by Palestinians in Gaza.

The steps he lays out are likely to fall short of the full set of demands made by Palestinian advocacy groups, but they will still be seen as a sign that the UK is moving beyond traditional rhetorical support for a two-state solution towards active steps to forestall the expansion of illegal settlements in the West Bank – widely seen as intended to destroy the prospect of a Palestinian state.

Israel has already threatened reprisals over Miliband’s previous claim that the Israeli military has held back aid into Gaza, and the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, has claimed the Labour government is gripped by Jew hatred. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, spoke to Donald Trump and key Gulf allies such as Qatar on Monday to brief them on the government’s plans in the region.

Miliband’s intervention comes as polling released to the Guardian shows Britons across the political divide strongly favour banning trade with illegal Israeli settlements by a margin of more than two to one.

The polling, conducted by Opinium and published by the European Council on Foreign Relations, shows that only 18% of UK adults oppose a ban on trade in goods with Israeli settlements, compared with 46% in favour. Support rises to nearly three-quarters when those who did not express an opinion are excluded.

Miliband’s statement will stand by his claim that the Israel Defense Forces, in the name of security, are placing unnecessary controls on aid entering Gaza, creating a horrific situation. It is understood, however, that he is sceptical of the UK’s leverage to resolve the situation apart from calling for the restrictions to be lifted.

His claim that aid had been held back was hotly denied by the Israeli foreign ministry at the weekend.

Miliband is also likely to go further than his predecessors in placing the settlement measures firmly in the context of upholding international law, including the findings of two key institutions, the international criminal court and the international court of justice (ICJ), two bodies under attack by the US.

The package is not likely to include sanctions over aid restrictions into Gaza, or to describe what has happened in the territory as a genocide. The UK has kept open the option of joining countries such as South Africa at the ICJ to claim Israel is in breach of the court’s previous rulings.

But by acting decisively on trade, Miliband has set aside warnings that a polarising UK intervention might help Benjamin Netanyahu’s chances in Israel’s 27 October election. British sources pointed out that even Israeli military officials have warned their prime minister that the IDF will struggle to defend new settlements and outposts in the northern West Bank, because they lack basic security infrastructure and were established for political rather than security reasons.

Despite US criticism of the UK stance, Washington has also been putting pressure on Netanyahu on the settlements issue to the point that he has called for some to be dismantled, saying they were not established with the necessary permits. Israel has previously demolished some outposts, but they are often rebuilt soon after.

The UK ban on trade in settlement goods, long parried by the Foreign Office as impossible to implement, is in line with the ICJ advisory opinion in 2024 requiring governments not to aid or assist an Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory, not just illegal settlements. The UK government has never formally replied to the opinion, but ministers in Keir Starmer’s government said it was broadly compliant.

The measures on settlements may require primary legislation to ban the trade in goods rather than an easier statutory instrument, while the trade ban will extend to some services including financing and advertising illegal settlements.

The Foreign Office has previously argued that it was impossible to distinguish between products emanating from illegal settlements and those from Israel. The UK officially regards all Israeli civilian settlements built on territories captured during the 1967 six-day war as illegal under international law.

Total trade in goods and services between the UK and Israel in 2025 was £6bn, and the scale of the disruption may depend on Israeli reprisals.

Products produced in Israeli settlements located within the territories occupied by Israel since 1967 have not been entitled to preferential tariff treatment upon entry into the UK since 2005. The country has also issued guidance on misleading labelling and urged businesses not to trade with or be engaged in economic and financial activities in Israeli settlements. The new measures make such investments unlawful.

The UK reset was made more urgent by Israel’s E1 settlement project east of Jerusalem, which is poised to effectively cut the occupied West Bank in two from November. But the Burnham government also feels compelled to act because of the increase in settler violence in the West Bank and the failure of Trump’s Board of Peace after six months to secure the twin objectives of Hamas’s disarmament and Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza.

Labour is also under domestic pressure from the Greens on Palestine. The party leader, Zack Polanski, is expected to stand in the 8 October Holborn and St Pancras byelection triggered by Starmer’s resignation as an MP. The new Labour policy may give the party’s candidate some political cover against Polanski.

In a sign of the potential ramifications for Miliband, Netanyahu’s older son, Yair, suggested last week that the Falkland Islands belonged to Argentina and not to Britain.

He is not a minister, but after his comments Trump indicated that Washington could reconsider its position on British sovereignty over the islands.

Trump said last Thursday that he would not back Britain if Argentina were to invade the islands, telling GB News: “Your country was not there to help me” when the US and Israel began their war on Iran in February.

The Foreign Office declined to comment when approached by the Guardian.
