‘Safety, security and service’: behind the scenes with police at Arsenal v Chelsea

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 18:00:14 GMT

Facial recognition and spotters part of operation at Emirates that involved a dozen incidents and two arrests

The concourses are silent when, deep in the Emirates Stadium’s bowels, Chief Inspector Pete Dearden’s briefing begins. Arsenal’s 4.30pm kick-off against Chelsea is still hours away but the fixture carries significance as a London derby and because the Premier League champions are hosting a realistic challenger.

Dearden is a senior officer in the Metropolitan police’s public order command and Sunday’s matchday commander. He is, to borrow football jargon, giving the pre-match team talk, running through intelligence and in-game tactics. “Set the right style and tone,” he says. After Dearden has finished, the police room becomes a pseudo-station for the afternoon, with all incidents triaged by the same crime officer. Football offences can be found in niche legislation, and the Met wants London’s matchdays to be, so far as possible, policed uniformly.

Matchday is the iceberg’s tip. The Met’s 17 dedicated football officers (DFOs) each work full-time on one club, planning each fixture with the matchday commander. All 500-plus games the Met covers per season are risk-graded using factors such as risk level of supporters, proximity, recent history and kick‑off time. Dearden labels Sunday’s game “medium medium”.

“Our mantra is safety, security and service,” Dearden says. “We appreciate that with 60,000 people in the stadium not everybody is going to behave, but we want to reduce the overall risk of the likelihood of disorder.”

Three police support units (PSUs), each containing an inspector, three sergeants and about 21 constables, have been assigned to the match. In addition, there are the senior team and 20 operational football officers, or “spotters”, on duty.

Clubs also have their own in-house safety teams, with, in effect, both parties doing their homework before collaborating. Arsenal’s operation involves about 1,000 stewards and response team members. They are the first responders to any incidents within Arsenal’s footprint. When a Chelsea fan overzealously reacts to his team’s early lead, the response team remove him.

Stadiums are not policed as standard, but clubs can request (and, if the request is accepted, pay for) special police services (SPS). Arsenal asked for one PSU to work within the Emirates for Chelsea’s visit but even then, police intervene only when required. Dearden estimates policing football costs the Met £23m a season, with approximately 10% recovered from clubs for SPS.

The Met is looking to close that gap, with aspects such as road closures and hostile vehicle mitigation now managed, and financed, by clubs. Dearden says his department is looking at “mitigation measures to reduce risk, which means that we don’t have to have as many police resources and we don’t compromise safety and security”.

Using spotters is one such measure. They work under the DFOs, are usually locally based for their day-to-day duties and operate consistently with one club. Dearden estimates that their expertise allows them to do the work of double the number of public order officers that would otherwise be needed. “They will go to pubs in the wider footprint where these people gather and try to identify what their plans are, get a good feeling for their mood and the numbers,” Dearden says.

Some Chelsea spotters are in Holborn and will follow when supporters journey to Arsenal by tube. Fans being unwilling to engage with spotters may indicate they are planning something. “You can get a good idea of whether they are potentially going to cause problems at a game because of that lack of engagement,” Dearden says. “It’s that communication approach again – even with some of the supporters that cause us problems, albeit a minority, there’s still engagement to be had. There are still opportunities to say: ‘Don’t do that.’”

Immediately before the match one spotter performed CPR on a supporter. The intervention was life-saving.

Outside the Emirates, two blue vans contain officers monitoring the data from cameras scanning passersby as part of an intelligence‑led live facial recognition pilot. The trials were funded thanks to a multimillion-pound Premier League investment.

Passing the cameras is voluntary, with signs alerting pedestrians to their presence. Faces are biometrically scanned and compared with a watchlist containing the several thousand people subject to football banning orders (FBOs) and individuals wanted for more serious crimes.

“We are targeting high-harm offenders, sex offenders, those with FBOs, who, if they came to an event, could spoil it for others, commit crimes, or exploit opportunities such as crowded spaces,” Dearden says.

The two-hour pilot yields six interventions, one while Guardian Sport is present. Officers intervene to speak to the individual, who is with their family. They have an FBO, although are not restricted from being around the Emirates. They have also recently been released from prison for human trafficking and are wearing a tag.

Dearden feels half a dozen hits is proportional to what would be expected. “What we can’t measure is the deterrent effect,” he says.

Noticeable is the relative lack of police visibility compared with recent years. That is by design, not accident. A heavy police presence does not necessarily make an event feel safe. “We don’t work on a ‘just in case’ basis these days,” Dearden says. “We deal with known knowns.” Arsenal fans in Naples on Wednesday are likely to meet a vastly different approach.

Immediately before the match, the Guardian laps the ground with the day’s three-person violence against women and girls (VAWG) team. “We want to change the culture of what perhaps in the past was tolerated,” Dearden says, giving the example of staff being targeted with misogynistic abuse.

“We’ve had people at football matches come forward and say: ‘I’ve heard you talk three or four times now and I’m now confident enough to report that I think I’m a victim of domestic abuse and controlling behaviour.’”

The VAWG team are also watching for those who may target vulnerable individuals.

For the match, Dearden heads to the command room with Arsenal’s safety team and the other emergency services. Proximity and open dialogue are vital. Because of the game’s risk level, there is a bronze commander, Inspector Rachel Duckett, at ground level. A half-time briefing allows all parties – including medical, the London fire brigade, the local authority, the Premier League, and British transport police – to compare notes and address issues. Dearden and Duckett then discuss the strategy for the game’s end.

For all the planning, much of what happens at football is result-driven. With Arsenal 2-1 up and time running out, a late Chelsea equaliser might have changed the mood. Home and away fans cross paths after, outside the 3,000-strong Chelsea end, where there is no cordon. Arsenal supporters gloat; some Chelsea fans react. A pair of Chelsea content creators try to record in the middle of the departing crowd and receive an expletive-laden reaction from passing Arsenal fans. They are advised to move on for their own safety.

Striking is the speed at which potential flashpoints are spotted and then defused. Officers are calm, not confrontational, and act as an external subconscious: “‘C’mon, think – do you really want to do that?’”

An hour after the final whistle, the stadium is silent again, and Dearden and his senior team debrief pitchside. A dozen incidents occurred around the game, with two arrests made – one for assaulting a steward and another for racial abuse and assault. A further 10 people were reported for offences including drinking in view of the pitch, missile throwing, low-level assault of a steward, homophobic chanting and possession of drugs.

Dearden says the number is “slightly higher than we’d like” but points out that it demonstrates proactivity. For example, stewards are told not to tolerate pushes as simply part of the job. Outcomes will be proportionate and consistency is key. In the days and weeks ahead, everything will be analysed, assessed, fed into data. Incremental improvement will be sought and further action may be required for the reported incidents.

But, for a few hours at least, all involved can reflect on a matchday’s work completed well.

Farage still Reform’s best hope as rivals struggle to match appeal to party faithful

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 17:58:46 GMT

Despite series of scandals, members remain loyal to their leader as questions over his successor grow

Few British politicians unleash the kind of evangelical zeal among their party faithful as Nigel Farage. Despite being weighed down by weeks of scandal, last weekend’s Reform UK conference showed that – as far as the membership is concerned – the lustre has not come off their man.

So it was notable that Farage felt compelled to reassure his disciples that he wasn’t going anywhere. “I’m only here because of the failure of our political class, and I am determined to lead Reform to victory at the next general election. That is my job,” he told them during his speech.

While support within the party for Farage remains rock solid, the same cannot be said for the wider public. Dogged by financial controversy and with a parliamentary standards investigation hanging over him, as well as the police looking into Reform, it is unsurprising that his ratings have slumped.

The steady drumbeat of speculation over his future has continued. But while he has publicly declared he intends to fight the next general election – and beyond – sources close to Farage have told the Guardian that if Reform UK loses that particular contest, it will be his last.

By 2029, the likely date for the next election, Farage would be 65 years old. That would make him the same age – he tells friends – as Winston Churchill in 1940, the oldest first-time prime minister to take office in the modern era. Another five years at the helm would put Farage well ahead by that measure.

Yet four out of five Reform UK members say they would want Farage to continue as leader even if the party is not in government after the next election, according to a poll of 850 members by Lord Ashcroft in June. Just 13% said he should step down if they don’t win.

There are those inside the party who don’t think Farage will stick around even until the next election. “There are all sorts of reasons why Nigel could throw in the towel before then,” one Reform official said, citing family, security and money. “He’d have an easier life on the outside.”

What almost everybody inside Reform agrees on, however, is that if Farage does decide to stand down, it would be on his own terms. The party base is so fervently behind him it would be virtually impossible for a rival to stage a coup.

Whether Reform UK could carry on making the political weather to the extent it currently does without him at the helm is far from clear. So while any doubt remains over his plans, speculation over a possible successor will continue.

One Reform insider said that if Farage did depart, the race was expected to quickly turn into a battle between Zia Yusuf and whichever “anyone but Zia” candidate seemed best placed to beat him, with the home affairs spokesperson a divisive figure even inside the party.

“Everyone loves Zia when he’s on policy and focused, and when we were polling at 32%, they didn’t mind when he wasn’t,” they said. “But now it’s more like 23%, and every vote counts, there is a concern that he puts off possible switchers, especially from the Conservatives.

“If you lead a party you have to be able to build internal coalitions, and he’s so combative I can’t see that happening.”

Yusuf’s social media outbursts have prompted even party loyalists to urge him to rein it in. Nadine Dorries, the former Tory culture secretary who defected to Reform last year, said at the weekend: “I think Zia’s got a problem with Twitter and someone needs to take his phone off him.”

One close ally of Farage said the party leader was “unimpressed” by some of Yusuf’s comments, which he felt distracted from Reform’s attempts to make itself look ready for government. “Nigel thinks he’s a wanker,” they added.

But when asked unprompted who they would like to see as the next Reform UK leader, party members were most likely to name Yusuf, with the backing of 22%, according to the Ashcroft polling.

Reform insiders believe he wants the top job – the backstory video he launched online at conference looked every bit like a veiled leadership pitch – even though party bosses have to date appeared less than enthusiastic about finding him a seat to stand for parliament.

Richard Tice, the party’s deputy leader, was almost level, on 21%. Tellingly, just 6% suggested Robert Jenrick, the economy spokesperson, who is viewed with some scepticism among Reform activists because he defected from the Tories after losing that leadership contest, and was also a key member of the last Conservative government.

“My view is there’s an acceptance that it probably can’t be a former Tory MP, and that Richard would have the authenticity to beat Zia,” one Reform insider said. “It doesn’t mean that Robert wouldn’t think about it, but if it was him against Zia, Zia would probably win.”

Tice, who led the party for three years until Farage’s return to frontline politics in spring 2024, probably has greater public appeal than Yusuf, and as a more moderate figure could win more votes from the Conservatives.

Yet neither Yusuf’s provocative outbursts, nor Jenrick’s ruthless ambition, nor Tice’s more mainstream leanings are ever likely to deliver the same level of cut through that their boss has achieved, and so electoral success could end up eluding them.

For now, despite his increasing toxicity with the general public, Farage remains Reform’s best hope.

German chancellor vows to stay in office despite AfD triumph in state election

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 17:48:37 GMT

Friedrich Merz said his conservative CDU was shaken ‘to its very foundations’ after far-right victory in Saxony-Anhalt

A “shocked” and chastened Friedrich Merz has vowed to stay in office despite the far right’s triumph in a state election that has brought anti-immigrant, pro-Kremlin politicians within striking distance of power.

The German chancellor, appearing ashen-faced in front of reporters in Berlin, said on Monday that the landslide victory by the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt had shaken his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) “to its very foundations”.

The unpopular Merz, who had pledged to halve the AfD’s support at the national level, has watched the nativist party rack up electoral gains, none as convincing as its utter rout of the CDU in the eastern region on Sunday with nearly 44% of the vote.

The AfD and its candidate Ulrich Siegmund fell short of an absolute majority but could yet create Germany’s first far-right state government since the Nazi period.

Merz appeared contrite and willing to work on his “communication” with voters. “This is the worst electoral defeat the [CDU] has suffered in years, in decades,” he said. “Of course this will have to have consequences.”

Exit polls indicated the state’s voters were driven by deep dissatisfaction with the political establishment and its stewardship of Europe’s biggest economy, with one showing that only 9% approved of Merz’s performance.

Siegmund, a media-savvy former fragrance salesman, was also able to tap into a sense of grievance in the former communist east, where complaints abound that voters there are treated as “second-class citizens” more than three decades after the fall of the Berlin Wall.

Siegmund, 35, mocked the 70-year-old Merz as “a very good campaigner” for the AfD.

Only 16 months in office, Merz conceded his own low poll ratings had played a role in his party’s loss. “I know that I personally was a constant topic in this election campaign,” he said. “We must try – myself included – to reach people more effectively, in the full range of their emotions.”

The CDU’s junior coalition partner, the Social Democrats, indicated a willingness to water down contentious measures to shore up the statutory healthcare and pension schemes.

However, Merz insisted: “My determination to continue on the path of reform is unbroken,” saying a sustainable system was essential for the sake of “our children and grandchildren”. He added: “Giving up is not an option for me.”

Merz said he wanted to assure Germany’s allies that “our institutions are resilient and stable” and its own vulnerable minorities that the country would stick to its values and constitution even if the AfD took power in Saxony-Anhalt. “We know that Germany carries special responsibility because of its history,” he said.

He also promised to stay the course on Ukraine, stressing he would “not budge a single millimetre from my fundamental conviction that we must defend our freedom against Russia as well”.

Merz said Moscow would cheer the AfD’s success in Saxony-Anhalt and accused it of lending support to the far right’s campaign, with another two German state elections still to come this month amid alleged Russian interference and sabotage.

Although the CDU rallied behind its chancellor and party leader, several influential commenters openly called for his immediate replacement – a complex step under German law.

Germany “needs a clean slate, a fresh start, and that starts with Friedrich Merz”, said the Der Spiegel editor-in-chief, Dirk Kurbjuweit. “He is evidently the wrong man for this office in these times.”

The AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt chapter is listed as “confirmed rightwing extremist” by the domestic intelligence service. It has pledged mass deportations of unwelcome immigrants and asylum seekers, which critics have said would be illegal, while promising massive boosts in social welfare spending with unclear financing.

The AfD has also taken aim at state support for public broadcasters and cultural institutions it deems “unpatriotic”, sparking fears of “cultural hegemony”.

The party did not win enough seats to elect Siegmund as state premier, but AfD leaders said they seek to pick off rebel lawmakers from other parties willing to play kingmaker. It is only three seats short of a majority.

The conservative-left populist BSW party, which also favours restoring ties with Russia and largely blocking immigration, signalled an openness to working with the AfD but before the election ruled out joining the state government.

In the 13 years of the AfD’s existence, the mainstream parties have maintained a “firewall” against the far right, refusing any formal cooperation that would allow it take power. The strategy meant to sideline the party has appeared to backfire, however, as the permanent “outsider” role appeals to legions of voters fed up with politics as usual.

The CDU state premier, Sven Schulze, acknowledged his party had “no mandate” to govern given its humiliating 17% result, even if it managed to cobble together an unwieldy coalition with all the other parties in the legislature.

Although Saxony-Anhalt forms part of the AfD heartland as a relatively poor, ex-communist region, the party has begun making inroads in the west as well amid alarming signs of decline in the steel, chemicals and automotive sectors.

Germany faces another two regional elections on 20 September, in Berlin and in another eastern state, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where the AfD is also strong.

The party co-leader Alice Weidel, beaming after Sunday’s vote, said the AfD was now targeting 40% at the next general election, due in 2029. It is polling at about 28%.

The Guardian view on the far right’s real weapon: it is the politics of powerlessness

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 17:48:01 GMT

From Dover to Saxony-Anhalt, extremists thrive when voters believe established parties can no longer deliver security, prosperity or meaningful change

What links the thuggish masked agitation in southern England this weekend and the far-right Alternative für Deutschland’s (AfD) best-ever result in a German state – where it more than doubled the 21% vote it received five years ago? Several hundred men in balaclavas blocking an A road are not the same as a party winning a landslide election. But both events draw on the idea that the political system has lost control. The extremists in Dover and Portsmouth dramatise this claim; the electoral result in Germany threatens to institutionalise it.

The prospect of Germany’s first far-right-led state government since the second world war carries real consequences. In Saxony-Anhalt it could see power handed to a party hostile to migrants, Islam, LGBTQ+ rights and climate policy. Alarmingly, it has senior figures linked to former neo-Nazi groups. About 170,000 foreign nationals live among 2 million people in Saxony-Anhalt – and roughly a fifth of the state’s doctors were born abroad. The grim paradox is that an AfD government could oversee the very state intelligence service that has classified the party as “rightwing extremist”.

In England, the “Patriot Platform” agitation is far-right vigilantism that claims it will “stop the boats” if the authorities won’t. The AfD is a political party which presents its success as a repudiation of established parties that, it claims, have failed – most notably on immigration. The intimidation seen in England and the AfD’s extremism are, however, two sides of the same coin: a broader politics in which migration is felt to embody a sense of powerlessness – not just over borders but over state institutions, economic change and national identity.

The AfD polls highest in Germany’s eastern states. These have a post-reunification history of population loss and high unemployment. Britain has its own political geography and history. The small boats are a live political issue. More than 33,000 people arrived by that route in the year to June 2026. Nearly all will claim asylum. But arrivals were 23% lower than the previous year. The street escalation is occurring as numbers are falling.

Across Europe, the far right keeps rising because immigration has become a test of whether states can still govern effectively. Cutting migrant numbers or asylum claims does not lessen the issue’s potency. Studies suggest that, in Germany, political alienation is more important to AfD support than deprivation. That is also why, in Britain, using facts alone – that crossings are falling, or that migrants aren’t responsible for NHS waiting lists or stagnant wages – may have little electoral effect. The reality answers the far right’s argument, but doesn’t dispel the deeper belief that the country is becoming ungovernable.

Borders, in that sense, are a symptom of a bigger problem: voters increasingly distrust democracy to make things happen for them. In Germany, politicians can point to the constitutional settlement and coalition arithmetic and say that their hands are tied. In Britain, they defer to the bond markets and the Bank of England. The language is different, but the message can sound the same: you can vote for change, but the government is limited in what it can achieve. The answer is not to pretend that inflation or legal constraints are irrelevant. It is to show that they do not amount to a permanent veto on democratic choice.

The Guardian view on skin cancer: fear the heat of the sun

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 17:47:42 GMT

With melanoma cases rising, the UK must learn from public health campaigns elsewhere

New climate risks bring with them new health risks. An exceptionally warm and dry summer in Europe meant that outdoor workers, and those who choose to spend leisure time in the sun, were confronted more directly than usual by the need to protect their skin from ultraviolet (UV) radiation, as well as avoid dehydration and overheating. In the UK, the annual total of new melanoma cases was reported to have risen above 20,000 for the first time earlier this year (the two most common forms of skin cancer, basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma, are less dangerous).

As with other cancers, the increase in cases reflects an ageing and a growing population. A third of those diagnosed with cancer in the UK are over 75. But with the NHS struggling to cope with the number of those seeking treatment, and melanoma the fifth most common cancer – after prostate, breast, lung and bowel (and excluding other skin cancers) – there are growing calls for behaviour change aligned to stronger public health measures. In May, a group of MPs proposed a ban on advertising sunbeds, which – along with sunburn and tanning – are linked with a raised risk of skin cancer. Last year, a group of experts advocated banning their commercial use altogether, as in Australia and Brazil.

There are lessons to be learned from other countries besides new laws. In Australia, melanoma is the third most common cancer, and strong public health warnings have been the norm for decades. In 1981, a cartoon seagull was the face of a “slip, slop, slap” campaign aimed at persuading people to slip on a shirt, slop on sunscreen and slap on a hat. At school, children are expected to follow a “no hat, no play” rule (meaning no games in sunny outdoor spaces for those with bare heads). While some British nurseries and schools have adopted similar policies, awareness of the risks remains far lower. Many people still habitually welcome bright sunshine and high temperatures.

That is partly because these remain much rarer in the UK, especially in northern areas. For good reason, melanoma is less likely to be a priority for health authorities in Scotland than in south-east England. But with global temperatures predicted to keep rising, and given their commitment to shift towards prevention in healthcare, UK ministers and local health bosses should look again at the risks of UV radiation and the factors driving it (the National Cancer Plan has already committed officials in England to seek further evidence on sunbeds). In Australia, doctors have objected to tanning apps promoted by influencers; in the UK there has been an increase in the popularity of tanning among young people, due in part to promotion on social media.

Personalised care for many cancers, in the form of immunotherapy, has led to the present being termed a “golden age” for oncology. Such advances deserve to be celebrated. But there are tensions between the desire to focus on innovation and the need to improve access to more established services, and invest in prevention and public health. Melanoma is one of many diseases in which behaviour has a role (cancers linked to obesity are others). After a tightening of the law on tobacco and vapes, and following this summer’s record high temperatures, there is a strong case for renewed efforts to communicate the risks associated with the sun as well as artificial UV light – in time for summer 2027.

Bernie Ecclestone questioned after shotgun found on his private jet in Portugal

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 17:45:35 GMT

Former F1 chief says firearm was for clay-pigeon shooting

Police quiz 95-year-old over lack of documents for gun

Bernie Ecclestone was detained in Portugal on Monday after customs authorities found him in possession of an undocumented shotgun. The Guardian has independently confirmed the incident with multiple authorities involved in the matter.

The detention of the 95‑year‑old took place at Tires Aerodrome in Cascais, shortly after the former Formula One chief’s private jet landed. After a routine inspection of the aircraft and its passengers, authorities reportedly discovered a shotgun in Ecclestone’s possession. He was stopped for questioning by Portuguese officials and said the gun was for use in clay pigeon shooting.

Under standard procedure in such cases, the firearm is seized and the person found carrying it is formally made a defendant in criminal proceedings. It is not yet known what the outcome of Ecclestone’s case will be.

Responding to reports he had been arrested, Ecclestone told the Press Association: “No. The police were very helpful and doing all they could to stop us from having to do what we had to do.”

Explaining the events, Ecclestone told PA: “I was going to take part in Portugal in a clay pigeon shooting competition, which I only knew about a few days ago because Fabiana [his wife] met someone when she was coming back from Brazil to Portugal. He said he was entering into a clay pigeon competition.

“So she called me and said: ‘There is something here you should go and look at. Why don’t you turn up and join?’ And I said: ‘Well, that wouldn’t be a bad idea.’ … As I have got guns already in Switzerland, which have been imported properly, because we do a bit of clay pigeon shooting there, I brought the gun in with me.

“I went through customs and the people know me very well. They said: ‘Anything to declare?’ I said: ‘No, nothing really, just all the usual personal things.’

“So I walked out and, as I got out, one of my people with me said: ‘The police have asked if you would go and see them.’ I went to see the police and said: ‘What can I do for you?’ And they said: ‘We would like some information on this gun you brought in.’

“I didn’t even unzip the case. I said: ‘Well, it is a shotgun and this is the reason.’ And they asked where is the blue book for the gun? And I said: ‘I don’t know, I have never heard about a blue book in my life.’

“They said: ‘Yes, well anyone with these guns should always have the book, it is like a passport. Incidentally, I want to look at your passport, too,’ which they took.

“I said I bought the gun in England and took it into Switzerland through all the normal channels. And they said: ‘Where is the blue book?’ And I said: ‘I just told you, I don’t know about the blue book.’

“There were about four police guys and they said: ‘What you have done is try to import a gun into the country.’ I said: ‘I have not tried to do that. I have come through customs, and here I am with you’.

“So all this nonsense went on. We went back to the customs, and the police had complained to customs, and the customs officer said: ‘You need to surrender the gun here in Lisbon and then we will look at it there, and do you want to import it? And if so, you will have to pay duty on it and ask for a temporary import, and we will deal with it like that.’ So I said: ‘Well we’d better do that.’”

This is not the first time Ecclestone has faced scrutiny from authorities over a firearm while travelling by air. In May 2022, the former F1 chief executive was arrested in Brazil for illegally possessing a gun while preparing to board a private plane bound for Switzerland.

On that occasion an X‑ray of Ecclestone’s luggage revealed an undeclared LW Seecamp .32‑calibre pistol. He admitted that he owned the firearm but said he was unaware that he was carrying it.

Ecclestone was taken to a facility at Viracopos Airport in Campinas, where he posted bail before being released to continue his journey.

Ecclestone’s wife, Fabiana Flosi, was linked to a property purchase about 15 miles west of Lisbon. The deal was reportedly the largest private sale of a house in Portugal, with the price said to be around £35m.

Ecclestone has been involved in Formula One since the 1950s, starting out as a driver and businessman before becoming a team owner and a key negotiator of the championship’s television rights.

He was the sport’s most influential commercial and political figure for decades, playing a central role in securing commercial partnerships, sponsorships and agreements with racing circuits around the world.

Ecclestone’s official involvement with F1 came to an end in 2017, when Liberty Media acquired the commercial rights to the championship. He has nevertheless remained an inescapable figure in the sport and is widely credited with transforming F1 into a global mass-market phenomenon.

Jonathan Reynolds is right, Jaguar Land Rover doesn’t warrant use of public money

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 17:22:51 GMT

The 4,000 job cuts cannot be compared to a VW-like existential crisis and, as JLR presents them, are about staying competitive

Jaguar Land Rover confirms plan to cut 4,000 jobs over two years

A default reaction to news of job losses in the UK car industry is to ask what the government is going to do about it. So, well done business secretary Jonathan Reynolds for giving the correct response to the question of whether public money will be used to support Jaguar Land Rover, which on Monday confirmed 4,000 job cuts over two years. His answer was no.

It is the right stance because JLR’s cost-cutting cannot be compared to a Volkswagen-like existential corporate crisis. In common with most European carmakers, JLR has had a rotten 12 months thanks to Donald Trump’s tariffs, luxury taxes in China, inflation in the cost of raw materials and, in its case, a big cyber-attack. Yet the company continues to talk bullishly about double-digit growth around the next corner as it prepares to launch five new models.

Here, for example, was the big-picture outlook assessment in May’s full-year results: “Looking ahead, JLR remains resilient and well placed to address the geopolitical, inflationary and regulatory challenges the industry faces. Investment spend is planned to remain at £18bn over the five-year period from FY24 [full year 2024].

Monday’s job losses were characterised as a major – but not exceptional – programme to keep a lid on costs by finding £1.7bn worth of annual savings. Instead of breaking even, cash-wise, when it has sold 350,000 units, JLR wants to get back to 300,000, which was the level in 2024. That seems a reasonable ambition in a trickier market, especially after a period of heavy investment. As Reynolds said, car manufacturers have always flexed the size of their workforce at different points in the business and product cycle.

Note, too, that the 4,000 job losses – out of 44,000 people globally and 34,000 in the UK – will be heavily skewed towards what JLR calls “salaried and management” roles, or white-collar workers in old lingo. In other words, there will be relatively little impact on factory workers who are paid hourly. An outsider may wonder if JLR isn’t simply overpopulated with managers.

Either way, the appropriate role of government is the normal one of assisting with retraining and re-employment and so on. One assumes action on that front will follow after talks with unions on Tuesday. State financial assistance might be a different matter if we were talking about new battery factories or other big capital programmes, or schemes to take the edge off the UK’s horrendous industrial electricity costs. But the job cuts, as JLR presents them, are simply about staying competitive – and there’s no reason for government to interfere in that process.

The big corporate test ahead is chasing the US “luxury” market (and a starting price of £154,070 for the new electric Range Rover means the vehicle definitely qualifies as a luxury item) and avoiding what the chief financial officer calls “the killing fields of mass automotive”, a reasonable shorthand for Volkswagen’s predicament under competition from China. The next couple of years will be critical for JLR.

By the same token, one cannot call the job losses a blow to Andy Burnham’s ambitions for “reindustrialising” the country. They’re unwelcome, obviously, but were signalled in May and are part of a specific corporate story.

Indeed, the wider reindustrialisation challenge is working out what the prime minister means. On that score, Reynolds’s early contributions on his return to his old job have been less impressive. His descriptions of reindustrialisation have fallen into mushy “backing the industries of the future” generalities. Work to do on that score – but the position on JLR is correct.

A Reform UK without Nigel Farage used to be unthinkable. Not any more

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 17:08:06 GMT

The scandals are building, his touch perhaps not quite what it was. And, most of all, his party rivals are beginning to sense an opportunity

Nigel Farage didn’t know. He wasn’t told.

Sure, he was right there at the table when the undercover reporter he believed to be a rich American’s son spelled out very clearly how he hoped to channel his father’s money to Reform, in ways that certainly don’t sound too lawful.

But he wasn’t listening, you understand. God forbid that the man who insists his party takes compliance very seriously, and who never stops warning that the establishment is out to get him by any means possible, should actually pay attention to the details of a donation offered bang in the middle of a byelection that was fought over – of all the luck, eh? – some other questionable donations.

Farage’s defence is essentially that he was present but not involved, as Jeremy Corbyn once famously said of attending an event where someone laid a commemorative wreath for members of the terrorist group behind the 1972 Munich Olympics atrocity.

It didn’t work for Corbyn, any more than claiming to have tried cannabis but never inhaling worked an age ago for Bill Clinton, in part because some people just didn’t believe it. But mostly, perhaps, because critics found it revealing even that Corbyn would be at the kind of gathering where such things might happen. Most aspirant prime ministers take good care to avoid moving in circles where someone might end up venerating terrorists, or explaining exactly how they intend to get around the law. For good reason, it turns out.

What we are being asked to accept, in the instance caught on camera, is that at best Farage has been astonishingly sloppy; that he just turned up, tuned out, thanked the guy without even really knowing what for, and then went happily on his way. Take Farage at his own word and he is describing someone curiously semi-detached. Someone who, despite repeatedly claiming his enemies will stop at nothing to stitch him up, puzzlingly doesn’t seem to take such basic precautions against entrapment as noticing what’s actually going on around him. Someone for whom fighting a byelection in which nobody else of note is standing, bar a talking bin, is apparently so all-consuming that he can’t possibly be expected to concentrate on talking to donors as well.

If that degree of walking and chewing gum is a stretch, imagine what a shock running the country might be. No wonder some in Reform are starting to ask themselves if, deep down, that’s what he even wants.

What would Reform look like without Nigel Farage? Once upon a time that would have been a ridiculous question – without him, it would simply fall apart – but the party now is not quite what it used to be. Among the faithful, the fact he doesn’t seem to take the job too seriously is still part of his charm, and many Reform supporters will be nothing but indignant on his behalf at the undercover tactics used to catch him out.

But there are also people in Reform these days who have seen the very real possibility of seizing power to enact an agenda not seen before in Britain, just as Alternative für Deutschland is starting to do in Germany and as the National Rally’s Jordan Bardella (the star turn at Reform’s party conference this year) and Marine Le Pen threaten to do next year in France. They won’t want to let that opportunity slip through their fingers.

Having lost its lead in the polls, Reform finds itself ironically in a version of the dilemma Labour faced a few months ago: torn between those who think recovery depends on tacking left (in this case towards Tory voters who are Reform-curious but worry that it seems too extreme or sleazy) or tacking right (towards Rupert Lowe’s Restore, now consistently taking small but damaging chunks out of them, and other far-right groupings). Events like last weekend’s sinister black-shirted, paramilitary-style show of force in Dover by the previously little known Patriot Platform group – which even the government took a surprisingly long time to condemn in the decisive terms that chief secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds eventually did on Monday morning, after what looked like copycat demonstrations in Portsmouth – may now start to push those tensions into the open.

Are these their people, or not? Having ripped open Pandora’s box by saying what others would not on immigration, there would be a grim irony in Reform struggling to deal with the furies unleashed, if only the whole thing wasn’t so frightening for everyone else. Farage ended up calling the Dover mob “disgusting” because of their balaclavas, while suggesting he absolutely shared their anger about small boat crossings (now, of course, down to a seven-year low). But is covering your face at a protest the only line Reform won’t cross?

Some of its supporters clearly do want a leader prepared to say what Farage won’t, a niche that Zia Yusuf, Reform’s home affairs spokesperson, evidently aims to fill. Others more recently arrived from the old Conservative party might prefer a leader who treads a hard line on immigration, welfare and woke, but with some rougher edges sanded off (or so Robert Jenrick clearly hopes). Crucially, some in both camps will see the departure of close aide Dan Jukes – who along with head of policy, James Orr, has taken the rap for this latest donor scandal, though both deny wrongdoing – as an opportunity to replace Farage’s loyal and protective sidekicks with people less tied to him personally.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Historically, anyone daring to fly this close to Farage’s sun has got their wings scorched. But what if that sun doesn’t burn quite so brightly any more? What if the political judgment that always served him so well in the past is now fractionally off-key? For now, the idea that there could be an election any minute – forced, perhaps, by some future bond market crisis – is perhaps imposing a measure of discipline on the party. But what if that imaginary snap election never materialises?

For now, these are all still very much “what ifs”. Given his miraculous capacity for resurrection, it is a mistake to underestimate Farage or count him out when he is down.

But until recently, even the idea of Reform without its leader seemed ridiculous; he was Reform, to the point that without him it would cease to meaningfully exist. In the current climate, that assumption may no longer be safe. Bardella, after all, got his big break when Le Pen was brought down by a financial scandal. It’s time the other parties thought harder about the shape Reform might take without its maker, rather than assuming the battle begins and ends with him.

Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

A health MOT is just one step towards prevention

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 16:50:56 GMT

Tackling social and economic conditions must come first, writes Dr Louise Lawson. Plus letters from James Hibberd, Bob Forster and Dr Giles Youngs

Devi Sridhar is right to welcome free cholesterol testing on the NHS in England and blood pressure checks in pharmacies. Such measures can help identify health risks earlier. However, I would take issue with her suggestion that a “health MOT” is “precisely what prevention is all about” (Free cholesterol tests on the NHS are great – but here’s the five-point health MOT I’d really like to see, 2 September).

Sridhar’s proposed five-point health MOT is undoubtedly valuable, but it is better understood as identifying risk rather than preventing disease. Prevention is what comes next: enabling people to make changes that improve health and reduce that risk. Public health has long distinguished between upstream factors, such as poverty, housing, employment, access to affordable healthy food and safe green spaces, and downstream interventions focused on individuals. Screening and health checks sit much closer to the downstream end of that spectrum.

Interventions aimed at changing behaviour emphasise individual responsibility and often assume that everyone has similar economic, social and psychological resources to adopt healthier lifestyles. Yet those living on low incomes, in insecure work or facing linguistic and cultural barriers often have far less capacity to act on health advice. Such approaches can also reinforce stigma by implying that poor health results primarily from individual choices rather than the circumstances in which people live, while diverting attention from the drivers of health inequalities.

In England, people living in the most disadvantaged communities can expect about 19 fewer years of healthy life than those in the least disadvantaged communities. Free testing is welcome, but a genuinely upstream approach would focus not only on identifying risk, but also on tackling the social and economic conditions that make healthy choices possible in the first place. Dr Louise LawsonLecturer in social policy, University of Glasgow

Prof Devi Sridhar is right to emphasise prevention and the importance of identifying cardiovascular risk early. However, screening is only the first step. As a GP in London, I worry that suggesting annual “health MOTs” risks creating expectations that the NHS currently lacks the capacity to meet. Without substantial investment in general practice and community services, what happens after we identify millions more people with pre-diabetes, obesity, mildly raised cholesterol or borderline hypertension?

These patients will understandably seek advice, support and follow-up from their GP. Yet many of these conditions are driven less by a lack of diagnosis than by wider societal factors such as diet, inactivity, housing and poverty. They are not problems that can simply be solved with a prescription, or advice.

Articles advocating routine health checks without this context may also encourage patients to request annual MOTs from their GP when these are not clinically indicated or commissioned. At a time when primary care is already under intense pressure, increasing demand without increasing capacity risks diverting resources from those with established illness and greatest need. Prevention matters, but calls for screening programmes must be matched by realistic plans for what follows. Dr James HibberdBarnet, London

I always appreciate Devi Sridhar’s articles for their straightforward and sensible approach to health. However, could I humbly suggest that she reconsiders the inclusion of a press-ups test? For far too many of us, particularly those with the musculature of an anaemic grasshopper, nightmares of the school gymnasium spring to mind, with those familiar and ignominious collapses on to a sweat-speckled floor. Never to be forgotten. Bob ForsterShipton-under-Wychwood, Oxfordshire

I agree with Devi Sridhar that annual screening tests offer the prospect of improving the health of the nation, starting with NHS cholesterol testing for 40- to 84-year-olds. Alas, I’ve just had my 85th birthday, so I’m presumably fit only for the knacker’s yard. Dr Giles YoungsRetired consultant physician, Drinkstone, Suffolk

Contemporary Films had a global impact and influenced my career as a director

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 16:50:51 GMT

Ross Devenish says he owes a debt to the British film distributor, while Kal Hodgson invites Mike Leigh to join the Manchester and Salford Film Society

With regard to the article about 75 years of Contemporary Films by Andrew Pulver (‘Not just Hollywood crap’: Mike Leigh on the East End communist who brought world cinema to the UK, 1 September), it was not only in Britain that Charles Cooper’s impact was felt: it spread to many other parts of the world.

Contemporary Films made a major impact on me in South Africa before I even went to London to study film-making in 1959. In Johannesburg, as an 18-year-old, I discovered the Johannesburg Film Society. Through Contemporary Films’ distribution systems, the society was able to show Satyajit Ray’s film Pather Panchali, a film that has lived on in my mind while so many others have been forgotten.

Then, 13 years later, Charles and Kitty Cooper distributed my film Boesman and Lena, based on the play by Athol Fugard and shown in the Paris Pullman cinema, London. Years later they screened Marigolds in August, also written by Fugard, with a cast that included Fugard, John Kani and Winston Ntshona.

The Coopers showed me that the word “film” was not defined by Hollywood and that there were many ways to spell film. It encouraged me to believe that we could tell our own stories without necessarily being constrained by the diktats of Hollywood. We owe the Coopers a great debt. Ross DevenishCape Town, South Africa

Mike Leigh may have only watched “Hollywood and British movies” as he grew up in Manchester, but if he’d been a bit more inquisitive he could have joined the Manchester and Salford Film Society, which was at that time regularly showing world cinema; formed in 1930, it had been mentioned by the Manchester Guardian during its first year, when the paper noted its belief that “intelligent film will prosper [as] each visit to the film society shows”. Ewan MacColl, an early member, said that we presented “the cream of the world’s best films”.

Our volunteer-led society is still going strong, approaching our 96th season, and currently based at the Little Theatre in Altrincham. We are always happy to welcome new members, so perhaps Mr Leigh could join us for our showing of Tokyo Story on 12 September. Kal Hodgson Hale, Greater Manchester

AI transcriptions are no time-saving measure for doctors

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 16:50:41 GMT

Dr Mary Gibbs says there are a number of problems with AI, particularly its tendency to misunderstand, as Debbie Cameron can attest

I am an out-of-hours GP, and I am glad to see a news report on this issue, which has been causing me increasing concern at work (Doctors’ AI scribes get names of drugs and diagnoses wrong, NHS watchdog warns, 31 August). There are a number of problems with AI, particularly its tendency to misunderstand and contradict itself, which can lead to dangers for the patient, but I will concentrate on the supposed “time-saving” aspect.

Many of the patients I see will have been assessed by someone else first on the phone, and I am used to reading through a triage assessment before I call in the patient. My heart sinks when I see that AI has been used – the consultation is invariably long, with duplications, and sometimes contradictions. Often, any history I take turns out to be significantly different from what is listed. So I can never trust that it is correct – I can state with certainty that I find meaningful errors far more often in AI consultations than in those typed out by colleagues.

You may blame the original clinician, but anyone who has tried to proofread something they have created, particularly under time pressure, will know how difficult this is. So how can this save time, when the first clinician has to check through a long, repetitive account, and the second clinician can’t trust what is written and has to check it again?

In addition, turning an often complex history by the patient into a clear account that a colleague can assimilate quickly is a difficult skill to learn, as any medical student can tell you. If we do not learn and maintain this skill, we will lose a lot, and so will our patients. Dr Mary GibbsManchester

Re the risks of AI diagnosis and medication being mistranscribed, I have first-hand experience of the problems. A consultant I worked for as a secretary had a week’s trial of voice recognition software. He gave up the idea when “I recommend two weeks on lansoprazole” turned into suggesting a two-week holiday on Lanzarote. A prescription I’m sure the patient would have been more than happy to try. Debbie CameronFormby, Merseyside

Hamza Chowdhury says most of his fellow Green Camden councillors back him to contest 8 October byelection

Zack Polanski is facing unexpected opposition from his own party in his attempt to fight the Holborn and St Pancras byelection for the Greens, with a local councillor saying he is also seeking the nomination, and that the seat does not need “a politician you’ll only see on a leaflet”.

The intervention by Hamza Chowdhury, a Green representative on Camden council in north London, came as the date for the byelection was confirmed for 8 October, after Keir Starmer’s formal resignation as an MP.

This is also potentially problematic for the Greens, given the vote comes just a week after their conference, meaning the final weekend of campaigning takes place as many party activists will be gathered in Brighton.

In a post on Instagram on Monday, Chowdhury said he had received nominations from six other Camden Green councillors, meaning seven of the 10 Greens on the authority oppose Polanski being selected.

Among those backing Chowdhury is Lorna Russell, the group leader in Camden for the Green party, which is the official opposition to Labour.

Polanski, the leader of the Greens in England and Wales, announced on Thursday that he would seek the nomination to fight the seat vacated by Starmer, setting up a high-stakes byelection against Labour.

Local party members will vote later this week to select a candidate, and the Guardian has been told that they are broadly supportive of Polanski standing.

But such high-profile opposition is notable, especially given Chowdhury argued that Polanski, who lives in east London, would be unable to properly represent the area if he won.

Chowdhury wrote: “I know Camden because I live it every day. I know the challenges facing our communities, our estates, our broken lifts, our unpicked bins, our unclean roads and endless housing register waiting list because these are the places I have grown up and continue to call home.

“We don’t need another MP who arrives during an election campaign, puts out a few leaflets, makes a few promises and disappears once the votes are counted. We need an MP who is present, accessible and visibly part of the community all year round.

Barton, the former Manchester City and QPR midfielder, of Widnes, Cheshire, won one England cap and also played for Newcastle, Rangers, Burnley and Marseille. After stopping playing he moved into coaching and had managerial spells at Fleetwood and Bristol Rovers.

Painful, unconvincing, boring: welcome to John Healey’s late show

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 16:30:50 GMT

Chancellor has the look of a man born to announce the UK is under nuclear attack

Meet the new chancellor. Same as the old chancellor. Although, on reflection, that might be a little hard on Rachel Reeves. At least Rachel had given the job some thought before she got it. She had had some experience working at the Bank of England and, whether you liked it or not, she had some kind of plan. John Healey? Not so much. No one can remember him ever having given the economy much thought until Andy Burnham offered the job. He was more the strong and silent type.

As defence secretary, Healey had looked like a man of principle. A defender of the armed forces, a guardian of the realm. He had even resigned over Keir Starmer and Reeves’s refusal to guarantee increasing the defence budget to 3% of GDP by 2030.

Now that he’s in charge of the purse strings, he’s remained silent. Though not so strong. It feels as if he doesn’t know what he thinks. Or if he even thinks at all. Almost as if, were he to spend too much time in deliberation, he might have to resign all over again. He doesn’t even come across as a career opportunist. A well-trodden route for cabinet ministers over the years. Instead, he’s just a rabbit caught in the headlights.

There again, for your first major speech as chancellor, you’d probably prefer it if the cost of government borrowing wasn’t at a record high since the financial crash and that Jaguar Land Rover hadn’t chosen that morning to announce 4,000 redundancies. On the plus side, Healey could be guaranteed everyone’s attention. The trickier question to answer was whether he would want it.

Burnham had stayed away from the Manufacturing Technology Centre in Coventry because he didn’t want to steal his chancellor’s sun. Amazingly though, Healey somehow managed to eclipse himself. It was like watching a man in negative space. The lights were off and no one was at home. One of those occasions when to have barricaded himself in the Treasury, refusing to come out, would have been a massive improvement all round. With John, less really is more. At least that way there’s the possibility of authority.

You would have hoped Healey’s ability with numbers was rather better than his time-keeping. He was 15 minutes late for his own debut and the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, and the entire Treasury ministerial team were getting decidedly fidgety before his arrival. Perhaps they were wondering whether the chancellor was going to throw a sickie. Had decided he wasn’t the right man for the gig after all. We’d have all understood. It’s a tough job and it isn’t for everyone. I’d hate to do it.

It was a very nervy-looking Healey who eventually appeared. Occasionally having to grab hold of the lectern to make sure he didn’t fall over. Not the most reassuring sight. Less rock. More Northern Rock. Even when you know the news is going to be bad, you want your chancellor to appear strong and coherent. In the same way you want your doctor to tell you she has a plan and you are not going to die, in the same breath as she has said you have a life-threatening illness. A chancellor is someone you need to believe in. Not someone who will agree with you that we are probably all screwed.

Healey started downbeat. The global situation was terrible. The Tories had trashed the economy. Politicians don’t get to choose the time and circumstances in which they are asked to serve. It rather suggested he would have much preferred not to have landed up at the Treasury just now. But hey! We were all in it together so we might as well make the best of it. He would do what he could to make things a bit better, but if it didn’t work out he hoped there would be no bad feelings. You couldn’t help feeling it was the blind leading the blind.

Then came the continuity Rachel stuff. Fiscal discipline was his priority. He would be maintaining his predecessor’s fiscal rules. He would be honest about government spending. Manifesto promises would be honoured. It made you wonder why we had changed prime minister if it was all going to be much the same. Had we been through all that psychodrama just to get someone with a little more personal charm, had twinklier eyes and who looked good in a T-shirt?

Having made all his excuses, Healey turned to the good vibes stuff. The hallmark of Andy’s two months in office so far. Yes everything was terrible. Yes everything was going to stay the same. But not to worry because if we all just sat in a circle, chanted “Om” and had positive thoughts then we could turn this around. We were going all out for growth through devolution. He wanted to bring hope to every postcode. John is one of the few people who can make hope sound like a sexually transmitted disease.

after newsletter promotion

It was all a bit painful. Unconvincing. Boring. You longed for him to stop because the speech was as painful to listen to as it was for him to give. Healey isn’t cut out for all this positivity stuff. It dies on his lips. He was far better off where he had come from. He has the look and the gravitas of a man who had been born to make a television announcement that the UK was under nuclear attack. It was time to hide under the kitchen table with the dog and a can of baked beans and wait to die in half an hour’s time. Thank you and goodbye.

The questions were no more revealing. Everything was either met with a dead bat, “You can’t expect me to comment before the budget” or was brushed aside with mindless waffle as Healey tried to fill the dead air. Still, his speech didn’t cause any extra volatility in the bond markets, so that was something. Then again, as he had spent half an hour saying nothing of interest, it would have been remarkable if the bond markets had moved. Perhaps he had sent the traders to sleep for a thousand years.

They wouldn’t be the only ones. The whole of the government appeared to be in a Healey-induced sense of torpor. There was no sign of the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood. Normally, she would have been quick to crack down on the balaclava protesters in Dover and Portsmouth. But she too had been silenced. Almost as if the government wasn’t quite sure if it was OK to call out the protests.

Strange that, given even Nigel Farage thought they weren’t OK. It was fine to attack migrant women and children, just so long as you did it out in the open. Take a leaf out of the Reform conference where members had been filmed apparently attacking female protesters. That was the Britain we all knew and loved.

Why does the hard right have such a high tolerance for domestic abusers in their midst?

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 16:20:25 GMT

The ‘stop the boats’ narrative is increasingly presented as if it stems from a concern for women’s safety. This is just the laundering of thuggery

It was a busy weekend for the insurgent and hard right, as Reform party delegates redoubled their commitment to women’s safety by physically attacking a female protester and Patriot Platform, a new group established by Danny Tommo, real name Daniel Thomas, arrived in Dover on Saturday, then Portsmouth on Sunday, dressed in balaclavas. No arrests were made in Dover, and therefore the protest was deemed peaceful. “A message was sent!” Thomas exclaimed later on his socials. “Now imagine how powerful the next message will be.” The next powerful message of peace the following day spurred the issuance of a dispersal order from Hampshire police, alongside some smashed windscreens (of police cars) and advice for local people to avoid the area.

The “stop the boats” narrative, along with a lot of Reform’s anti-immigrant rhetoric, has become increasingly bound up with a concern for the safety of women and children. It might be a slyly vague sentiment from Robert Jenrick, in which he doesn’t want his daughters sharing a neighbourhood with men “who broke into the country illegally, about whom we know next to nothing”, or it might be Zia Yusuf’s much more explicit complaint that the nation is prepared to “sacrifice British women and girls on the altar of diversity”. Protesters outside hotels housing asylum seekers get all their righteous wrath from the danger posed to women from foreign nationals, and Thomson stated his aims straightforwardly on Instagram – posting video of Saturday’s protest, he wrote: “Protect our country! And more importantly our women and children! This is our warning!”

Observers trying to remain neutral and fair-minded accept that there certainly is a crisis of violence against women in this country, but point out that more than 90% of perpetrators of rape and sexual assault in the UK are known to their victims; anyone serious about preventing this violence would not start with the spectre of recently arrived refugees. But the Home Office’s literature for recent arrivals about the importance of consent just plays into the hands of the hard right, which then – this is Yusuf again – call this “an implicit admission that, as we all know, these undocumented fighting-age men pose a threat to the British public and women in particular”.

It is pointless trying to battle this narrative with statistics, because it is cynical and strategic rather than a mistaken point of view, authentically held. It is worse than pointless trying to meet it halfway as a “legitimate concern”. And we can see that from the remarkably high tolerance these protest movements have for domestic abusers within their own midst. After the 2024 Southport riots, it later transpired that 41% of the nearly 900 arrested had been reported for crimes associated with intimate partner violence; one police force had that figure as high as 68%.

In the higher ranks of Patriot Platform, meanwhile, Thomas has served prison time for a botched kidnapping, Kevin Jones of the Thanet Patriots has pleaded guilty to wounding and assault of his partner and her mother, and Adrian Clark, also of Thanet, gave a rousing speech in August which climaxed: “We’ve all done stupid shit, but if any of these other people want to sit out there and say ‘Oh you’re a domestic abuser’, what do you think these people on the boats have a better criminal record than me? You having a laugh?” It should be stressed that only one of these lieutenants has been convicted of violence against women, and some are merely violent towards other men. It should also be stressed that nobody at Reform’s conference has been arrested, despite viscerally unpleasant footage of one man trying to grab a woman by her neck and another apparently trying to whack her with his crutch (to be fair to West Midlands police, they have appealed to the woman to come forward).

So yes, Danny Tommo is right: Patriot Platform is sending a message. Zia Yusuf is right: people should be terrified. But that message is: “Anyone taking our commitment to women’s safety seriously is a mug.” And what we should be terrified of is the laundering of this thuggery by what claims to be a mainstream political party.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

Sale’s Courtney Lawes ‘not worried about legacy’ in drive to make England return

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 16:00:23 GMT

Lawes is back in the Prem after two years in France and has unfinished business at international level

Courtney Lawes was not expecting to be named in Steve Borthwick’s pre‑season England squad over the weekend. While the 37-year-old has made clear that his return to the Prem with Sale Sharks is in no small part down to his ambition to feature in a fifth World Cup next year, much like the national head coach Lawes favours action rather than words.

Borthwick has explained to players such as Lawes, his fellow Sale arrival Joe Marchant and Newcastle’s new No 8 Hoskins Sotutu that in order to achieve England selection they must prove themselves against the players they are now competing with in the Prem.

As such, Lawes was circumspect when discussing what is privately a fierce determination to add to his 105 caps. “If I play well for Sale I’ll give myself an opportunity to play for England,” was his response, aware that Borthwick’s side have hardly kicked on since he last turned out for them at the 2023 World Cup.

What fascinates most, though, is why Lawes is putting himself through it at all.

There were times in his final years with Northampton and England that Lawes appeared bound together with gaffer tape. Peel away at the frayed edges and after years of what he describes as “balls-to-the-wall rugby” you feared he would crumple in a heap of exhausted parts. Nonetheless, the level at which he was performing at the 2023 World Cup and particularly his final, title‑winning season with Northampton was little short of stratospheric. After signing off from English rugby, winners’ medal secured, performing his valedictory press conference topless and wearing ski goggles, does his return not risk tarnishing that legacy?

“I don’t feel nervous,” he says. “I’m not too worried about legacy at this point. I’d much rather come back and not be able to make it than not know whether you’ve called time a bit early. I’ll give it my best effort and the cards will lie where they lie.”

To anyone with a passing interest in Lawes’s career, particularly from the point of his Test resurgence under Eddie Jones, it will come as no surprise that he worries little about legacy. He has four children but there is not the financial imperative either, even if a move to Sale – with whom his wife’s family has close ties – was brought about in part because Northampton could not afford to bring him back. There is a school of thought that worries Lawes is in for a rude awakening after two years in France’s second tier with Brive, but it is clear that he has a steely confidence that he can still perform. What has made Lawes one of the most likable England internationals of recent years is that he backs himself without any accompanying bravado.

“At Brive I don’t think I played more than three weeks on the bounce, and very often it was two weeks,” Lawes says. “So it probably prolonged my career a little bit, going out there and not having to play balls-to-the-wall rugby every single week. I wasn’t ready to retire last season. I was still playing really well and still one of the better players in the league. So I thought I’d go one more time. You’re a long time retired and I can still move really well so, why not when you’ve still got it in your legs?”

Those statements will be music to the ears of Alex Sanderson and his fellow coaches at Sale. Indeed, there is an unmistakable buzz around the place after the arrival of Lawes, who demonstrated his will to win by clinching the pre‑season padel competition with Dom Hanson. Young players are in awe of him and senior pros such as George Ford have been taken aback by the levels that Lawes can still reach. Given how highly he rates Ford’s opinion, that will be music to the ears of Borthwick too.

It seems inevitable then, that if he stays fit, Lawes’s return to the England fold will come in the autumn. It is a big if, but there are grounds for optimism. The season before the last World Cup, Lawes barely played for Northampton, making four appearances before mid-April. He had sustained what he thought was a head injury in September 2022 but further investigation revealed a problem with his vestibular system. He returned and performed superbly well for England during their World Cup campaign but he surprised even himself with the heights he hit in the following campaign with Saints.

By then, however, a move to France had been agreed and international retirement had been announced. That is not to suggest Lawes regrets his move to Brive, rather that after maintaining standards across the Channel, he believes he has unfinished business with England. All the more so because Lawes has always been an advocate of scrapping the Rugby Football Union rule that prevents players based outside England being selected.

“When some of your better players are out in France, I don’t see why you’d limit yourself,” he says. “No, I can see why they do it because they don’t want all their players playing abroad but I don’t think that’s necessarily going to be the case anyway. It’s important that you have the best players available for selection. If we want the game to develop and more people to watch it, I think [the rugby landscape] has to develop.”

Lawes is at pains to say that moving to France is not for everyone but believes he returns with a few more strings to his bow and says the key difference in France is one of autonomy. “You’ve got to have a very specific mindset,” he says. “I see why players, take your Sextons, that are used to doing things a certain way, a certain standard, how they struggle, because you have got to be adaptable, you’ve got to be relaxed as well and have the ability to say: ‘OK, let’s do it your way.’

“It’s much more individual focused rather than team focused. In terms of the players there, instead of moving the ball to space they’re expected to go for the space themselves, that kind of thing.” In other words, the kind of thing that Borthwick’s England are crying out for.

“Céline Dion is a force of bravery and an inspiration,” she said.

Lamy, who works in catering for a private clinic, had travelled from her village near Amiens in northern France to wait for 36 hours behind a metal barrier outside the Canadian star’s Paris hotel to get a glimpse of her.

Hundreds of Dion fans have been gathering each day to catch sight of the singer, as she rehearses for a long-awaited return to the stage in a series of sold-out Paris shows that begin this weekend.

Dion, 58, announced in 2022 that she had been diagnosed with the rare and incurable autoimmune disorder, stiff-person syndrome. She took a break from performing, later describing how the condition meant she had suffered muscle spasms so strong that her ribs were broken as a result. In the 2024 documentary I Am: Céline Dion she provided insight into the severity of her pain from the condition, including having a seizure.

“She is resilient, humane and humble,” said Lamy, who had seen Dion perform several times in the US and France and has tickets for a Paris show. “I’m happy she’s back on stage and I hope it’s a gentle comeback for her. I know it won’t necessarily be the same type of shows she put on before, because of her health, but I know she’ll outdo herself and it will still be very grand.

“I feel like she’s been there for me for every challenge in my life. I lost my husband around the same time she lost her husband, and her songs really helped me through. I first watched her singing on a French TV chatshow when she was 14 years old and I was eight and I’ve been a fan since then.”

Dion, who grew up the youngest of 14 children in a small town near Montréal in French-speaking Quebec, has a massive fanbase in France. Although she is famous worldwide for her 1997 song My Heart Will Go On, which featured in the Oscar-winning film Titanic and became the second-bestselling single by a woman in music history, in France she is known for her many French-language songs. Her 1995 album D’eux became the biggest-selling Francophone album of all time. In 2024, she sang an Edith Piaf song from the Eiffel Tower at the Paris Olympics opening ceremony.

Dion has made a point of greeting fans outside her Paris hotel, often dancing for them and chatting to them as they wait for her to come and go from evening rehearsals. She told fans a few days after arriving at the hotel that she was not going out in Paris except to rehearse because: “I’m trying to conserve my energy to give the best of myself.”

The pavement outside Dion’s hotel has become a gathering place that often resembles a street party, with office workers in the next-door building putting speakers on their balcony to blast her hits while the crowd dances along.

Marina, 31, a chemist for a cosmetics company, who has tickets for one of Dion’s Paris shows, said: “I thought I just have to get down here to her hotel as the mood seemed so good outside. My mother had all her CDs when I was a child and I also watched Titanic when I was small. Even if you don’t specifically listen to Céline Dion, you’re constantly surrounded by her music in France. It’s really positive that she showed her health condition so honestly. Lots of stars clearly feel they mustn’t show any difficult moments, but they’re human like us. I think it made her more real and close to her fans.”

Sylvie Lugans, a retired cafe worker, had been a fan since Dion won Eurovision in 1988 representing Switzerland. “She’s a wonderful diva on stage, but in real life, she’s so down to earth,” Lugans said.

Augustin, 21, who worked in the last remaining wallpaper factory in France, had also travelled from northern France to stand outside the hotel and had seen Dion wave at the crowd as she left.

“She’s brave enough to speak about the hardest moments of her life, and that’s very moving,” he said.

Pakistan launch player conduct investigation during dysfunctional England tour

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 15:00:57 GMT

Mobile phones of players confiscated as part of inquiry

Nine fined during Pakistan’s recent tour of Caribbean

Pakistan have launched an investigation into “discipline and conduct” during their highly dysfunctional tour of England, with two players understood to have had their mobile phones confiscated as part of the probe.

A spokesperson for the Pakistan Cricket Board confirmed on Monday that an investigation is currently under way and while no individuals have been named, it follows the removal of seven players from their original touring party last week in response to going 2-0 down with one Test still to play.

The Guardian understands that, as part of this, two players had data from their mobile phones captured by PCB security officials. This is said to have occurred during the aftermath of the team’s 194-run defeat in the second Test at Lord’s.

Amir Mir, the PCB head of communications, wrote on X: “The Pakistan Cricket Board has initiated an internal disciplinary inquiry following media reports concerning discipline and conduct, which are currently being reviewed internally.

“The PCB handles such matters in accordance with its standard procedures. The process is being conducted under PCB regulations, ensuring that all concerned individuals are given due consideration.”

The precise nature of the investigation – ie any potential wrongdoing or otherwise – is not yet clear, nor has a timeline been announced.

So far only Imam-ul-Haq has drawn the public ire of the PCB – and a large section of supporters – after the opener did not bat in either innings of the Lord’s defeat due to a low-grade calf injury suffered on day one.

Speaking in an interview with Geo News last week, Aaqib Javed, Pakistan’s director of high performance, said: “The Imam injury is a big question mark, and a deep disappointment.

“Players in the past used to get injuries, but they used to put on casts and still tried [to play]. We’ll take action against this. How is it possible that a pulled muscle ruled you out of batting in both innings? He should have tried and fought.

“He’ll have to face an inquiry; I can’t say he faked it, but a muscle pull like that cannot stop you from batting altogether.”

Imam has since been released from the squad, along with Mohammad Rizwan, Salman Ali Agha, Ali Usman, Khurram Shahzad and the unused Aamir Jamal and Muhammad Awais Zafar. Sarfraz Ahmed was also stood down as head coach, with New Zealander Mike Hesson moved across from his role with the white-ball team.

Speaking after training at Edgbaston on Monday, Pakistan’s newly arrived bowling coach, Ashley Noffke, said: “I don’t know too much.

“I sit outside that decision-making model above us as coaches. We try to keep the players focused on what they need to worry about.

“I guess that’s one thing I’ve learned about being in Pakistan and coaching for a period of time – nearly 15 months with the white-ball team – there’s always something going on in the background, whether or not it’s in or out of our control – and most of the time it’s out of the players’ control.”

As well as this ongoing investigation, the upheaval has also triggered news of nine players being fined during Pakistan’s recent tour of the Caribbean.

The Guardian understands this was considered a relatively minor issue. The players were supposed to stay within the Player and Match Officials Areas (PMOA) during their warm-up match in Trinidad, only for a group to break away to watch the Fifa World Cup final in a part of the ground not covered by the restrictions.
