Dover and Portsmouth showed us a new kind of far right – and the authorities were caught out

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 15:00:23 GMT

This is a new and dangerous development: a network of vigilantes who have mobilised as politicians and police have failed to act

Sadly, we’ve become used to far-right protests in recent years. Whether it’s the vast demonstrations led by Stephen Yaxley-Lennon (AKA Tommy Robinson) in central London, or the hundreds of local protests outside hotels and HMOs housing asylum seekers, the sight of far-right activists chanting anti-migrant slogans has become all too common.

What we saw in Dover and Portsmouth over the weekend feels different. At roughly 7am on Saturday morning, hundreds of balaclava-clad men, dressed all in black, began piling out of the backs of vans and blocked roads around Dover port. Shockingly, the police appear to have known nothing about it in advance.

Then, on Sunday evening, a group of men gathered near a Portsmouth beach to “block” the arrival of asylum seekers on a boat. The group had been monitoring maritime apps and tracking the progress of boats towards Britain. They put out a call for people to join them and dozens answered, including well-known activists from the neo-Nazi movement.

What we have seen over the past three days marks a dangerous new development in the far right. While previous protests – many of which descended into ugly racist violence – have been worrying enough, we are now faced with a new, more clandestine and confrontational threat.

Hope Not Hate was the first to identify that the Dover disturbance was organised by a far-right group called Patriot Platform. The balaclava-clad men blocking roads were part of a new network founded by Tommy Robinson’s right-hand man Daniel Thomas (AKA Danny Tommo).

Launched in June, the group unites a web of smaller localised anti-migrant groups into a single body. Current members hail from the Kent Patriots, Watford Patriots, South London Patriots, South-East Patriots, North-West Patriots, Surrey Patriots and Chertsey Patriots, to name just a few.

Patriot Platform is a self-professed Christian “army of patriots” formed to, in Thomas’s words, “reclaim our borders, restore order and send a clear message: Britain belongs to the British people”. The group functions as a vigilante unit to combat immigration and revive what it says are Christian values, ready to spring into action across the country at Thomas’s word.

Worryingly, there is an unusual degree of discipline to Patriot Platform’s organising. Rather than being a single entity, it operates as a network for the local groups. These groups utilise various social media platforms, most commonly Instagram, X, Facebook and TikTok, for their promotional output.

However, unlike organisers of previous public anti-migrant protests, Patriot Platform operates clandestinely, with event planning happening via closed groups and direct personal communication. Its means of operation have more in common with football hooligan gangs than with traditional anti-migrant protest groups. This is how its supporters managed to arrive in their hundreds in Dover unnoticed.

Rather than being met with the usual mealy-mouthed condemnations and talk of “legitimate concerns”, these “protests” need to be called what they are: far-right vigilantism. These aren’t fearful locals, they are organised far-right activists led by Thomas, a man who pleaded guilty to attempted kidnapping and was sentenced to two years in prison after taking part in an armed attempt to abduct a man during a drugs-related dispute.

Since the riots of 2024, Thomas has repeatedly spoken about the need to take to the streets and take direct action. He has been upfront about his intention to create a “patriotic army that is able to take control of the United Kingdom”.

Despite warnings from Hope Not Hate, the authorities have failed to act. They have allowed Thomas to agitate, organise and mobilise large groups around the country. Last weekend was the consequence of police inaction, and I fear that without decisive action things will only get worse.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Clearly, the government needs to be far more robust in dealing with far-right vigilantism. The Home Office is so preoccupied with being seen to be tough on immigration that it has neglected the safety of the very migrants and asylum seekers being targeted.

And the police response exposes serious failings in the authorities’ approach to far-right anti-immigrant violence more broadly. Time and again, they appear unaware of the strength of protests and unprepared for the violence that sometimes results.

The events in Dover and Portsmouth should be a wake-up call for anyone who believes that far-right extremism can be managed through inaction. This is no longer simply about angry protests or offensive rhetoric. We are seeing organised groups willing to mobilise quickly, operate covertly and confront those they see as enemies. The longer authorities fail to recognise the seriousness of this threat, the bolder these groups will become.

The government must act now, before vigilantism becomes normalised and far-right activists feel they can operate with impunity on Britain’s streets.

Joe Mulhall is director of research at the anti-fascism organisation Hope not Hate

Cravings ‘like heroin withdrawal’: what happens when weight-loss drugs don’t work?

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 15:00:21 GMT

GLP-1 medications have been a gamechanger in the fight against obesity. But for a minority of patients, their impact is negligible. Why?

When Mercedes was told by her doctor that she could be prescribed GLP-1 weight loss jabs in 2024, she broke down. “[When] she said yes, I cried in her office. And I didn’t really stop crying for a week,” she said.

“Finally, after being overweight my entire life, this was going to save me. My struggle, my burden, my shame was finally going to come to an end.”

But as time went on it was hope, not weight, that fell away.

“I was on [Ozempic] for nine months. And then I went on Wegovy for four months, then Contrave [an oral, non-GLP-1 medication], and then Mounjaro, and that was for a few months, and then nine months ago I started on Zepbound,” said Mercedes. “Nothing has worked.”

A recently retired teacher in her 50s, Mercedes is among a small proportion of people for whom the powerful new weight-loss drugs, championed by celebrities for their transformative effects, do not work.

Ozempic, a type 2 diabetes medication, and Wegovy, which is licensed for weight loss, both contain a drug called semaglutide that mimics a hormone that occurs naturally in our bodies: GLP-1. These medications reduce the rate at which food is emptied from the stomach, suppresses appetite and increase the production of insulin – meaning many people lose weight.

Mounjaro and Zepbound, also now household names, have an even greater weight-loss effect. They both contain the drug tirzepatide which mimics both GLP-1 and another hormone.

The excitement around such “GLP-1s” has been hard to miss: the medications have grabbed headlines, with clinical trials suggesting they can help participants lose an average of 15% to 20% of their body weight. Studies suggest they could help with conditions ranging from heart problems and addictions to fatty liver disease. In some cases experts say the effects may not be entirely related to weight loss.

But not everyone experiences the benefits. Between 9% and a third of participants in clinical trials lose less than 5% of their body weight – depending on the type of drug and dose used.

Now researchers are trying to work out why – something they say could help doctors tailor the use of the drugs, maximise cost-effectiveness and reduce side-effects.

For Mercedes, the impact of non-response has been profound.

“Aside from the fact that it’s not working and that it’s so expensive, to say it’s hard on the self-esteem is a humongous understatement,” said Mercedes, who lives in Canada. “It’s been a real struggle, with shame and regret and big bills and disappointment that my own body is not working the way it should.”

Prof Alexander Miras, an obesity expert at Ulster University, said the efficacy of the drugs could not be blamed on patients. “If the drug does not reduce hunger and food intake for someone, it is just not going to work,” he said.

Mercedes said she has tried hard to stick to lifestyle changes alongside the medications but, for her, the jabs did not suppress constant, intrusive thoughts about food.

“I just thought: ‘No, I’ve got to get somewhere … I’m going to die of obesity’,” she said. “I was really strict with myself for a month – but the cravings, which I can only call like heroin withdrawal … it’s just overwhelming. And the food talk never ended.”

The extreme effort paid off, to an extent. “I can honestly say I lost 20 pounds in that month, but not because of the medication,” she said.

Mercedes is certainly not alone: the Guardian has heard from dozens of people for whom GLP-1 medications have had little effect.

Yury K, 57, also from Canada, said he tried a number of weight loss programmes before starting Wegovy for obesity. He exercises about five days a week, mainly with kettlebells, and does not eat junk food or fast food.

While Yury said he saw some improvements in his blood sugar levels and cholesterol while using the medication, as well as a reduction in food noise and appetite, he found his weight barely changed.

“I started Wegovy at about 242lb and, after six months, I was still about 242lb. My weight can fluctuate a little because of water, but essentially there was no meaningful weight loss,” he said. He also experienced unpleasant side effects, including constipation and sensitive skin.

“There is so much discussion about GLP-1 medications as if they work for everyone, and that was not my experience. When you put in the effort with diet and exercise, take the medication exactly as prescribed, and still see little benefit, it is difficult not to feel disappointed,” he said.

Lucille*, 53, who is based in Luxembourg, told the Guardian she has been taking GLP-1 medications for four years – initially to help with insulin resistance – starting on a daily injection of a GLP-1 medication called Saxenda, before switching to Ozempic.

Yet despite being effective at first, Lucille says the medications no longer help her lose weight – even after switching to Mounjaro and taking the highest dose. “It’s as if nothing is having an effect any more,” she says. “The Mounjaro 5mg [dose] is outrageously expensive and so far none of these medications have been approved by my health insurance,” she adds.

At present, the reason for such variations in response remains unclear. “The short answer to why some people don’t respond is we don’t really know,” said Miras.

He said research had suggested factors such as motivation, intelligence, education and socioeconomics did not predict how patients would respond to GLP-1 medications.

But other characteristics might do. “We know, for example, that age plays a role – so older people lose less weight. Sex plays a role – men lose less than women,” said Miras. “[And] people with type 2 diabetes lose less weight compared to people without.”

Studies have also suggested ancestry might have an impact, with the medications most effective in people of European ancestry, and least effective in people of African American ancestry.

Dr Mahesh Umapathysivam, an endocrinologist and clinical researcher at Adelaide University in Australia, said it was plausible that hormones could have an effect too.

“There is growing evidence that oestrogen alters GLP-1 response. We see that with the difference between male response and female response. Also, we know from some of the physiological studies that time of menstrual cycle also alters GLP-1 response,” he said.

“Finally, the use of menopausal hormone replacement therapy – which contains oestrogen – is associated with greater weight loss in semaglutide users.”

Then there is the matter of genetics. A recent study highlighted the potential role of a genetic variant that affects receptors in the brain upon which the drugs work.

“People carrying the genetic variant, we found lose about an extra 0.76kg (1.6 lbs) on average, and people who carry two copies of the variant double that,” said Adam Auton, vice-president of human genetics at the 23andMe Research Institute, and the senior author of the study.

“For people with two copies, this accounts for about 10% of the weight people might expect to lose on these medications.”

Umapathysivam and colleagues have recently published a study into two genetic variants that affect the production of an enzyme, known as PAM, that modifies many hormones including GLP-1. The team found people with such variants appear to show resistance to GLP-1.

“GLP-1 resistance simply means a given amount of GLP-1 has less effect on the body,” Umapathysivam said. “The implication for treatment is that a certain dose of GLP-1 in someone with resistance might mean less weight loss, less glucose lowering, less insulin secretion or less slowing to the gastric emptying.”

Despite emerging research, it is not yet possible to accurately predict who will respond to weight loss jabs and who won’t.

But there are reasons for people like Mercedes to be hopeful. A series of promising new drugs are in development. “Another option is to change patients to a non-GLP-1 based drug called Mysimba [the UK brand name for Contrave]. It works in the same parts of the brain, but just slightly differently and therefore may be worth trying,” said Miras. “It is not available in the NHS, just privately.”

For some who struggle to lose weight with GLP-1 medications, weight-loss surgery may be the only option left. And, Miras says, “[A] lack of response to GLP-1 based drugs does not predict lack of response to [bariatric] surgery.”

And for those who lose little to no weight on GLP-1 medications, the message is clear. “It’s not your fault and it’s not the drug’s fault either, this is purely luck,” said Miras. “I’ve seen it before, it’s not very common, but it does happen.”

Mercedes began GLP-1 medications with huge amounts of hope and expectation. “There was just so much publicity around it. So many people [using the drugs said]: ‘Oh, I forgot to eat lunch,’ that I suppose subconsciously I just sort of ignored the prospect that … the drugs didn’t work,” she said.

“I wish I knew if there were other people out there, like me, for whom [GLP-1s] are just not effective at all.”

*Some names have been changed

Netflix announces production of third Inbetweeners film

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 14:40:22 GMT

Creators Damon Beesley and Iain Morris return as writers and directors, with the original cast reprising their roles

Netflix has announced that production has begun on a new Inbetweeners film, with the original cast members reprising their roles.

It will be a continuation of the popular Channel 4 sitcom, which aired on E4 from 2008 to 2010, followed by two films in 2011 and 2014.

The actors Simon Bird, James Buckley, Blake Harrison and Joe Thomas will star as Will McKenzie, Jay Cartwright, Neil Sutherland and Simon Cooper. The coming-of-age comedy followed the misadventures of the four teenage friends at the fictional Rudge Park comprehensive as they navigated school life, friendship and failed sexual encounters.

The trailer announcing the new film begins with a garage door being opened and pairs of feet making their way towards a car, revealed to be Simon’s yellow Fiat Cinquecento. The four men are then seen in the car, and when it fails to start Simon says: “Ah, for fuck’s sake.”

He gets the engine going and drives the car out of the garage with the number three written on the rear windscreen. The trailer ends with the announcement: “Now in production.”

The Inbetweeners creators, Damon Beesley and Iain Morris, will return to write and direct the film. They said: “It’s been super-fun hanging out with our friends again, and we’re going to work hard every week to ensure there are no problemos making this new film for humans.”

In the first film, which grossed £65.1m at the box office, the group of friends head to Crete in Greece for a post-sixth form break. It made history as the biggest opening weekend for a UK comedy at the time, according to Netflix.

The 2014 follow-up, which grossed £46.6m, reunited Will, Simon, and Neil as they travelled to Australia to visit Jay during his gap year.

It is not known whether Emily Atack will return in her role as Charlotte Hinchcliffe, or if Emily Head will come back as Carli D’Amato.

Trump administration attacks UK plans to boost traditional media on social platforms

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 14:20:12 GMT

US embassy says Downing Street’s plan to give BBC, ITV and other established media more online visibility carries risk of ‘censorship’

The Trump administration has raised “serious concerns” over Downing Street’s plan to force YouTube and other digital platforms to hand more prominence to established broadcasters, warning the move risks “facilitating censorship”.

In a pointed intervention, the US government said the proposals to boost traditional media outlets in social media algorithms could “establish a template that authoritarian regimes could invoke to justify more control over online content”.

It also warned it could undermine “independent journalists” and amount to “extraterritorial censorship of protected speech by Americans online”.

The statement, made via the US embassy in London, raises the stakes in the plans to give the likes of the BBC, ITV and other established media more visibility on increasingly dominant digital platforms.

Ministers, regulators and public service broadcasters have suggested new rules are needed to counter growing misinformation online as people increasingly turn to less regulated online platforms such as X, YouTube and TikTok.

In a consultation this year, the UK government said it would consider legislating should the platforms not act to prioritise trustworthy content. However, Washington claimed such a plan risked effectively removing the content of “independent journalists” over established outlets.

“Preserving a free, open internet and protecting freedom of expression online are top priorities for the Trump administration,” it said. “A framework that empowers governments to influence which sources receive preferential visibility risks becoming a mechanism for viewpoint-based censorship.

“If the UK compels platforms to boost government-preferred media in algorithmic feeds, the effect on a government-disfavoured speaker or media source’s reach is not meaningfully different than outright removal. The US government would likely consider such a measure as facilitating censorship.”

The administration has asked what safeguards will be in place to ensure “any biases and preferences of UK government officials and third-party organisations” do not influence the plan in ways that disadvantage “independent or minority-viewpoint journalism”.

A spokesperson for the Department for Culture, Media and Sport said: “We welcome engagement and responses to our media green paper. We believe strongly in free expression and fair competition, and any action we take will ensure these are protected.”

Insiders say any measures would only affect the UK. The US complaint highlights its readiness to fight for the largely US-based tech companies that run the world’s largest digital platforms.

If you have something to share about this story you can contact Michael using one of the following methods:

The Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.

If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.

If you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can email michael. savage@theguardian. com.

You can message Michael using the Signal Messenger app. Use the ‘find by username’ option and type ‘michaelsavage.01’.

Finally, our guide at theguardian. com/tips lists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.

Donald Trump also has a long record of attacking and bypassing the established media, regularly accusing major outlets of “fake news” and biased coverage. He often tries to reach supporters online.

The US president is still engaged in his lawsuit with the BBC over an episode of Panorama in which it spliced together one of his speeches. The BBC has apologised for the edit, but stated the show did not defame Trump.

Social media companies have previously been sceptical about artificially boosting the prominence of traditional media, arguing that it goes against the principle of creator content.

Online content creators have compared the proposals to state control and fear their content would be pushed down the rankings as a result.

Simon Squibb, a UK YouTube creator, said he was encouraged that his concerns were shared by an “entity that I think politicians will listen to”.

“This is a very dangerous potential direction for the UK to go in,” he said. “I’m happy that the USA has stepped in.”

Supporters of the enforced prominence plans have couched them as a way of dealing with misinformation and preserving culturally British content.

However, the government has also been clear that it wants to help public service broadcasters survive the economic turmoil created by the rise of digital platforms, which all media companies are confronting.

September is the real new year: 39 brilliant buys to supercharge school, work and everything in between

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 14:00:53 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

From loafers to lunch boxes to fancy stationery, these picks for kids, teens and grownups will bring that new-term energy, whatever your age

Don’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

Shiny shoes. Freshly sharpened pencils. New rucksack. Back-to-school season is here, and even for those of us no longer in full-time education, the energy of this time of year is undeniably one of fresh starts and renewed momentum.

A couple of well-chosen items, from a notebook to inspire ideas to a lunch box that might encourage you to bring in your own food, are often all it takes to feel a touch more pulled together after a languorous summer. So whether you’re looking for school kit or your own stuff, here’s our pick of the best back-to-the-grind products for kids, teens and grownups.

Munchkin kids’ bento box lunch box

If your child has ever written off an entire lovingly prepared meal because of a single stray parsley leaf, this is the perfect lunch box. The enticing, rainbow-coloured compartments allow you to serve them separate snacks to power them through maths and beyond. Plus, it’s dishwasher-safe, BPA-free and comes with stainless steel cutlery.

Klean Kanteen kids 355ml water bottle

BPA-free and with a leakproof sports-style flip-cap, this bottle comes in a pattern to suit most interests – sharks, dinosaurs, unicorns, you name it. Also, crucially, it’s dishwasher-safe.

For more, read our guide to the best water bottles

Clarks shoe cleaning kit

Embarrassingly, my dad is still the only person who can be bothered to take some polish to my shoes, when he gets the chance. Make sure your kids get used to cleaning their own footwear early – a valuable life skill – with this kit for school shoes. Courtesy, of course, of Clarks.

Frugi navigator backpack

Fun but with an expedition’s worth of pockets, this unisex Frugi backpack says start-of-term sensible but also adventure. The reflective details feel smart as the nights draw in, and the Arctic polar bear scene adds a bit of magic.

Yolla Studio pencil case

If you want to avoid polyester, this hand-printed waxed cotton pencil case is a good alternative. Once your child tires of it, you can reuse it as a wash bag.

Legami mushroom pencil sharpener

A pencil sharpener and an eraser in one feels like an efficiency win. But the cottagecore/goblincore aesthetic is what really sets this piece of kit apart. The most fun-gi in any kid’s pencil case.

Kitpas crayons, set of 12

Chunky, smooth and, most importantly, washable, Kitpas crayons are a delight to colour with. Plus, they’re made from rice bran wax that would otherwise go to waste.

Legami erasable pens

Pens you can rub out once felt like the height of sophistication. These Legami ones still feel special, if not sophisticated, coming in a range of playful animal designs. They’ll liven up any desk and are refillable.

Regatta waterproof packaway jacket

It’s the season of mist and unexpected downpours. Kids need an anorak that can be packed away small and light, but is there when they need it. This design from Regatta comes in enough delicious colours to keep everyone happy, with sizes for ages two to 14.

M&S scallop hair bow and scrunchie

Putting your hair up is a bit like pulling your socks up – it signals a readiness for knuckling down. Marks & Spencer has a great selection of accessories, including scrunchies and a bow in school uniform-adjacent coloured gingham.

Helix Oxford stationery set

A one-and-done approach might be easiest when you need all the stationery for secondary school. Helix is a classic academic brand that provides the complete set.

Leuchtturm1917 ballpoint pen

But that doesn’t mean one super special pen isn’t worth investing in. This Bauhaus-inspired ballpoint from heritage German stationery brand Leuchtturm1917 will make writing feel like a treat. It’s refillable and comes in a few different colourways.

Kokuyo x Noritake Haco Haco pencil case

Minimalist but fun, this pencil case is part of a series created in collaboration with Japanese illustrator Noritake. The sub-compartments will be as perfect for a pencil sharpener as for some contraband chewing gum.

Ykra mini wallet

With a rope and carabiner attachment to keep it safe, this mini wallet is made from sturdy cotton canvas and will fit cards and some loose change. It’s the colourful work of Ykra, a Hungarian company inspired by the design of 70s climbing gear.

Clarks Wallabee shoes

First released in 1967, Clarks Wallabees have a rich fashion history. According to GQ, they’re “still loved by Liam Gallagher, Tyler, the Creator and basically half of Tokyo’s menswear scene”, so wearers will be in illustrious company.

The North Face Chuckwalla daypack

This bag is available in three colourways and understated enough to appeal to teens who like to blend in, but it can also provide a canvas for some extrovert DIY bag decorating. Plus, it’s big enough to fit a 16in laptop and lunch.

Post-It notes

An oldie but a goodie, and never not useful for adding some purpose to pandemonium at the start of the new academic year.

Papier academic year diary

The perfect space to plan the year ahead, revision and all, including pages for goals and to-do lists. The only downside is that there will no longer be any excuse for missed deadlines.

William Morris was a Marxist socialist, making him an interesting choice to decorate a bank card holder. But modern life is full of contradictions, and this is a beautiful way to bring some order to an untidy bag this September.

When the Duke and Duchess of Sussex landed back in England earlier this summer, six years after they moved to California and quit as working royals, speculation was rife about where they would call home.

Now, members of the luxury countryside retreat Soho Farmhouse have said they spotted Meghan arriving for an early morning coffee, sparking speculation that the couple were settling down in the exclusive countryside enclave of north Oxfordshire. The correspondent for the Royalist Tom Sykes said the duchess was seen arriving at the Comfy Farm lounge before 9am, where she was introduced to senior staff members by name.

The Cotswolds club, set in 40 hectares (100 acres) of countryside and featuring a luxury spa, 40 discreet guest cabins, and an indoor-outdoor pool, is a hotspot for celebrities.

If it is true that the Sussex family are staying in a property near the club, their neighbours will include the Beckhams, who live within walking distance of Soho Farmhouse and are often seen enjoying dinners and strolls in the grounds.

Paul McCartney also visits with his fashion designer daughter, Stella, who has a house nearby. Meghan and Harry previously rented a house in picturesque Great Tew, a village full of thatched chocolate-box cottages a stone’s throw from the Beckhams.

Another potential neighbour is Geri Halliwell-Horner and her husband, Christian Horner, who live in a £9m former vicarage in nearby Banbury. They share a love of animals with Meghan and have a menagerie on the estate including miniature donkeys. The Telegraph reported that the Sussexes left their rescue chickens back in Montecito but would transport their dogs over.

There have been rumblings of a royal return in the Cotswolds, with the local papers reporting on their move. Their children, Archie and Lilibet, are enrolled at a school for the new term, and parents at a school in the area have reported being sent letters reminding them to maintain the privacy of other children and parents and not to take pictures or share any information about others there.

Although the more than 200,000 members have made Soho House feel less exclusive to some, Soho Farmhouse is still a favourite venue for A-list stars including Taylor Swift, Kate Moss, Tom Cruise and Harry Styles. This could be because it costs £325 a month to be a member, which screens out many members of the public, and taking photographs inside any of its venues is strictly forbidden. The chain recently announced it had banned Meta glasses over privacy fears.

There could also be more royal reunions in the offing, as Princesses Beatrice and Eugenie are regulars at Soho Farmhouse. Eugenie was the first member of the royal family to visit the couple when they moved out to the US.

King Charles wrote to the government on Monday to reiterate that the Sussexes would be private citizens in the UK. He said that would bring the couple “personal latitude … in respect of financial independence and protection of their privacy as they would wish”.

It is a venue that is likely to feel safe to Meghan. In Harry’s memoir, Spare, he wrote that Soho House on Dean Street was “her headquarters whenever she came to London”. He added: “Sometimes she just left her luggage at Soho House for weeks. They stored it without question. The people there were like family.” The couple met there for their first date.

During the same 2016 visit, Meghan was pictured cycling around the grounds of Soho Farmhouse with the Made in Chelsea star Millie Mackintosh. She also reportedly hosted her hen party at the Cotswolds retreat in 2018.

Meghan is a close friend of the Soho House executive Markus Anderson, who is thought to have introduced her to high society in London when she visited in 2016. The two met in 2011 in Anderson’s home country, Canada, as she filmed the TV show Suits.

Harry has several charitable events in the UK planned, including the WellChild awards in London at the end of this month. He will also be getting ready for the Invictus Games, to be held in Birmingham next summer. It has been reported that Meghan may be seeking acting roles, and she recently said she “sometimes” missed her old job and liked being around a crew when filming her Netflix cookery show.

The pair “love” the Oxfordshire countryside and reportedly made the Cotswolds their base when they visited earlier this year to see King Charles. They also rented a place when they were still working royals.

In Spare, Harry wrote: “We thought we could move into Oxfordshire full-time.

“We loved it out there. The air fresh, the verdant grounds plus, no paps.” It seems, perhaps, they have finally achieved this.

Soho House has been approached for comment. A spokesperson for the Sussexes declined to comment.

The AfD’s win in Germany is a dark day for Europe. Time is running out to stop the far right

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 13:56:21 GMT

This party is among the most extreme in Europe. To protect our democracies, liberal parties must urgently change their tactics

The far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) narrowly failed to secure an outright majority in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt. But nobody should take comfort from that. The party still won by a landslide. Decades of far-right election gains have made them seem normal to the point where only the biggest victories are deemed newsworthy. But 44% of the vote for a party that is officially classified as “extreme right” is not normal. It is a black day for European democracy, even if it occurs in a small east German state.

While Saxony-Anhalt (and Germany itself) may have dodged the worst outcome because the AfD won’t automatically fulfil its ambition of forming the first far-right state government in Germany since the Nazi era, there is no reason to assume it will be so lucky at the next election. Neither will other German states, such as Mecklenburg-Vorpommern in two weeks’ time, or other countries, such as France next year. No country is immune from the far right and, perhaps even more worryingly, no far-right party or politician is too extreme for political success (as the US has shown). We must therefore update our analyses and strategies.

Although Saxony-Anhalt, and east Germany in general, is an extreme case, it reflects similar trends in the rest of Europe. Far-right parties are going from strength to strength, with old dominant parties decimated, and party systems fragmented. Consequently, coalition formation is becoming increasingly complicated, particularly if we want to keep the far right out of power. In many countries, provinces and cities, most democratic parties are having to govern together to exclude the far right. This often leads to inefficient and unstable coalitions, in turn feeding yet more political dissatisfaction and far-right support.

Sunday’s results will only intensify an ongoing debate in Germany about the so-called Brandmauer (a firewall maintained by mainstream parties against cooperating with the AfD). Actually, Germany is one of the few EU countries to still have a far-right cordon sanitaire. Throughout Europe, from Italy to Sweden, far-right parties have been normalised and integrated into the political mainstream. In most cases, the (rightwing) parties that collaborate with the far right claim that the latter have moderated and are now “conservative” – a claim that is factually wrong, but increasingly popular with the electorates and members of these parties, and much of the media.

This will remain almost impossible to claim in Germany. The AfD is among the most extreme parties in Europe, and its most successful branches, including the one in Saxony-Anhalt, are among the AfD’s most extreme. This will not prevent some rightwing politicians from claiming that the AfD is less of a problem than the left, and there is even a fear that some parliamentarians from the conservative CDU in Saxony-Anhalt will defect to give the AfD a majority in the state. On the other side of the political spectrum, calls for an AfD ban will become even louder, and while this might be legally possible, it could create a massive popular backlash, going well beyond Saxony-Anhalt.

Both approaches share a too-limited interpretation of the problem. The idea of maintaining the Brandmauer is that the only (or main) problem is outside the system. Yet the system is falling apart as it is. Yes, the AfD (and the far right in general) is a fundamental threat to liberal democracy, but so is the fact that a sizeable and growing part of the population no longer feels represented by its politicians. While many still come out to vote for democracy, they increasingly vote against a party rather than for one.

Even worse, most mainstream politicians have accepted that they are unpopular and try to remain in power by arguing that they are the lesser evil and mobilising people to come out to vote against the far right. Ultimately, this is unsustainable. If democratic parties do not develop inspiring manifestos for what they want to achieve in government, liberal democrats will refuse to come out to vote and the far right will win a majority of votes – even if they represent only a minority of the population.

Developing such manifestos will require realism from politicians, but also from the media and voters. In fragmented party systems with large far-right parties, no party will be able to implement most of its preferred policies. There are no majorities for social democratic, Christian democratic or Green parties and policies. But this should also not be the main concern at this moment. When the far right gets close to governing alone, or dominating coalitions, the main goal should be to strengthen liberal democracy – in terms of institutions and values. This should be something that all liberal democratic parties can agree on.

This does not simply entail strengthening democratic institutions – the judiciary and regulating social media, for example – and promoting inclusion and tolerance. It also means listening to the many concerns and preferences of the majority of voters who do not vote for the far right. In other words, mainstream politicians need to go beyond crime and immigration and focus also on such things as increasing housing provision and public spending, limiting economic and income inequality, fighting the climate crisis and strengthening European integration. And it means accepting that you don’t get everything you want – now or in the near future.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

Of course, many countries are not as close to a far-right majority as Saxony-Anhalt is. But we should not forget that in the state’s 2021 election, the AfD had “only” 20% – and the average score of the far right now is roughly 25% across Europe. In other words, there may not be much time left. And, as we can see in countries such as Hungary and the US, the democratic struggle becomes harder and less fair once the far right establishes power.

Democratic politicians must therefore realise that today’s key fight is for democracy, rather than for party or power. This requires both fighting the far right and strengthening democracy. Neither the banning nor the normalisation of the far right can achieve this. Democracy neither be strengthened in isolation, nor by the politics of fear. It requires a collective effort from democratic politicians, citizens and journalists, who must show realism, resilience and restraint. And the time for that fight is now.

Cas Mudde is the author of The Far Right Today, and is the Stanley Wade Shelton UGAF professor of international affairs at the University of Georgia

‘The more famous I got, the bigger my beehive got’: how Mari Wilson made Just What I Always Wanted

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 13:45:05 GMT

‘I was trying to bring back some glamour. The backcombed hair was like architecture really. It took more than 45 minutes to style’

Just What I Always Wanted had already been in our live set, but with different verses. When we’d gone on David Essex’s Showcase earlier in 1982, in the middle eight I sang “A wink from Wilbur, a kiss from Kurt, don’t tell Hank, he might get hurt” – all names of my backing band the Wilsations. But when it came to recording, I said to Tot Taylor, who wrote most of my early singles, including Love Man and Baby It’s True, “We can’t sing that because no one will know who they are. What about, ‘A mink from Paris, a ring from Rome, a whole new wardrobe in my home?’” Tot, such a brilliant writer, took it from there.

We’d brought in Tony Mansfield, whose futuristic New Musik had enjoyed hit singles with Living by Numbers and This World of Water, to produce the song and my debut album Showpeople. He brought a modern feel but captured our warmth and sense of fun. The trumpet solo was actually a synth, as was the timpani, but Paul Bultitude recorded his very loud snare drum fills in a studio corridor. I’m at the top of my range at the end of the middle eight – something a lot of Motown artists did to make the voice sound more plaintive.

My older sister had a beehive which I’d loved. When I first got mine in 1980, I remember walking through Brent Cross shopping mall and everyone staring. It wasn’t long after punk and no one wanted that look. However, the more famous I became, the bigger it got! It took more than 45 minutes to style, the hair backcombed to buggery – it was like architecture really. I was trying to bring back some glamour.

I’d just come from an interview when I laid down the vocal part in Pete Townshend’s Eel Pie Studios, so I was already in character. I was wearing a crimplene dress and because of my beehive, the headphones had to go under my chin.

The artwork for the single and album covers was inspired by classic Julie London and Peggy Lee LPs of the 1950s. I never wanted to be just an 80s pop singer and later I shifted to jazz. Some people come to my shows and say: “I didn’t know you could sing like that.” My new album combines pop, jazz and soul – a hybrid of what I’ve been performing live all my life.

My earlier singles had reflected my love of 60s soul. I remember being in a studio with the Wilsations when Just What I Always Wanted was discussed on BBC Radio 1’s Round Table. We were excited and had the broadcast relayed through the speakers, but they were saying: “She’s meant to be retro, but she’s gone synthy.” Fortunately, the public were more enthusiastic and it became my biggest seller.

I knew something was up when I walked from my local Post Office to Tesco and heard the single playing loud and clear over the sound systems in both places. Mari and her 12-piece band had been playing live in London for around a year. We’d released a couple of – now rare – singles on my record label the Compact Organization. This operated out of a cupboard in my one-bedroom flat, with a tiny backroom office off Portland Place in London. One of Mari’s singles, Beat the Beat, was an airplay hit and we thought Just What I Always Wanted was probably a likely UK indie hit, if lucky.

But massive radio play and a Top 10 position for three weeks exceeded all expectations. The initial idea for the song came to me when the band were at the BBC for a Radio 1 live session. I sat down at their beautiful Steinway grand piano in a tea break and out of nowhere this short-phrased tune came floating by. I grabbed it, and played it over and over so I could remember it.

Then, on the bus going home, I got a lyric idea for a shopping list of best things – real-life items, or examples of things that were happening to Mari. “A tune from Teddy,” came from my songwriting pseudonym, Teddy Johns. “An Ashworth snap,” referred to Pete Ashworth, the cult photographer who took the – much imitated – photos for the sleeve.

I’ve always believed the song did so well because it followed the list formula, as with Cole Porter’s You’re the Top. It brings a natural structure. Tony Mansfield’s outer space and out of sight production sounded good – and loud – on the radio. And Mari’s vocal is so figured out and “up” attitude-wise. It really shows off her velvet sound.

Mari Wilson’s new album Girl About Town is out now. She plays Cadogan Hall, London on 4 October, then tours

John Healey backs growth but says Labour must be honest on spending

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 12:54:05 GMT

Chancellor ducks questions on whether he will have to raise taxes but says he will stick firmly to fiscal rules

John Healey has said boosting economic growth will be his defining mission as chancellor as he warned Labour had to “be honest” about the need to control public spending at next month’s budget.

In his first big speech since taking the job in July, Healey said the top priority for his 28 October budget would be to support stronger growth across the UK while sticking firmly to the government’s fiscal rules.

“I want to be the chancellor that gets things done and I want to see growth driven from more places across the UK,” he said.

Against a backdrop of jittery global financial markets, the chancellor said he and Andy Burnham were “in lockstep” in their commitment to meeting the government’s self-imposed target to balance day-to-day spending with tax receipts by 2029-30.

With the public finances under pressure from soaring long-term bond yields, which hit an 18-year high last week, Healey argued that stronger growth was the most sustainable way to balance the books. However, he also signalled that his budget would require Labour “being honest about the need to control government spending”.

Economists have warned the chancellor could be forced to increase taxes or cut spending in response to rising spending pressures and the economic fallout from the war in Iran triggering turmoil in global bond markets.

The UK’s 10-year borrowing costs rose slightly on Monday amid pressure on governments worldwide, as fears over the impact of the war pushed the price of oil closer to $100 a barrel.

Aiming to soothe concerns in a speech to business leaders at a manufacturing centre in Coventry, Healey said Britain was continuing to pay a “Truss penalty” almost four years since the former Conservative prime minister’s ill-fated mini-budget triggered a meltdown in the UK government bond market.

With Labour under pressure amid questions over Burnham’s tax and spending priorities and as the UK carmaker Jaguar Land Rover – headquartered down the road from the venue for his speech – announced plans to cut 4,000 jobs, Healey said maintaining fiscal discipline was important in an uncertain and volatile world.

“It makes our task in government harder. It makes the task of every business looking to invest much harder, too,” he added.

Business groups said they welcomed the chancellor’s pro-growth message, including pledges to devolve tax and spending powers to regional mayors and also his promise to “take an axe” to regulations he said were holding back business investment.

Louise Hellem, the chief economist at the Confederation of British Industry, said: “Firms will welcome the positive signals of intent from the chancellor and will now be looking ahead to the budget to see whether the government can match its ambition with decisive action to cut business costs and give firms the headroom they need to invest.”

The chancellor’s critics said his speech was light on detail despite the mounting pressure on the economy.

Andrew Griffith, the Conservative shadow chancellor, said: “John Healey sounds increasingly like continuity Rachel Reeves. Warm words about growth will not make growth a reality, or cover up the enormous damage Labour have done to businesses and family finances.”

Robert Jenrick, Reform UK’s Treasury spokesperson, said: “On the day 4,000 people are losing their jobs, Healey gave a dire and dreary speech that will change absolutely nothing.”

Refusing to be drawn on the details of his tax and spending plans less than two months before the budget, Healey promised to stick to Labour’s manifesto commitments not to raise taxes on working people. However, he signalled the government could look at finding savings from the welfare bill by tackling youth unemployment.

“As the prime minister has said, there is a need to bring down welfare costs. And most importantly for me we have to get more of Britain working again,” he said.

The chancellor ducked questions on whether taxes would need to rise and also a suggestion from the British Chambers of Commerce that the government should scrap the pensions triple lock to fund a cut in employer national insurance contributions to help support youth jobs.

The government is awaiting the findings of a highly anticipated review into youth worklessness by the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, which Healey said would “address this scar of youth unemployment”.

Healey said there was a “moral duty” and a “fiscal duty” to supporting young people to find work.

“A person coming off benefits and into work saves the taxpayer money. And that becomes a win-win when those people start paying tax themselves,” he said.

Next overturns equal pay ruling that raised basic wages for shop staff

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 12:45:59 GMT

Retailer wins appeal against 2024 decision forcing it to pay shop workers the same as warehouse employees

The UK retailer Next has overturned a 2024 court ruling forcing it to pay its shop staff the same higher basic pay rates as its warehouse workers under equal pay rules.

The chain, led by the Conservative peer Simon Wolfson, said it had “won a landmark victory in its ongoing equal pay litigation”. It has succeeded in its appeal to the employment appeal tribunal “on the key issue of basic pay”, it said.

It comes two years after 3,540 claimants won a six-year legal fight for equal pay, which the fashion and homeware retailer then appealed against. Shop workers accused Next of paying its retail sales staff – who are predominantly female – lower hourly wages than its warehouse workers, the majority of whom are male.

Since that employment tribunal ruling in Leeds, several thousand more Next staff have brought equal pay claims, bringing the total number of claimants involved in the litigation to more than 6,400. Next employs more than 20,000 store staff across 458 stores in the UK and Ireland.

Next said the appeal judgment endorsed its position that it “should not have to pay shop assistants and warehouse operatives the same amount of basic pay, in circumstances where the market and working conditions are very different”.

The retailer argued that it had to pay a higher market rate to warehouse staff because of recruitment and retention pressures, which it said did not apply to the workforce in its stores. It added: “Next believes this element of the judgment is not only correct in law, but also a victory for common sense.”

The retailer said the judgment affirmed: “Employers must be able to pay what is necessary to recruit the people they need; and that doing so does not oblige them to raise the pay of other employees where there is no reason to do so.”

The law firm Leigh Day, which represents Next store workers, described it as a “mixed ruling” as it rejected Next’s challenge to the tribunal’s findings that it had failed to justify lower rates of night-time pay, overtime pay and the failure to provide paid rest breaks to store workers.

Next also failed to persuade the employment appeal tribunal that lower Sunday premium payments to store workers were justified. The appeal tribunal held that the issue remains to be determined and should return to the employment tribunal.

The Next case, which covered the period from 2012 and 2023, explained women made up almost 78% of retail sales jobs, while men made up about 53% of warehouse staff. During that time, some warehouse staff were able to earn between 38p and £3.13 more an hour than retail sales workers, according to Leigh Day.

Elizabeth George, a partner at Leigh Day representing the claimants, said: “I am pleased that the employment appeal tribunal rejected Next’s arguments that its pay practices do not disadvantage women. They plainly do and the appeal tribunal firmly recognised that. I am also pleased that the tribunal upheld the findings on night-time premiums, overtime premiums and paid rest breaks.

“The appeal tribunal’s conclusion on basic pay is disappointing. Next pays market rates in both its stores and its warehouses in order to recruit and retain staff. The market rate is higher in the predominantly male warehouse labour market, even though the work carried out in stores has already been found to be equal work.

“While the store staff and their legal team welcome many aspects of this appeal judgment, we respectfully disagree with this approach to justification. We remain confident in our clients’ position and intend to appeal.”

Next had argued that the equal pay ruling created a threat to the viability of many of its stores, and that it put retailers operating their own warehouses at a “material disadvantage” to rivals that contract out their warehouse operations.

The original employment tribunal and the appeal tribunal found that there was no direct discrimination. The employment tribunal found: “It was all about cost. Gender did not enter into the equation” when Next set pay rates.

Next said it had won the vast majority of the terms challenged in the equal pay litigation, including bonus pay to warehouse staff previously, and now basic pay. It intends to seek permission to appeal in relation to other terms.

“This judgment has come at the right time, the UK economy desperately needs jobs and the loss of this appeal would have represented a hammer blow to retail employment in the UK,” the company said.

Four people have been arrested on suspicion of murder after a three-month-old girl died in Staffordshire while camping with her family.

Staffordshire police said they attended the scene in woodland off Strawberry Lane near Great Wyrley and arrested four people on suspicion of murder. This includes a 42-year-old man and 30-year-old woman from south Staffordshire, a 20-year-old woman from Wolverhampton and an 18-year-old man from Walsall.

Officers said all four had now been bailed with conditions while the investigation continued. DI Josh Lee, from Staffordshire police’s child protection team, said: “I want to assure the local community that we are working around the clock to investigate the circumstances of this tragic incident, which has understandably caused concern.

“While we can confirm that all four people have been arrested on suspicion of murder, we are still working hard to obtain further evidence and we are keeping an open mind as to the circumstances of the death at this very early stage, which we are treating as an isolated incident.

“All four people were arrested at the scene of the incident and have been released on bail.

“While we fully understand that speculation into the nature of this incident is likely to take place, we’d ask people to follow this page for factual, accurate updates as our investigation unfolds and to avoid sharing unconfirmed and speculative claims online.”

A spokesperson for West Midlands ambulance service said: “We were called to reports of a medical emergency near to Strawberry Lane at 8.39am on Saturday. Two ambulances, two paramedic officers and a helicopter from the Midlands air ambulance charity attended the scene.

“On arrival we discovered one patient, a female child. Ambulance staff immediately began administering advanced life support but sadly, despite their best efforts it became apparent nothing could be done to save her and she was confirmed dead at the scene.”

TV has never been so nerve-jangling: 10 years of the agonising Motherland

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 11:55:59 GMT

The rage, the wine, the power mums, the PTA horror – the BBC sitcom was a spot on send-up of life at the school gates. A decade on, we remember its most awkward bits

If Uncut Gems was about the school run instead of gambling debts, it would look like Motherland. It is now 10 years since the BBC sitcom jangled the already frayed nerves of all parents watching and turned Anna Maxwell Martin into the most frazzled woman on television in the name of skewering middle-class motherhood.

Whether she was marching her children to buy school shoes the night before term started (“Don’t be closed. Pleeeeeaaaaase don’t be closed”) or having a meltdown at temporary traffic lights en route to a school drop-off that proved redundant because she’d forgotten it was half-term, Maxwell Martin’s Julia would undoubtedly have a more chilled-out time in the kitchen of The Bear than raising her kids.

Originally created by Sharon Horgan, Holly Walsh, Helen Serafinowicz and Graham Linehan (with Barunka O’Shaughnessy joining from series two, after Linehan departed), Motherland arrived into a TV landscape where mothers were no longer images of parenting perfection. But while the likes of Malcolm in the Middle and Outnumbered had embraced the humour in the warts and all of child-rearing, the experience of mothering on television was still mostly centred on the kids themselves: tantrumming toddlers, precocious primary schoolers and stroppy teenagers.

Motherland took a different tack. It was never about the offspring, who rarely amounted to more than the occasional school uniform bobbing into view (rare is a Motherland fan who can name all – or indeed any – of the sprogs). Instead, it was more like a workplace comedy, focusing on the adult experience of motherhood: the passive aggression, the barely disguised competition, the begged-for favours, the ulterior motives, the whingeing and the copious bottles of wine. While it had been considered progress to see women on television who were more than just mothers, Motherland acknowledged an uncomfortable truth: that the mothering bit can really take over, at least for a while there. That being a mother sometimes – often – feels like a constant fight against being flattened into two dimensions.

Alongside Maxwell Martin’s perma-stressed Julia was unflappable Liz (Diane Morgan), token dad Kevin (Paul Ready), long-suffering Anne (Philippa Dunne) and Amanda (Lucy Punch), a vividly heinous alpha-mum creation who always saw herself as the centre of the universe and now literally is, in spin-off Amandaland. The series two introduction of Meg (Tanya Moodie), a high-flying Black woman who appeared to have it all together, gave us a more diverse group but Motherland was carefully hyper-specific to its well-off west London demographic. The horrors here took place at interminable PTA fundraisers, joylessly non-competitive sports days and skin-crawling swimming pool birthday parties (devastatingly, not a drop-off situation).

In Motherland, panic rises faster than house prices in a good school catchment area, and there is always someone to witness you making a colossal balls-up such as panicking about forgetting World Book Day and sending your child in holding an umbrella … as the novel Umbrella by Will Self. Obviously.

The show gamely took on the utter weirdness of mother-to-mother relations: attempting variously to bond with, impress and one-up a group of people who just happen to have given birth around the same time as you. The thwarted efforts to join carpools and get your kids into after-school clubs, all the while doing just enough to appease this gaggle of onlookers eager to judge (if only to convince themselves they are doing OK).

Amanda may be the obvious villain, but Motherland never stopped reminding us that motherhood will, at times, make sinners of us all. Having children does not suddenly wash away our foibles; if anything, it probably magnifies them. Motherland understood that being a mother frequently involves your spirit hovering somewhere above your body, watching yourself mutter Latin gibberish in an attempt to get your kids into a Catholic school, and silently screaming: “How did it come to this?”

As the series progressed and the bonds formed at the school gates transitioned into real friendships, the stakes got higher. But Motherland never lost sight of the relentless nature of parenthood: even as divorce, illness and death reared their heads, lunches still had to be packed (and probably left at home).

It’s a show that really should have had parents diving for the remote rather than spend their evenings reliving a hellish half-term cottage break or attempting to curb a nit epidemic. As Julia hissed when she ended up back at Anne’s house for an afterparty (a special bottle of cava and some dubious homemade paté): “This is my worst nightmare come true – surrounded by mums at night.”

But while it’s too close to the bone to be a comfort watch, sitting down in front of Motherland is an act of catharsis – a reassurance that even when you’re trying really really hard, you still might lose someone else’s child while trick-or-treating. If you no longer identify as a Carrie or a Samantha, perhaps being a Liz or a Kevin feels more appropriate.

It stands up as a triumphantly messy monument to a stage of life that passes in a blur of doctor’s appointments and sponsored bike rides and forgotten swimming kits. Less laugh till you cry and more laugh to stop yourself crying, Motherland holds out a hand to mothers watching. Not to help, of course, but to cling on to across a pub table as you try to fathom how on earth you’ve agreed to sort out the collection for the school’s poorly caretaker.

WSL talking points: Palace result in doubt after substitution nightmare, Arsenal signings shine

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 11:20:32 GMT

Promoted side’s thrilling win may be overturned after they used four substitutions windows while Georgia Stanway show the way for Gunners

Kirsty Howat’s 60-second cameo deep into injury time could ruin what was a memorable day for Crystal Palace on their return to the top flight. An impressive 1-0 victory over Everton was celebrated emphatically by Jo Potter and her players but that joy would have been replaced by concern and frustration not long after. On Sunday evening WSL Football revealed that there had been a breach of the rules – the Eagles used four different substitute windows rather than the regulated three – which had not been picked up by either the coaching staff or the match officials. An investigation has now been launched with punishment to be decided (there is a potential for the result to be overturned). The needless error has put a dampener on what should have been a positive afternoon thanks to England Under-23s forward Lexi Lloyd-Smith’s winner on her WSL debut. Sophie Downey

It was not the first time Chelsea have struggled to kill off games under Sonia Bompastor and, on the basis of Saturday’s 1-1 draw with Aston Villa after an almost excessively dominant performance, it seems the issues of last season have not been put to bed. “I think in a few games we had last season we were in the same scenarios,” said Bompastor. “So, yeah, if you analyse the performance today and the statistics of the game you can say that it’s crazy we couldn’t win the game.” It felt all too familiar, with last season’s 1-0 defeat to Everton in December, which ended a 585-day unbeaten run in the WSL, particularly springing to mind. Then, Chelsea accrued 79% possession, had 30 shots and hit the woodwork three times but came away with a loss. The fear for Chelsea fans will be that, in the 10 months since that defeat, the issues that were becoming increasingly evident have not been resolved. Suzanne Wrack

Match report: Chelsea 1-1 Aston Villa

Much has been made of Arsenal’s recruitment over the summer with many believing that Renée Slegers now has a team primed to challenge for the title. Four of their new signings started in the 1-0 win over Brighton, with two standing out. Recognition of Lisa Baum’s potential came to the fore with a series of impressive showings in pre-season. The 19-year-old caught the eye on her WSL debut on Sunday not just for her well-taken goal but for her direct, positive style of play. Meanwhile, Georgia Stanway showed exactly why Slegers was so keen to bring her in. The England international has added balance to the midfield, allowing Mariona Caldentey to operate more creatively. Stanway controlled the middle of the park, ranking first for touches – at 131, she had 25 more than anyone else – joint top for accurate passes (86%), first for passes into the final third (23) and second for chances created (2). SD

“Just give her the ball and then something happens!” Andrée Jeglertz said of Lauren Hemp after her 200th appearance for Manchester City. The England winger was on typically strong form during the 3-1 victory over Birmingham City and became only the fourth Manchester City player to reach that landmark of appearances. Jeglertz was full of praise for the 26-year-old and continued: “One thing that is fascinating with Lauren is, if you come and watch one of our training sessions, she has the same joy for playing football. It’s also shown in the games. Our job is to put her in situations where she can show how good she is. [She] shows young players what it’s about. They need to love to go to work and love to go to the football field. It’s not just a job. It’s also an identity.” Tom Garry

Many believe the biggest challenges faced by the London City Lionesses manager, Eder Maestre, is integrating a squad that has experienced a high turnover of players and balancing the demands of an expectant cast of superstars. There have been eight arrivals this summer and seven players have departed. Teams that have experienced a high turnover of players after a strong WSL season have previously struggled. On Friday night, however, Maestre’s team showed signs they could buck that trend with a 2-1 win over Manchester United. It wasn’t always the prettiest of performances but fledgling connections were forming in Bromley, with the individual quality of players helping to cut across any lack of cohesion. Gelling players is not easy though. “I think it’s one of the most challenging situations for any coach,” said Maestre. “We have talented players, but we have a clash of cultures. I’m trying to align everybody in the same place, trying to create something big where everybody can feel represented … I’m very happy with the performance.” SW

It was a worrying start to the season for Charlton Athletic fans, as the newly promoted side were convincingly beaten on home turf by the club that finished second from bottom in the WSL last season. Not only that, Charlton failed to register a shot on target during Liverpool’s 4-0 victory and the hosts could only manage two efforts off target, as Gareth Taylor’s visitors’ enjoyed 76% of the possession. It had been a much closer-fought affair when the two sides met on the same ground on April in the Women’s FA Cup quarter-finals, when Liverpool eventually squeezed through after extra-time, but the Merseyside club appear to have strengthened significantly over the summer whereas Charlton clearly have significant work to do. Kirsty Hanson wasted no time making her mark at Tottenham, scoring twice on her debut to secure a 3-1 victory over West Ham after joining from Aston Villa this summer. The forward opened her account with a first-time finish after an assist from Signe Gaupset and then produced a superb left-footed strike into the top corner. Hanson was the third-highest scorer in the WSL last season, behind Bunny Shaw and Alessia Russo, with 12 goals in 22 matches. She was one of several key transfers made during the window with the club believing she will add a new dimension to their attack. Speaking to Spurs Women social media about her performance, the manager, Martin Ho, said: “The movement for her first one was outstanding, and the second was a wonderful strike. Ratko Mladić, the ‘Butcher of Bosnia’, given hero’s funeral in Serbia

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 11:20:15 GMT

Fanfare at Belgrade funeral of man convicted of genocide raises questions from EU over Serbia’s membership plan

Ratko Mladić, a Serbian general convicted of orchestrating the worst massacre in Europe since the second world war, has been given a hero’s funeral attended by thousands in Belgrade despite international alarm.

Known as the “Butcher of Bosnia” for ​his role during the Balkans genocide in the 1990s, Mladić died in prison in late August aged 84 while serving a life sentence for war crimes and crimes against humanity.

Mladić was found guilty of genocide in 2017 for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, in which about 8,000 Bosniak Muslim men and boys were killed after Bosnian Serb forces overran the UN-designated enclave.

But he has remained a beloved figure among many Serbs, with the president, Aleksandar Vučić, arguing last month for him to be released early from a UN detention facility in The Hague so he could die on Serbian soil.

Vučić, an ultranationalist leader, has dominated Serbian politics for more than a decade and is due to run again for prime minister in a snap election announced on Monday.

Mladić’s coffin was flown to Serbia last week on a government plane, draped in national flags and carried from the aircraft by uniformed soldiers.

On Monday morning, thousands of people gathered in front of a small church in the Serbian capital to pay their respects to Mladić. Armed forces stood guard at his casket, on top of which was laid his signature military cap, as well as a sword. A display of medals lay in front.

“We know that his name will remain deeply etched in the memory and prayers of the majority of our Serbian Orthodox people, who feel and nurture a deep sense of gratitude towards him,” said Porfirije, the patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox church.

After the service, a street procession moved with the coffin towards the cemetery, where Mladić was buried with military honours including a three-volley rifle firing salute.

Scenes of military pomp drew condemnation from the European Union’s enlargement commissioner, Marta Kos, who cancelled a forthcoming visit to Serbia on Friday. “The return of his remains to Belgrade reminds Europe of the darkest pages in our recent history,” she said on social media.

Serbia has been negotiating EU accession since 2014, but the process has stalled in recent years.

“The glorification surrounding [Mladić’s] death is incompatible with the values on which the EU path is built,” said Kos. “That path requires confronting the past, genuine reconciliation and respecting the victims of war crimes.”

An EU spokesperson repeated the warning on Monday. “Any glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism contradict the most fundamental European values and have no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries,” he said in a statement.

On Sunday evening, ​football fans displayed a huge image of Mladić and chanted his name at a match in Belgrade.

While Monday’s ceremony was not an official state funeral – probably to avoid further damaging international relations – it mirrored a state event, with large police and military delegations. Vučić said he had a prior engagement, but his son Danilo attended along with several other Serbian ministers, as well as Russia’s ambassador to the country.

During the early 1990s Balkans conflict, when Mladić was a military officer, Vučić was entering politics as part of the Serbian Radical party, a far-right nationalist party that sought to secure land for a “Greater Serbia” by removing non-Serb populations.

Decades later, Vučić has managed to remain in office – once as prime minister and twice as president over 12 years – while vacillating between keeping close ties with Russia and seeking EU membership. But anti-government anger was galvanised after the 2024 collapse of a railway station roof that killed 16 people, with widespread claims of corruption threatening his hold on power.

On Monday, Serbia’s government said it intends to ⁠dissolve parliament and set a date for a snap election, a year ahead of a planned December 2027 vote. The current prime minister, Djuro ‌Macut, said: “If we want to mitigate tensions in society there ‌is no better way than to ask people.”

The election has been seen as a chance for Vučić, who cannot legally run for president for a third term, to stay in high office, and his ruling party has nominated him for prime minister.

Marko Vujić, an assistant professor at the Faculty of Political Sciences at the University of Belgrade, said he did not believe the government had planned the snap election announcement to coincide with Mladić’s funeral. “But once his death occurred, the regime took advantage of the momentum surrounding the event and used that day, among other things, for the dissolution of parliament.”

Mladić was one of the main architects of the policy of ethnic cleansing during the Bosnian war, which killed more than 100,000 people and displaced more than 2 million.

Key among his crimes was the 1,460-day siege of the Bosnian capital, Sarajevo, where the civilian population was subjected to daily shelling and sniper attacks from Serb nationalist forces, and more than 10,000 people were killed.

The three-year conflict culminated in the 1995 killing of at least 8,000 Bosniak Muslims in the town of Srebrenica, a crime that shocked governments in Europe that had spent decades working to prevent mass killings after the mid-century horrors when Nazi Germany killed 6 million Jews.

In Srebrenica, Mladić’s forces were filmed handing out sweets to children and promising their safe passage before thousands of Bosnian men and boys were rounded up, killed, and their bodies bulldozed into mass graves. “We give this town to the Serb people as a gift,” Mladić said at the time in filmed comments.

The killings have been pointed to as an international failure, especially as Srebrenica had been designated a “safe haven” under the protection of the UN, a global body created immediately after the second world war specifically to help prevent such bloody future global conflicts.

Mladić was arrested in Serbia in 2011 after 16 years as a fugitive, and sentenced by a UN tribunal in the Netherlands to life imprisonment in 2017.

While in detention, Mladić had been in ill health after having a series of strokes.

The Balkan war started after the June 1991 breakup of Yugoslavia, when Slovenia and Croatia declared independence. Bosnian Serbs quickly took control of more than two-thirds of Bosnia and launched the siege of Sarajevo. After three years of bloodshed, the Dayton agreement was signed in Dayton, Ohio, ending the war and creating the independent state of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

Leader of group behind flag campaign in England charged with 14 offences

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 10:43:44 GMT

Ryan Bridge, who co-founded Raise the Colours, to appear in court on charges including racially aggravated harassment

The leader of a group responsible for raising union jack and St George’s flags across England has been charged with 14 offences, including racially aggravated harassment, threatening behaviour and assault.

Ryan Bridge, 45, of Bromsgrove, Worcestershire, co-founded Raise the Colours, which describes itself as a “grassroots movement for unity and patriotism”.

The group’s members have been erecting union jack and St George’s flags on roundabouts, lampposts and other street furniture across England since August last year.

Thames Valley police said they had charged Bridge with 14 offences from a two-month period in Oxfordshire from 31 January 2026. He is due to appear at Oxford magistrates court on 3 November.

The offences are:

Seven counts of using threatening words or behaviour to cause harassment, alarm or distress.

Three counts of using threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour with intent to cause fear of, or provoke, unlawful violence.

Two counts of racially aggravated intentional harassment, alarm or distress.

One count of racially aggravated fear of violence.

One count of common assault.

Officers said a file was prepared and submitted to the Crown Prosecution Service after a review of the evidence, including witness accounts and available footage.

Oxfordshire county council was granted an injunction against Bridge and others to prevent anyone from raising flags on public property, citing safety concerns as well as trespass and obstruction.

Birmingham city council announced last week it was seeking a similar injunction against Bridge and others. The application will be heard at the high court on Tuesday.

Bridge attended the Reform UK conference in Birmingham at the weekend, and told the Guardian he was invited by the party. “We got an invite, so we thought we would come along,” he said. There were no general admission tickets to the Reform conference for members of the public, where attenders were almost entirely members.

Farage praised Bridge and his group’s efforts at a conference event on Saturday, telling him: “What your campaign has done is wake up vast parts of this country.”

At the time, Bridge was on bail after he was arrested by Thames Valley police on suspicion of causing racially and religiously aggravated harassment, alarm or distress earlier this year. Bridge has previously denied any wrongdoing.
