The pet I’ll never forget: Harold, the halls of residence cat, who looked after me when I first left home

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 10:00:48 GMT

He was the gorgeous furry tabby who made my day, even when he waltzed into my flat just to finish my takeaway. Now he’s a campus celeb, with a part-time job guarding the doors of the village shop

In 2022, when I moved into halls of residence at the University of Sheffield, my biggest concern was no longer having a furry friend to come home to, as I’d had a cat since I was 11 years old. Then I met Harold.

My first encounter with this gorgeous tabby was quite unusual. One day, in our 10-bed flat, a flurry of messages appeared on the group WhatsApp chat after my fellow roommates caught an intruder on the sofa, innocently munching on my leftover pizza.

As in many homes for first year university students, there were plenty of unfinished takeaways lying around the kitchen. And Harold was a smart cat with a clear goal: food. Any time he saw a snack or sensed one from a distance, he would come running. A can of tuna. A block of cheese. The occasional pancake. And I was more than happy to feed him – he probably had a better diet than me.

With the area housing more than 4,000 students, Harold was in high demand. He would choose a different home every night (we never found out if he had an actual owner), so I felt honoured when, from time to time, he would turn up meowing at my door. Catching him after a night out waltzing into our flat always cheered me up. It was the perfect end to an evening – as long as he stayed away from my chips.

You’d often find him stretching out in the sun, eyeing up his next treat, or waiting for the lift to his third flat of the day. But, once the novelty of the university pet wore off, some of my flatmates were less keen on letting him in, as they knew his game. For me, he was too charming to refuse.

At times I felt as if I was cheating on my childhood tabby, Pippa, who still lived in my family home – there was no other animal I could have a greater love for. But I cherished Harold in a different way. For a pet-loving student getting to grips with independent living, he was a home away from home.

At the end of my first year of university I moved out of the buildings Harold used to roam, but I would still occasionally see him strutting from flat to flat. Later on, I became a residence mentor, supporting first year students living in university accommodation. “Do not let the cat inside any student flats,” the managers told me during my training. On a few occasions, I may have turned a blind eye.

Today, Harold remains a campus celeb, with 10,000 followers on Instagram as Harold the cat of Endcliffe (the name of the halls where he was found). He is always posing for the student paparazzi on social media, and even has a part-time job – guarding the doors of the village shop.

I’ll always be grateful to Harold for the laughs, the late-night chats and, most importantly, for being a much-needed anchor in my first year as a student.

Why are so many people stealing from restaurants?

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 10:00:47 GMT

About a quarter of British adults admit to having pilfered something from a pub or restaurant. Is it an Insta-fuelled craze, or just old-fashioned greed?

Knives, candles, a toilet roll holder complete with screws and Rawlplugs – that’s just some of the stuff Michelin-starred restaurants in France complained about clients nicking in a recent news report. I’m not sure why the screws were presented as the ultimate absurdity – if you want to use your stolen toilet roll holder, you’ll need them – it’s just common sense!

A Québécois restaurateur complained about similar thefts in July – a picnic table, a painting and even the thermostat had been pinched – and British restaurateurs confirm it happens in the UK, too. Jan Ostle of Wilsons in Bristol told the BBC’s World at One that the mother-of-pearl spoons he uses to serve herb sorbet are a particular target: “Every few months I have to buy another 28.”

It’s an age-old, frequently aired story – all down to a sense of entitlement, or the desire for a souvenir, or booze-fuelled bravado – but it seems awfully retro. Wasn’t trousering a Conran restaurant ashtray a quintessential 90s petty crime? We’re supposed to be into “experiences, not things” now, and isn’t the whole point of posting a boring Instagram carousel of seven badly lit amuse-bouches to show everyone you’ve been somewhere fancy without stealing a side plate?

But our basest instincts are still seemingly awoken by tableware in a hospitality setting: a survey by catering equipment supplier Nisbets found 27% of British adults had nicked something from a restaurant or pub. I’m not above such crimes: there’s a dinky spoon in the drawer here we definitely didn’t buy. It must have arrived nefariously, but I just don’t remember when or how (exactly what a criminal would say). We also eat our dinners off Quick trays my husband may have liberated from the Belgian fast-food chain in the 1980s.

What can restaurateurs do? Some have tried putting price tags on stuff, confronting suspected spoon smugglers (chef Tom Aikens caused a kerfuffle doing this to a customer in 2012), and even amnesties (Mexican chain Wahaca promised free tacos to customers who returned its covetable brightly coloured spoons).

The boring solution is passing on costs with higher prices; my (marginally) more fun suggestion is bringing back branded matchboxes and matchbooks, which were a colourful, legit way to brag you’d been somewhere. They’ll need to tell clients they’re forbidden to take them, though – it’s all about the thrill, not the thing.

‘Like an AI agent’: Wolff hails Antonelli’s Italian GP victory in title charge

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 09:48:06 GMT

Mercedes principal likens 20-year-old to F1 greats

‘No stopping him when a driver and car are one’

Toto Wolff has compared Kimi Antonelli to the greats of Formula One after the Mercedes driver’s remarkable victory at the Italian Grand Prix where he came back to take the flag from 19th place on the grid.

The Mercedes team principal cited the win as similar to some of the best made by Lewis Hamilton, the seven-time world champion, and said that Antonelli would likely remember the race as one of the greatest of his career.

Antonelli, 20 years old and in only his second season in the sport, delivered an exceptional drive to take victory in Monza, fighting his way through the field and ultimately beating his Mercedes teammate, George Russell, who had started in second on the grid, into the runner-up spot.

Wolff, who had been insistent that bringing Antonelli into the team last season was the right decision despite questions being raised over his youth and relative inexperience, felt Antonelli had definitively proved himself.

“We’ve seen it with other great ones in the past – Lewis, who did it at some of the races – that’s what he’s shown,” said Wolff. “There’s just no stopping when a driver and a car are one, there’s nothing that can stop them.”

Antonelli now leads the world championship by 66 points from ­Russell and 76 from Ferrari’s ­Hamilton with 10 meetings remaining and is in a commanding position in the title race.

In 2024 he had made his debut for Mercedes in the first free ­practice at Monza and was left disappointed when he crashed out at the ­Parabolica corner, leaving some questioning his credentials. His win on ­Sunday, Wolff felt, had finally put the ­incident to bed.

“This is one that I will remember. It’s how the circle closed,” he said. “Two years ago in first practice it was probably the toughest moment in his career for himself and his family. A moment where everyone doubted, including himself.

“Then two years later, it’s the ­biggest glory, the biggest moment of his career that’s probably going to be one of his biggest moments overall in the future. Even if he wins another 200 grands prix, that one will always remain special.”

Antonelli endured a difficult first season in F1 last year as he learned the ropes but has come on with extraordinary alacrity. He now has seven wins this season, including a run of five in a row, is in a strong position to close out the championship and Wolff compared his ability to learn and improve to that of advanced artificial intelligence.

“He came out after the winter out of the blocks in a way that no one saw coming,” Wolff said. “The ability, how he processed last year. He’s been at all the races, he’s seen the pressure of the media, the attention that he gets. It’s in a way that the system has been processed and saved.

“That’s why the results that we’ve seen afterwards. But it is still surprising and amazing to see how quickly he develops. For me it’s like an AI agent that continuously self-improves and learns.”

Russell, the more experienced driver at Mercedes, has a huge task ahead and admitted his teammate was all but uncatchable.

“It is definitely Kimi who is in ­control of it and he is deserving to be in control, I am not even thinking about a fight or a comeback,” he said. “It is going to be exceptionally challenging to overcome that gap. I am sort of accepting that is what it is and I am going to try and enjoy it from here on in and win as many races as possible.”

25 years ago, two strangers met in the twin towers and escaped on 9/11. What happened next?

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 09:00:30 GMT

Stanley Praimnath and Brian Clark were two of only four individuals known to have survived above the impact zone in the south tower

He has told the story hundreds of times, but it never seems to fade. If anything, it only becomes more vivid. “Oh, gosh,” exclaims Stanley Praimnath, his voice cracking with an “ooooooh!” as if bearing a weight. “It’s like reliving that day.”

Nearly 3,000 people died in the terrorist attacks on New York City and Washington DC on September 11 2001. But Praimnath and another office worker, Brian Clark, were two of only four individuals known to have survived from above the impact zone in either tower of the World Trade Center. The two strangers met in the smoke and fire of the 81st floor of the south tower, and walked down 1,620 steps into the rest of their lives.

Their split-second decisions that day made all the difference. Over the next 25 years, both men moved from middle age into old age and retirement. Both enjoyed family weddings and watched children and grandchildren grow. Both saw US presidents come and go as old wars ended and new wars began. They remained friends through it all.

They also told their story – countless times – in churches, schools, TV studios and elsewhere. “It could be 800, 1,200, a number like that,” Clark estimates.

Praimnath, in a separate interview, muses: “People refer to me as ‘the 9/11 guy’. It doesn’t feel repetitive. It is like unloading baggage from my shoulder, like washing my soul with tears. It is comforting to know that people out there still want to hear.”

Clark is now 79, living in retirement in northern New Jersey with his wife; he has 11 grandchildren and two great-grandchildren. Praimnath, a decade younger, lives in Valley Stream, Long Island; he is a pastor, grandfather and empty-nester who speaks of his survival not as luck, but as an act of God’s grace.

Their recollections of 9/11 are still as clear as the cloudless sky over Manhattan on that September morning. Clark, a Canadian who was executive vice-president at the financial brokerage firm Euro Brokers, arrived at his office on the 84th floor around 7.15am. Down on the 81st floor, the Guyanese-born Praimnath had settled into his desk at Fuji Bank, where he worked as a loan officer.

At 8.46am, the peace was shattered by a deafening double boom as the hijacked American Airlines Flight 11 slammed into the north tower. Clark recalls: “The lights above me flickered and I spun around in my chair and my peripheral vision caught flames against the window. It was surreal. Two or three seconds later, the flames dissipated and the airspace was filled with singed paper.”

Having volunteered as a floor fire warden after the 1993 World Trade Center truck bombing, Clark sprang into action. He retrieved an official torch marked “WTC fire safety team” from an overhead cabinet and began shepherding staff toward the building’s central corridor.

Co-workers crowded against the north-facing windows, gazing up nine stories at the raging “ring of fire” consuming their twin building. Thinking the emergency was confined next door, Clark phoned his wife at home and his father in Toronto, reassuring them that he was safe.

Three floors below, Praimnath was on the telephone with a colleague in Chicago who had witnessed the north tower explosion on television and begged him to evacuate. He was looking towards the Statue of Liberty when he spotted another plane – so close that he could make out the “U” on the tail of United Airlines Flight 175.

“On a given day, it was normal for a plane to zoom by a half a mile to a mile away,” he recalls. “But this plane is coming towards me. I made eye contact. I dropped the phone and screamed and said, ‘Lord, I can’t do this. You take over’. I don’t know why I said that – but thank God I said that.”

Praimnath dived under his desk in the foetal position, weeping and praying as the Boeing 767 bore down on his window. “With the most thunderous sound, the plane came and crashed into the building,” he says.

The aircraft struck diagonally at 9.03am, cutting through the 77th to 85th floors. The impact flattened entire walls, severed electrical wiring and sent a shock wave of jet fuel and debris through Fuji Bank’s offices.

Praimnath says: “That big orange glow that you see there – I’m stuck in the middle of it. Upon impact, it looks like a demolition crew came with a big giant wrecking ball and ripped the entire office. Every wall is flattened. I remember a large chunk of the plane was broken off and stuck in the office doorway.

“I remember flames all around me, as if somebody took a giant bag of cement, threw it in the air and I can’t breathe. The floor above me collapsed and it’s hovering over the desk and I’m like, ‘Oh, my God, I’m going to die. It’s gonna totally collapse, crush me to death, or I’m gonna get sucked out by the air pressure.’ You can hear the sound.”

At the memory, he sets his teeth and blows down the phone to recreate the terrifying whoosh.

Three floors higher, Clark was standing on the west side of the 84th floor when the aircraft sliced into the building’s eastern trading floor. “Our room exploded,” he says. “Everything came out of the ceiling – air conditioning ducts, lighting, the whole works. For five seconds the building swayed to the west and then it swayed back to vertical. For those 10 seconds I was quite terrified, thinking the building was going to roll over. But it didn’t.”

When the tower steadied, Clark gathered a group of six or seven colleagues and led them toward the central core. The impact had demolished stairwells B and C, but stairwell A, tucked furthest away on the north-west side, somehow remained open.

The group began descending stairwell A. On the 81st floor landing, they were halted by a man and woman coming up the stairs. “She was insistent we not go down,” Clark says. “‘No, no, no. You can’t go down,’ she said and, because she stopped us, it allowed me to hear a call for help from within the 81st floor, a muffled cry: ‘Help, I’m buried. I can’t breathe.’”

Clark squeezed through an opening where the door frame had been ripped from the drywall and stepped into the dark 81st floor, guided by Praimnath’s desperate shouts.

Inside the office, Praimnath prayed for rescue. “I can still remember the flames encroaching and I’m screaming, ‘Lord, send somebody, I don’t want to die.’ I’m crawling away from the flames, dodging all the cables that were hanging in the ceiling, short-circuiting because the sprinkler system came on,” he recalls.

“I’m like, ‘Oh my God, I’m gonna die.’ Somebody had a flashlight on the other end of the floor. The person’s saying, ‘I’ll wait for you’, but I couldn’t hear because I got temporarily deaf when the plane hit the building. As I’m crawling away, the flames are coming closer, licking up the office space.

“I got to the wall. The person’s saying, ‘Bang on the wall, I know where you are’. I hit the wall and the person says, ‘Climb over there.’ It had a hollow ceiling, a 10-foot sheetrock wall, a drywall. I remember that so vividly.”

Clark’s torchlight had picked out a hand protruding from a hole in the 10-foot sheetrock wall. He grasped Praimnath’s hands and hauled him over the partition. The desk beneath Clark gave way, and both men crashed to the floor in a heap.

Clark recalls: “We fell and he gave me a big kiss. I said, ‘What’s going on, what are you doing?’ I stuck out my hand and said, ‘I’m Brian Clark.’ He says, ‘I’m Stanley Praimnath; we’ll be brothers for life.’ I said, ‘Well, I don’t have any siblings.’”

Clark noticed that Praimnath had a puncture wound on his palm, while his own hand was cut and bleeding from moving debris. Clark recalls his instinctive gesture of solidarity: “I smooshed our hands together and said, ‘In fact, we’ll be blood brothers for life. Come on, buddy. Let’s go home.’”

When they returned to the stairwell, Clark made the critical decision to ignore the warning of the woman on the landing. Pointing his torch down the staircase, he saw no flames. Clark and Praimnath turned downward. Most of the colleagues who had been with Clark, however, chose to head upward, believing safety lay on the roof. They died in the collapse. At Euro Brokers, 61 of Clark’s colleagues perished.

When Clark and Praimnath finally emerged on to the street, police and emergency workers yelled at them to run. Minutes later, the south tower collapsed in a cascade of steel and concrete, sending a rolling cloud of debris surging through lower Manhattan. The two men dived inside 42 Broadway to escape the choking dust.

In the chaos, Praimnath reached into his pocket and handed Clark a business card from a small home business he and his wife operated. Separated in the confusion, Clark used the number on that card to reach Praimnath late that evening, confirming that both had made it home.

While Clark suffered remarkably little long-term psychological distress – describing his lack of post-traumatic stress as an unearned “gift” – Praimnath’s return to the living was fraught.

Arriving home on Long Island on the evening of 9/11, Praimnath says he suffered profound memory loss. “I wanted to know what this strange woman was doing in our house with two children, not going home. I refused to go to bed because this strange woman was in that room.”

His wife, Jennifer, quietly cared for him without judgment. “She would hobble me into the bathroom, fill the tub with warm water and Epsom salts, and tell me to soak,” he says. “Then she would put me on the couch. Every day, she would leave an apple, a sandwich, a bottle of water and a notepad. I don’t know how long I was in that state. All I know is that one day, I got up, looked at her, recognised her and snapped out of it.”

When Praimnath returned to work in October at a temporary office in Jersey City, he still could not navigate on his own. “I had to draw out my commute on a map and color-code it,” he recalls. “When I got to work, people would say, ‘Stan, can you please sign this?’ I didn’t have a clue what I was signing. But they were kind, patient managers. Gradually, the pieces came back.”

In the quarter-century since that Tuesday morning, the lives of Clark and Praimnath have remained intertwined. They shared family milestones, celebrated at each other’s daughters’ weddings and phoned one another regularly.

When Clark’s eldest daughter married, Praimnath and his wife were seated at the head table. Praimnath says: “Brian introduced me to all his friends and family as his blood brother. You could see people looking around, thinking, ‘Something doesn’t quite fit the picture!’ But Brian didn’t care. That’s who he is. He is the big brother I never had.”

For Praimnath, surviving 9/11 opened a deep spiritual vocation. In 2006, he became a pastor, joining the staff of the church where his father-in-law was senior minister. Over the past two decades, he has travelled to churches, military bases and schools worldwide, delivering his testimony as a sermon on redemption.

“On 9/11, I was crying out to the Lord under that desk, ‘Lord, let me live to walk my daughters down the aisle,’ and God answered. I walked Stephanie and Caitlin down the aisle. I’ve lived to see my grandchildren, Hannah and Ezra. They don’t call me Papa – they call me ‘Papaya’. Stephanie even bought me a shirt that says ‘Papaya’.”

Yet Praimnath’s resilience has been tested repeatedly. In 1993, he narrowly escaped the first truck bombing at the World Trade Center. He was diagnosed with leukaemia and a severe bout of Covid-19 scarred his lungs with bilateral pneumonia. Then, after a trip to Europe with his wife, doctors discovered that his four coronary arteries were severely blocked, requiring emergency quadruple bypass surgery.

“My question has always been: how many times do you try to kill one man?” asks Praimnath, who retired from the Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation two years ago. “I’m living by grace. I still travel. I still do exactly what I used to do before.”

He and Clark know they have more years behind them than lie ahead. On the 25th anniversary, Clark will attend a memorial service at his local town square in New Jersey, beginning at 8.45am, before spending the day quietly with his wife. Praimnath will be at a church in Virginia, telling his story once again, with gratitude.

Both men find themselves speaking to a generation for whom 9/11 is not a living memory, but history. Clark, who retired in 2006, says: “I don’t have to teach history anymore – the textbooks have that covered. What textbooks don’t have is the emotional reality, the optimism that life carries on despite terrible evil. But whenever I speak at schools, 98% of the time, the very first question the kids ask is: ‘Are you still in touch with Stanley?’”

Praimnath experiences the exact same phenomenon. Just recently, he addressed 700 students over Zoom at a Christian school in Tampa, Florida. “These children weren’t even alive when the towers fell,” Praimnath says. “Yet when you describe the roar of the jet engine and the wing slicing through the office, you can hear the audible gasp in the auditorium. It becomes real to them.”

The blood brothers look out at the contemporary US with a mixture of sorrow and perplexity. Clark has become an outspoken pacifist, dismayed by the decades of overseas conflict that followed the attacks.

He says: “With 25 years of time to think about it, I realise more and more the utter futility of war. I think of Germany, Italy, and Japan being our greatest allies today. What on earth are we doing to ourselves? Dropping bombs on residential areas in Ukraine, Russia, Gaza – what a senseless waste of energy and human life.”

Clark’s aversion to vengeance ran so deep that he was repulsed by the street celebrations following the killing of al-Qaida leader Osama bin Laden in 2011. “I was disgusted when people were driving around in pickup trucks chanting ‘USA!’ and cheering for another human being’s death. Capture him, interrogate him, lock him away – fine. But taking lives and celebrating it? No. That is not who we should be.”

Praimnath recalls the profound but fleeting sense of unity that blossomed after 9/11. “After that infamous day, the entire nation rallied around each other,” he reflects. “All the churches were packed. A month later, everything went back to normal.

“But I still believe we are a resilient people. We may have our political differences but at the end of the day we know that, when tragedy strikes, the labels fall away. On the 81st floor, there were no Republicans or Democrats, no Black or white. We were just brothers trying to find the way out.”

Friendships meant everything to me as a child. I worry today’s young people are being robbed of that

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 07:00:28 GMT

We sat in the park, laughing for hours, talking about nothing. Today’s childhoods are digital – and the result is an epidemic of loneliness

I saw an old friend recently – the kind you’ve known for so long that you clear a whole day for them, as you might a family member. We laughed and laughed like we were teenagers again, and drank martinis before lunch, and it felt almost like it always did when we were young, except we could afford better than cheap cider, and he owns a house and I’m someone’s mother.

Another old friend – one I’ve known even longer, since I was six – described me and the other girls who made up our little group as “fake siblings”. That is how lifelong friendships feel. There’s an easiness and acceptance that comes with longstanding intimacy. You know each other’s secrets, you’ve been inside each other’s parents’ houses, shared beds and cigarettes, witnessed heartbreak and foolishness, tears and whiteys, before the more serious stuff piles up: weddings, births, illnesses, life crises, deaths. You talk about the serious stuff, of course (there has always been some serious stuff, but teenage friendships often provide a refuge from it), but when you need it that old friendship is a portal, transporting many of us to a time of lightness and freedom that is otherwise hard to access.

I don’t know where I’d be without these friendships, which is why it makes me sad to read that young people today aren’t making them, or at least not in the same way. According to a new report from the Institute for Public Policy Research titled The Loneliest Generation, the number of young people with no close friends has risen fivefold since 2014, with 11- to 24-year-olds becoming dramatically more isolated. One in 20 16- to 21-year-olds say that they have no close friends at all.

The report cites digital childhoods and austerity measures such as youth club closures as factors in eroding the foundations of a good adolescence. My own friendships owed much to the digital realm (specifically MSN Messenger), but they were still largely and crucially face to face, and that seems to be one of the things that has changed. We did not have internet childhoods, and so the skill – and I do believe it’s a skill – of making friends was crucial, and acquired young. The things that bonded us – circumstances, subcultures, music and, most of all, humour – took place mostly offline. We spent hours sitting in parks or around campfires, just talking and joking. We went to gigs and club nights and festivals. We rode our bikes or begged lifts or walked five miles home. It’s strange seeing these ways of relating to one another being idealised by younger people, spoken of wistfully in social media posts and comments as though something has been lost. I suppose we idealise the countercultures of our parents’ eras. People simply conversing without a phone present shouldn’t be seen as radical, but it’s being framed that way.

We are right to be worried about this mass loneliness among young people. To spend adolescence without friends can leave a lifelong trace. Even the friendships that didn’t last affect us, even – perhaps especially – those that were not so straightforward. Therapists are fond of the phrase “rupture and repair” because it’s accurate – falling in and out and in again with friendship groups can be educative. It can teach you to be kinder to one another, to tolerate difference, and to learn what behaviour you are and aren’t willing to put up with. These are important life lessons but they are increasingly overstated – the online language of friendship, which emphasises what a friend “gives” you or “adds” to your life seems intense and transactional to those of us raised in less psychobabbly times.

These sorts of bonds take time and energy to establish. Many, many hours of sitting and fooling around. The art of friendship is as much the art of doing nothing. Of mooching. Hanging out. Watch an old sitcom such as Seinfeld and friends are always running errands together. When did you last go to the dry-cleaner’s with somebody?

Much has been written about the decline in third spaces and its impact on social relationships. Places to hang out, outside home or work, are essential to the art of real-world friendship. So is time to talk, to wander and to linger together. When it comes to the crisis in friendship, a social media ban for under-16s is a good thing: it makes relating to one another in person more of a priority, and leaves more time for those activities that bond us together.

It’s only as you get older that you realise how precious those adolescent years are. People don’t talk about fun enough – how important it is to wellbeing and survival. So much about technology makes our lives smoother and quicker, but I am not sure it makes it more fun. Not like gathering four or five or six people around a campfire and drinking cider before all jumping naked into a river, or exploring an abandoned house (not something I would ever endorse, but something we used to do). Memories of adolescence and the people we spent it with have been found to be more vivid. They call it the “reminiscence bump”. It is a crucial time for development and, as I’ve found myself, those memories carry us through our lives. In my dreams, I still explore abandoned houses with those kids, my fake siblings.

What will be the long-term wellbeing impact if those years are filled instead with the flickerings of other lives on a screen, gobbled up and then swiped past, forgotten? We must preserve the art of friendship before it’s lost for ever.

‘It’s the Bayeux tapestry of TV!’ After six decades, the seminal series bows out with 70 Up

The Guardian Mon, 07 Sep 2026 04:00:25 GMT

The ‘hugely important artefact’ that’s followed 14 children since they were seven is set to air its final instalment. The now-septuagenarians and director Asif Kapadia talk about breaking new ground for 63 years – and changing TV for ever

Described as the Bayeux tapestry of television, the groundbreaking ITV documentary series Seven Up is coming to its final conclusion.

In 1964, a group of randomly chosen seven-year-olds from different backgrounds were brought together and filmed in an attempt to answer questions about the effect of fate, class and environment on people’s aspirations and outcomes.

Designed to test the Jesuit maxim of “give me the child until he is seven and I will show you the man”, it began as a one-off World in Action film for the regional ITV company Granada. But the producers then returned to the children every seven years, charting their progress and creating a snapshot of Britain’s social history.

Viewers’ own lives, loves and losses have been reflected in the experiences of the contributors, such as Neil Hughes – the bright Liverpudlian schoolboy who dreamed of attending Oxford University but became homeless and then a local councillor – and Jackie Bassett, the straight-talking Londoner who was ahead of her time in challenging conventional norms.

Now the series is bowing out with 70 Up, which has noticeable differences from previous iterations. The Oscar-winning director Asif Kapadia has taken over from his long-running predecessor Michael Apted, who died in 2021. Many thought Apted’s death meant the end of Up, but the producer Claire Lewis – the custodian of the brand since 28 Up – got a call from one of the group, Nick Hitchon, who had terminal cancer and wanted to record a final interview.

Hitchon died hours after Lewis recorded his thoughts, which she said was heartbreaking, so “we all decided that we should make another film and [began] looking for a director”.

Knowing the concluding series needed someone skilled in archive and interviewing, she tracked down Kapadia – as his films about Ayrton Senna, Diego Maradona and Amy Winehouse “blew me away” – and discovered he was a fan of the series and that Apted had met and admired him.

With Kapadia secured, Lewis then had to persuade the contributors to take part one last time. There may yet even be another incarnation of their stories, she said.

Kapadia’s involvement helped convince Hughes to do 70 Up, “because I knew this was going to be a fresh start, a very different sort of enterprise”. It was also “a chance to meet some of the other participants, probably for the last time,” he said.

But he also reveals he feels that the portrayals of the struggles he has faced mean “I constantly try to clean up my image”. Hughes thinks Apted was very professional but “knew what he wanted”.

“Michael was selectively using the material he had. Now I don’t criticise that; that is within the gift of a director.” But Hughes “relished the chance to say to people, ‘Well, I’m not quite maybe what you think I am’.

“With the greatest respect to viewers of the show … they didn’t see the real me. There’s a me here who Michael never discovered.”

Now living in France, Hughes does not watch TV, not even the Up series. He says it is “partly a self-defence mechanism” but also that “I’m very sensitive to screens. I don’t have a mobile phone”.

Hughes has spoken before on screen about his struggles with depression and says in 70 Up: “If somebody has a mental health problem, it doesn’t mean they are odd. It doesn’t mean they have chosen to be weird or antisocial … It’s not something they chose. It’s what they are.

“I’m as happy as I could be given my life … I’m still quite lonely at times, but this is a common characteristic of our age.”

I ask him if he thinks his life might have been different if there had been more understanding of neurodiversity when he was younger.

“Yes, I think so,” he said. Because now “it is about recognising people’s individuality”.

There have been “pluses and minuses” to being in the series, he said, and he wonders existentially if television’s artifice means taking part has influenced the outcome of contributors’ lives.

Overall he thinks he has benefited – notably his friendships with Lewis and fellow participant Bruce Balden. As is common in TV, the participants also were paid so “because my life’s been a struggle to keep afloat financially … the little contributions from Granada have helped from time to time”.

Duty of care to contributors has been paramount for Lewis. She says it was important to ensure she didn’t influence them at the “same time as having a relationship that was honest and trusting”. Hughes credits her for creating an “extended family” feeling among the group.

For the 1964 film, “all the parents were talked to” about their children being involved, she said. “But not in the same way that they would be today”. Plus “it was completely innovative” and nobody knew it would run for so long.

As British TV’s first social experiment, it paved the way for reality shows such as Big Brother and the rise of content creators.

Kapadia, for whom directing 70 Up is a “dream come true”, says it is a one-off and the “most beautiful thing I’ve ever made”.

“A lot of people have copied it and been inspired by it. But none of them will ever do this ever again,” he told the recent Edinburgh TV festival.

His main aim has been to be “true to the series [and] answer the question that’s asked at the beginning: is your life defined at seven?”

Born to Indian Muslim parents, Kapadia thinks it is “impossible not to watch it to think about your own life, your own parents, your relationships, your kids … it’s about them, but it’s about us and there’s nothing else like it”.

Lewis feels Kapadia’s fresh viewpoint chimes with questions being asked about authenticity and unconscious bias in the world of television, making Apted the “15th character in the series”.

Kapadia explains: “Who shoots it [and] who picks who is important” in shaping a documentary, along with “how do you cut it [and] who is judging what’s interesting or what isn’t interesting?”. Unlike Apted, he did not go to Oxbridge and “had free school meals” growing up in east London, so “what is your norm is how you always make projects”.

The biggest takeaways from the participants include Hughes saying it is “remarkable, and maybe this is one of the things that Michael discovered” that he and Balden had become friends despite their different backgrounds. “It’s good for us to recognise that that can happen,” he said.

Another key conclusion is some male contributors wishing they had spent less time at work. Lewis says Apted also “realised he didn’t spend as much time with his family as he should have done, and he really regretted that”.

She thinks one of the most profound concluding statements comes from Symon Basterfield, who grew up in care and now fosters children. He said: “The one thing I’ve taken from this programme is my story is special because it’s been seen; not because it is special, just because it’s been seen.”

A vital part of the “beautiful” and “genius” films, said Lewis, is that Apted and his original team ensured the series featured “ordinary people … they are somebody you could have been living next door to”.

Bassett said: “It’s been wonderful to be part of. It’s been difficult at times, but I think we always knew that while it started about class … it ended up being about us and how different audiences relate to us.”

The stories of the 14 individuals and Apted may have a new lease of life, as Lewis reveals: “What I would like to do now, because we have the material, is to make hour-long films about each person.”

She is looking for funding from universities or media for the new edits, which will tell the participants’ individual stories and show how the conventions of television and our society have changed.

As ITV’s factual controller, Jo Clinton-Davis, puts it, the Up series is like the Bayeux tapestry, with all who have worked on it feeling the responsibility of “looking after this hugely important artefact”.

“It sort of belongs to all of us,” she said.

70 Up airs at 9pm on 15 September on ITV1 and ITVX. All previous episodes in the Up series are streaming on ITVX in the UK

Brushing Aside Trump’s Threats, Canada Retaliates on Tariffs

The New York Times September 07, 2026

U. S. Tariffs and Trade

Advertisement

Supported by

New Canadian levies of up to 50 percent are expected to begin Tuesday, even as Washington warns of a new round of American tariffs.

By Ian Austen

Reporting from Ottawa

With an insulted and angry nation solidly behind him, Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada is charging ahead in a bitter trade war with the United States, risking a further fraying of what once was one of the world’s closest friendships.

Retaliatory tariffs, set to take effect at 12:01 a. m. Eastern time on Tuesday, demonstrate Mr. Carney’s defiance toward increasing bombast by President Trump, who has been trying to humiliate Canada economically after more than two weeks of finger pointing and threats.

Mr. Carney’s response has distinguished him as one of the few world leaders standing up to Mr. Trump as he lashes out at American allies on a range of issues.

The new measures will double the rate of existing tariffs that Canadian businesses pay on imported American steel and aluminum products and affect about 700 products, including aluminum foil, railway locomotives and steel bridges.

Polls show that Canadians strongly back Mr. Carney’s decision to end trade talks with Washington last month and hit back with tariffs on about $20 billion in American products entering Canada. But there is also concern over what might happen next. Mr. Trump has repeatedly threatened another round of American tariffs if Canada follows through on its plan.

Some in Canadian industry say they are inclined to take Mr. Trump at his word, at least on this threat.

People in the Trump administration “are willing to hurt themselves, their own sectors and industries, in pursuit of their goal, however misguided I think it is,” said Flavio Volpe, the president of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers’​ Association of Canada. “So they may escalate. I hope that we don’t end up in a tit-for-tat situation.”

In what appeared to foreshadow Mr. Trump’s latest intensions, he announced on Monday that Bombardier, the Montreal-based aerospace company, would be banned from selling in the American market unless it built in the United States.

“They live off American Buyers, American Companies, American Airports, and American Service — All while Canada blocks our GREAT American Banks, and Companies, throughout the U. S. A.,” Mr. Trump wrote in a social media post announcing the ban.

Mr. Carney announced Canada’s new tariffs after he pulled Canadian negotiators out of talks in Washington last month — an ultimately unsuccessful attempt to stave off 50 percent American tariffs on $20 billion in Canadian exports and to reduce or eliminate tariffs of up to 50 percent on Canadian steel, aluminum and automobiles.

The Trump administration said the tariffs it imposed last month were in part a response to retaliatory tariffs Canada placed last year on some U. S. imports, particularly autos. American officials have repeatedly noted that only China and Canada retaliated against the United States since Mr. Trump began upending global trade.

Since trade tensions began to rise with Canada at the start of Mr. Trump’s second term, the United States has lashed out in ways both substantive and symbolic, including threats to block the reopening of a U. S.-Canada bridge and an executive order to rename Lake Ontario to “Lake America.”

At a news conference after a sternly worded speech announcing the tariffs, Mr. Carney declared that Canada had been attacked by the United States and that the two countries are now “at war.”

Last week, Scott Bessent, the U. S. Treasury secretary, rejected that framing, arguing that Canada is too small an economic power to battle the United States. “I don’t think you can be in a tit-for-tat with someone who’s 13 times larger than you are,” Mr. Bessent said on CNBC.

On Friday Mr. Trump escalated his trade rhetoric even further. He said that he might “end all trade with Canada” and other countries that have trade surpluses with the United States. Mr. Trump has frequently made dramatic threats during trade negotiations that have gone unrealized, such as floating the idea of a 100 percent tariff on Canadian goods in January.

Separately, the U. S. commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, said Mr. Carney had shut down the talks to gain “political leverage” at home, not because of what the U. S. side had offered.

Mr. Carney made clear last week that he was in no hurry to return to negotiations and was focused instead on diversifying Canada’s trade and expanding its domestic economy.

“At the appropriate time, the conversation will happen,” he said. “But the most important thing we can do is not to spend all our time waiting by the phone, waiting for a call, refreshing on social media to see what’s coming across.”

Many of the American items that will soon face Canadian tariffs of 15, 25 or 50 percent mirror the Canadian exports that now face 50 percent American tariffs, particularly clothing and wood products. Canada revised the list to remove dozens of fish products after the Canadian fishing industry said that tight cross-border integration meant its members would also be harmed.

Canadian officials have suggested that many of the targeted American items come from states where voters supported Mr. Trump, though some political analysts question how much pressure that will actually put on the White House. The list also includes items with little significance for the Canadian economy, including the metal bands that attach erasers to pencils, migratory bird identification bands and fish egg incubators.

Mr. Trump has not imposed tariffs on some of Canada’s largest exports, including oil and gas and many minerals, and has exempted many products with enough North American content to move duty free under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement. Auto parts, for example, are subject to a 25 percent tariff but generally cross the border without incurring it.

As a result, Canada’s overall average tariff rate remains low compared with what most other countries face and the majority of its trade, by dollar value, is still duty free.

After the talks collapsed, Mr. Trump threatened to impose 50 percent tariffs on autos and auto parts in January, apparently without the U. S. M. C. A. exemption — a move most analysts believe would be devastating for Canada’s auto industry. Mr. Trump has not taken formal steps to carrying out the threat, though some in Canada speculate that rather than target new products or raise existing tariff rates, the Trump administration may instead strip away the U. S. M. C. A. exemption for many goods.

Mr. Volpe said that auto parts makers were not intimidated. He said that last year, when the Trump administration proposed collecting tariffs on Canadian auto parts, “they understood that it would shut down the auto industry in a week.”

He added: “Ultimately, I think they will back off that. But if they don’t, they can have at it.”

Zane Irwin contributed reporting from New York.

Ian Austen reports on Canada for The Times. A Windsor, Ontario, native now based in Ottawa, he has reported on the country for two decades. He can be reached at austen@nytimes. com.

As people who receive a lot of packages, we at the WIRED Reviews team have a foolproof way of making sure an important delivery shows up: step into the shower. If you’re sitting at your desk with your shoes on, waiting and ready, I guarantee that every knock or ring will be from someone trying to sell you something or convert you to an obscure and weirdly expensive religion.

Even if you’re working in your backyard or hungover in bed, the best video doorbell can help you tell which knocks are worth lunging for and which ones can wait until next time. We've tested these smart doorbells for months, peering at Instacart deliveries and stray raccoons from the safety and comfort of our couches. The Nest Doorbell is our current favorite, but you'll find plenty of alternative picks that might work better for some folks.

Don’t see anything you need here? Check out our other guides, including the Best Indoor and Outdoor Security Cameras, the Best Subscription-Free Security Cameras, and the Best Personal Safety Devices and Alarms.

Updated September 2026: I added mentions for doorbells from Aqara, Ezviz, and Ecobee, updated the Reolink Video Doorbell with my latest testing impressions, and updated prices.

Google

Amazon

Walmart

Best Buy

Google

I’ve had Google’s third-generation Nest Doorbell (wired) installed by my front door for months, and overall, I’ve been quite happy with the experience. It’s one of the most attractive video doorbells on the market—design is important; it’s the first impression of your home, after all.

I used the predecessor for a few years, and while it did the job, I ran into connectivity issues more frequently; it occasionally had trouble operating in cold weather, too. Now that I’ve been through a rather frigid winter in New York City with the third-gen Nest Doorbell, I’m happy to report that things have improved. It’s hard to pinpoint whether some of my issues with the older model were due to my previous router, but I upgraded my mesh system to Wi-Fi 7 right around the same time I installed the latest Nest Doorbell, and I haven’t had any major connectivity problems. Sometimes the live view takes a beat to load, and very rarely I get “live view unavailable,” which usually resolves itself after a little while.

The best upgrade is the 166-degree wider and taller field of view with the 1:1 aspect ratio. You can see far more in the frame—including packages left at the bottom of your door—and the system intuitively zooms in on people and important subjects when the notification arrives on your phone. The resolution is sharp at 2K, and the scene is well-exposed thanks to HDR, day or night.

I have Google’s TV Streamer, and when the TV is on, I can get notifications that someone has rung the doorbell with a live view right on the big screen. (My other Nest displays and speakers blast that the doorbell is ringing around the house because I don’t use Google’s included chime.) You can communicate through the doorbell, and delivery drivers seem to hear me just fine when I ask them to leave a package by my trash can or that I’m not home.

I’ve set up activity zones through the Google Home app, and the Nest Doorbell does a good job of only bothering me with whatever happens in those zones, though it can occasionally pick up a stray person walking down the street. You don’t have to subscribe to Google Home Premium Standard or Advanced, but it’s worth it if you want more than six hours of event video previews. I also get Familiar Face detection through the subscription, so the Doorbell announces when a friend comes over, but the accuracy is hit or miss. It frequently mistakes me for a few different friends.

It’s annoying that Google gatekeeps the Gemini-powered home automations into the subscription, because these can be very useful. I asked Gemini to make sure my smart floodlights turn on only after midnight when it detects motion, and it set it up within seconds. You can’t even search your video history without the Advanced plan, which feels a little ridiculous. The daily summaries included in this plan are also not super helpful, especially when they get things wrong or suggest that my friend was in my front yard when they weren’t. I do like that I can search “Did I get a package today?” and subsequently find the clip where FedEx hid a package behind my trash can. But once again, this isn’t always accurate. There are times when I know I got a package, but Google says it didn’t detect one.

If you’re in the Google Home ecosystem and are in the market for a video doorbell, I think you should give the Nest Doorbell a shot, and if things go well, then consider subscribing if you think you’ll take advantage of the extra features. —Julian Chokkattu

Arlo

Walmart

Best Buy

Amazon

The Arlo Video Doorbell 2K (2nd Gen) comes a close second. I love the crisp video with HDR support, and this video doorbell has the widest field of view of any I tested at 180 degrees. Alerts come through quickly, and you get useful animated previews.

You need a subscription for the best features here, including person and package recognition, activity zones, and more. It starts at $8 a month for a single camera, jumping to $18 for unlimited cameras. That includes a 60-day video history, and Arlo's cloud videos loaded quickly for me. The live feed also loads quickly in Arlo's app.

Battery life will vary depending on how busy your door is, but mine has lasted around a month before needing a charge. You can hardwire it to continuously charge the battery. The Arlo doorbell works well with Alexa and Google Home, and you can have smart displays or speakers announce callers, alongside the alerts on your phone. There is also now support for Apple Home, but it requires you to connect the doorbell to an Arlo SmartHub or Base Station (this also enables local storage).

While the resolution is very good, the frame rate drops to 15 at night, resulting in choppy footage. The smart recognition features are great, but not quite as good as our top pick, and the live feed has a slight (second or two) lag on the action. That said, this is the best video doorbell if you already have an Arlo system. If you're willing to pay for the Premium subscription ($25/month), you can also get 24/7 professional monitoring and response, potentially scoring you a home insurance discount. There is also a cheaper HD Arlo Video Doorbell ($59), which has a lower video resolution.

Eufy

Amazon

Best Buy

Walmart

People often buy video doorbells to keep tabs on deliveries, but they don’t always capture a perfect view of your front porch, and they tend to have a blind spot directly below. Eufy’s solution is the Video Doorbell Dual, which combines a standard 2K camera with a secondary camera that’s angled down to take in your doorstep and porch floor. I reviewed the original Eufy Video Doorbell Dual S330 a while back. The E340 is very similar but works without having to connect to a HomeBase hub (though it can connect to the HomeBase 3 if you want). It has 8 GB of built-in storage and a removable battery, and it can connect to your existing doorbell wiring.

Local storage is a definite selling point for Eufy, and the E340 also has onboard AI to detect people and packages (it can even recognize familiar faces, though it’s not always accurate). I set it to only alert me about people or packages, and it works well. Combine that with activity zones and motion sensitivity, and it is easy to cut out false positives. By default, the main camera offers 2K footage that is crisp and clear, but if the sun is up, it can blow out areas of the picture. The downward-facing camera has lower resolution, but it's perfectly adequate for tracking parcels or spotting that the cat is waiting to get in. The dual camera lights allow color footage at night, but they take a toll on the battery life.

Alerts and the live feed are swift when I’m at home on the same Wi-Fi network, but there can be considerable lag when I'm out and about. It can also take a while to load recorded videos. There’s no Apple HomeKit support, though it does work with Google Home or Amazon Alexa (the option to use Echo devices as chimes is handy). I don’t think the Eufy E340 is the best-looking doorbell, but it is relatively affordable and probably the best option for folks who don’t want a subscription. If you don’t care about the second camera, the wired version of the Eufy Video Doorbell C31 ($100) is its cheapest model worth considering and is often discounted.

Note: I stopped recommending this brand for a while after a few security breaches—when a security researcher identified cloud uploads from a supposedly local-only device, a report warned of video streaming without encryption, and a bug in May 2021 exposed some camera feeds to other Eufy users. After initial denials, parent company Anker acknowledged and fixed the issues, overhauled its policies, and instituted a bug bounty program. I spoke with third-party security researcher Ralph Echemendia, who was hired to conduct an audit, and decided to start testing Eufy cameras again.

Aqara

Amazon

Best Buy

Apple households seeking a battery-powered doorbell that doesn’t need to connect to existing wiring might be interested in Aqara’s G410. (It can be wired too.) Video is sharp, and the camera offers an expansive view. The lack of HDR is a problem if your visitor is backlit by bright sun. While it works with the Aqara app and Google Home or Amazon Alexa, it offers more when paired with Apple’s HSV (HomeKit Secure Video)—and this will preclude the others. I tried it both ways, but let's look at Apple HSV first.

HSV requires a HomePod or an Apple TV set up as a home hub and at least the 50-GB iCloud plan at $1 a month for a single camera. (The 200-GB plan supports five cameras for $3 a month.) You get unlimited recordings, alerts for people, packages, vehicles, and animals, motion zones, and even face recognition. It’s great when it works, with doorbell alerts instantly streaming live video on your iPhone, Apple Watch, or Apple TV, but it isn’t reliable. Occasionally, it inexplicably missed motion events that other doorbells caught.

Aqara’s G410 is one of the chunkiest doorbells I have ever tested, partly because the chassis needs room for a whopping six AA batteries. Sadly, it ships with disposable batteries that fell well-short of Aqara’s suggested four months—it was closer to one month. But I’ve since swapped them out for Panasonic’s rechargeable Eneloop, and they lasted a bit longer. Testing it without HSV, it performed more reliably, with the indoor hub recording video to a microSD card and doubling as a loud chime and Wi-Fi repeater. The G410 is not fully waterproof, so it's only suitable if you have a porch, or at least some cover at your front door.

The depth of features in the Aqara app is impressive, with options to configure loitering alerts and fine-tune detection zones. It’s also worth mentioning that you can record 24/7 video if you hardwire this doorbell. But as the only battery-powered option that currently supports HSV, that is its unique selling point.

The G410 is a good upgrade over the Aqara G4 ($90), which it replaces here. It offers a wider view that takes in more of the porch, sharper images, and enhanced connectivity that enables it to act as a hub for Matter and Aqara Zigbee devices. If the G410 is too big for you and you can hardwire your doorbell, check out the Aqara G400 ($100). It is slimmer, supports PoE, and has an IP65 rating.

Reolink

Amazon

Walmart

Best Buy

If you worry about how to secure your video doorbell, this local-recording Reolink doorbell can be hardwired. It also supports Power over Ethernet (PoE) for a speedy, reliable, and secure connection. Reolink offers a straightforward app that displays clear 2K video playback, and this doorbell records to a microSD card, so you're not bound to a monthly service fee. It even includes a plug-in chime in the box instead of trying to upsell you like many competitors. The Reolink doorbell has usable but choppy night vision (the frame rate maxes out at 20). Built-in speakers and a microphone allow you to plead with the FedEx driver to linger for 10 seconds before disappearing into the ether.

This doorbell is not battery-powered and does require a wired connection. You have three options: connect to your existing doorbell wires, plug into a power outlet, or connect via PoE using an Ethernet cable (ideal for NVRs). PoE is your best bet if you can run a cable because it ensures a rock solid connection and also protects your footage from Wi-Fi jammers. It supports both RTSP and ONVIF, and you can use it with your NAS device or NVR. It can also be configured for continuous recording.

There is onboard person detection and custom zone support without the need for any subscription. I found it worked well enough after tweaking the sensitivity, and it can reliably detect people versus general motion. Compared to something like Arlo's security camera app, Reolink's smart sensing is a bit behind. Smart home support is also limited to Amazon Alexa and Google Home (there's no Apple support). But if you're replacing a traditional wired doorbell with a video doorbell, this is a solid choice that avoids fees or dead batteries.

I've tested several other video doorbells. These are the ones that narrowly missed out on a place above.

SwitchBot Smart Video Doorbell for $100: I don't love the design of this wide doorbell, but it does come with a wee display that you can use to view who’s there and answer. This could be handy for folks who don’t want to rely on a phone and it lets anyone in the house check who is calling. Video quality is decent, though the frame rate is limited to 15, and the display is low res. You can record locally, and there’s a subscription option if you want cloud storage. Sadly, I found the display was often slow to wake up, and sometimes I had trouble playing back recorded videos.

Aqara G400 Select for $100: This wired doorbell from Aqara is a mixed bag. It’s affordable, comes with a chime, and offers decent video quality (up to 2K). There’s local video storage if you insert a microSD card. It supports PoE or regular doorbell wiring, and has onboard motion and person detection. But it’s a big, chunky lump of plastic, night vision is below par, and you need a HomeGuardian subscription to unlock smarter AI detection (faces, animals, vehicles, and packages), rich notifications with screenshots, and AI video search. The subscription starts from $5 per month ($50 for a year) and also gives you 90-day cloud storage. Alternatively, you can use this doorbell with Apple HomeKit Secure Video (though it will limit the resolution), or with your own NVR or NAS, as it supports RTSP and ONVIF. It also works with other smart home options (Amazon, Google, and Samsung), but it lacks the Matter and Zigbee connectivity of the Aqara G410 above.

Philips Hue Secure Video Doorbell for $170: After a fiddly installation, you get a stylish doorbell offering sharp 2K resolution day or night and a wide view that takes in your whole porch. Notifications are swift and reliable, and you can sync up your Hue lights in interesting ways. But if you don’t already have a Philips Hue setup, I’d pick something from above instead. There’s no local storage option and you must buy a Smart Chime separately. Although you can get 24 hours of video for free, the false alerts will drive you mad. You must subscribe (from $40 a year) to get vital features, like people detection, activity zones, and back-to-back video recording.

Wyze Battery Video Doorbell for $66: Another solid budget option, you get decently sharp 1536 x 1536 resolution video with a 150-degree field of view from this doorbell. You can record locally on a microSD card and there’s good smart home connectivity, but you need a Wyze subscription, from $3 per month, to get person, package, pet, and vehicle detection, back-to-back video recording, and rich alerts (it’s not worth getting without this subscription). The indoor chime is sold separately, and if you want advanced features like facial recognition or descriptive alerts you have to pay more ($10 or $20 a month).

Logitech Circle View Doorbell for $200: As close as you can get to an Apple video doorbell, this compact hardwired doorbell boasts a 160-degree field of view with a 3:4 portrait aspect ratio that takes in your whole porch. Video is crisp and clear, in bright or low light, and the live feed is impressively quick to load. The notification system can tell the difference between animals, people, and vehicles, and will start to recognize familiar faces over time. It works directly through the Apple Home app, though there are pros and cons to Apple's HomeKit Secure Video. Ten days of encrypted videos are stored in your iCloud account (if you have a 50-gigabyte subscription or higher). Alerts come via Apple devices, but your regular chime will also sound when this doorbell is pressed. I love that live video pops up on the Apple Watch or Apple TV when someone rings the doorbell. The complete lack of support for Android or Alexa will turn some people off, and I encountered several issues with this doorbell cutting out and having to be rebooted at the fuse box.

Amazon Blink Doorbell for $60: One of the cheapest doorbells worth considering, (wait for one of Amazon’s frequent discounts to save even more) the Blink Video Doorbell only needs two AA batteries to run for months. But you need a subscription unless you buy with the Sync module (I recommend it). The Blink Basic subscription is $3 a month or $30 a year. Video quality is 1080p with a limited field of view (135 degrees horizontal and only 80 degrees vertical). The lack of HDR shows in mixed light, with bright areas blowing out and shaded areas losing detail. If you have a person at the door with light behind them, it can be tough to see their face. Notifications lacked images or video and were slightly slower than some of the competition, but they always came through. The two-way audio is passable.

Nest Doorbell (Battery) for $200: If you can’t hardwire your doorbell, the battery version of our top pick is still a great doorbell. I tested it alongside several competitors, and it consistently outperformed them. Alerts are swift, and notifications include animated previews that make it easy to decide whether you need to act. While the resolution isn't the sharpest (960 x 1280 pixels), and the field of view is 145 degrees, Google compensates with HDR video at up to 30 frames per second.

Doro Hemma Doorbell for £150: A simplified smart doorbell for seniors is a solid idea, and Swedish maker Doro gets plenty right with the Hemma. It is a battery-powered doorbell that’s easy to install and use, offering a 1440 x 1440-pixel resolution with a decent frame rate (30 fps), local recording via microSD card, and a plug-in ringer that gets loud enough to hear throughout the home. It worked reliably during testing, and the mobile app is deliberately straightforward, with a handy option to pass calls off to a trusted friend or family member (they’ll need the app too). The two-way audio works well, there’s a handy zoom function when you livestream, and there’s a siren to scare folks away. It is simplified, so there are no privacy zones or package alerts, and it may be too sensitive for busy front doors, though you can set it to alert just for doorbell rings. Battery life is decent, though the battery is not removable, so you need to take the doorbell off to charge or use a portable charger. Sadly, it is only available in the UK and Europe.

SimpliSafe Video Doorbell Pro for $170: If you’re looking for a solid security system, SimpliSafe is likely on your radar, and for folks with a SimpliSafe setup, the Video Doorbell Pro fits in neatly. Former WIRED reviewer Medea Giordano found it sensitive at first, but, after an update, she says it worked nearly perfectly, sending swift alerts and offering a good, clear view of her porch. Footage maxes out at 1080p, but the camera supports HDR to banish glare and has a 162-degree field of view. It does have to be wired, and you need a subscription from $5 per month to record videos, but SimpliSafe also offers the option of professional monitoring (from $32 per month), which is a rarity for doorbells and might make sense if you have a complete security system with them.

TP-Link Tapo (D230S1) Smart Battery Video Doorbell for $109: For folks seeking a local storage option that doesn’t require a monthly fee, Tapo's smart video doorbell is worth a look. Notifications come through swiftly and include a still image; video quality is excellent, even at night, and the indoor hub takes a microSD card and doubles as a chime. On the downside, it is chunky, and the onboard AI (which is supposed to recognize people, pets, vehicles, and packages) is flaky.

We didn't like every video doorbell we tested. These are the ones we don't recommend.

Ezviz EP8 Ultra: It took me several attempts to set up this doorbell. Despite following the exact same process each time, it only worked on the third try. Once I was able to set it up, I found it to be a feature-packed video doorbell offering dual cameras for a view of your front step and visitor, two batteries so you can switch in a charged one when it runs low (it can also work with doorbell wiring), onboard AI motion detection that includes facial recognition without a subscription, local video storage with 32 GB built in, and a plug-in chime. There’s also a light, color night vision, and AI characters (panda, raccoon, or husky) that will delight kids, but likely confuse delivery people. The video quality is decent, though the fixed frame rate (15 fps) is disappointing. It worked well when it worked, but I had real issues with it going offline. Even after I moved it closer to the router just to test, it regularly showed as offline in the app, and I couldn’t access the feed. It still came to life and rang the chime when I pressed the button. The EP8 Ultra is only available in the UK and Europe right now.

Ecobee Smart Doorbell Camera: Formerly known just for smart thermostats, Ecobee dips its toes into the smart-home ecosystem world with this 5K HD smart doorbell whose feed can be viewed in the Ecobee app or right on an Ecobee Premium model thermostat screen. One of its main selling points is the 175-degree field of view, which is a dramatic improvement over the older Ring camera it replaced on my porch. However, notifications for movement and people are alarmingly slow and inconsistent; the app interface is clunky; and it has thought my totally standard-looking doormat was a package every day for the two months I’ve been testing it, sending a notification any time someone comes to the door. Ecobee’s smart thermostats are still best in their class, but I’d skip this doorbell add-on. —Kat Merck

Imou Doorbell 2S Kit: Aside from being large and ugly, the Imou doorbell offers crisp video recording up to 2K with a 166-degree field of view, and it has a unique trick: the lens can rotate through 30 degrees to track subjects. The large size allows for a big battery, but this doorbell can also be hardwired. The kit includes a plug-in chime with a microSD card slot for local storage. Unfortunately, testing side by side with the Arlo, it failed to pick up some events. I also had major connection issues after changing my router, despite retaining the same network name and password. I had to reset the chime, which temporarily deleted the doorbell. It's only available in the UK.

Reolink Video Doorbell (Battery): We liked Reolink’s wired doorbell, listed above, so I was excited to try its first battery-powered model, but it was a disappointment. It offers up to 2K footage with a 1:1 aspect ratio that gives you a complete view of the porch, but you must turn HDR on in the settings, and it has a relatively low frame rate (15 fps). I like the option to go subscription-free, but it means putting a microSD card in the doorbell itself, and this is a relatively easy doorbell to remove. Reolink suggests up to five months of battery life, but my first review unit died after less than two and refused to recharge. Reolink sent me a replacement, which is performing better, but when it does run out, the rechargeable battery inside cannot be removed, so you have to take the doorbell off to recharge it. Factor in the slightly confusing app, relatively slow loading times, and connection glitches, and this is impossible to recommend.

Ezviz EP3x Pro

Ezviz EP3x Pro: This is a far better-looking doorbell than Ezviz’s previous models, and it’s nice to see solar panels as an option for doorbells, though you will need a porch capable of catching some rays. The video quality is good, and you get a split view (like the Eufy above) that includes packages or waiting cats on your doorstep. The distortion correction works well, and there is optional color night vision with a built-in light, though it only works at very close range. I appreciate the 2FA, with fingerprint login, and 32 GB of onboard storage (cloud storage is an optional extra). Sadly, if you use the solar panel, you can’t connect to your wired chime. The lack of HDR is disappointing, human detection was a bit off (it frequently said I was a cat), and I had issues with alerts failing to come through on some Android phones. (Even after following Ezviz’s instructions, they never worked reliably on my Xiaomi 14 Ultra.) This model is not yet available in the US.

Botslab Video Doorbell 2 Pro: The flaky setup procedure required a couple of restarts, and physical installation was no better, as the screws supplied were so cheap that one of the heads broke off. The camera has a fisheye effect, but you can correct it with different views. I liked the VR mode, which provides a 180-degree view of your front porch. It comes with a handy plug-in chime, alerts seem reliable, there is an HDR option, and you can record locally (32 GB included) or in the cloud. You can also set a detection range, which could be handy for street-facing cameras. But the app is confusing, with an AI tab that lists various skills available for purchase. There is a login history and a limit of two devices signed in at once, but no 2FA, which makes this impossible to recommend. It is versatile but also relatively expensive.

Swann SwannBuddy Video Doorbell: This doorbell comes with a wireless battery-powered chime and the option of local storage, but the positives end there. The video quality is poor, the app is painfully slow to load and glitchy, and the doorbell frequently fails to register motion. I found the battery life disappointing. I must also question the decision to provide local storage via a microSD card inserted in the doorbell (the chime would make more sense and be more secure).

What Features Should I Look for in a Video Doorbell?

Here are a few factors that you might want to think about when shopping for a new video doorbell.

Resolution and HDR: The higher the resolution, the clearer the picture you get, but consider that higher-resolution video also requires more bandwidth to stream and takes up more storage space. If your front porch is in direct sunlight or strong shade, I strongly recommend opting for a video doorbell with HDR (high dynamic range) support, as it helps to prevent bright areas from appearing blown out or shadowy areas from being too dark to see. Sometimes it's called WDR (wide dynamic range).

Field of view and aspect ratio: If you want a head-to-toe view of the person at your front door, then think about the field of view and aspect ratio offered by your prospective pick. A wider field of view will take more in but can cause a fish-eye effect. Rather than a traditional landscape aspect ratio, you may prefer a square or portrait view to ensure you can see a visitor’s face and any packages that might be on your porch.

Local or cloud storage: If you don’t want to sign up for a subscription service and upload video clips to the cloud, ensure your chosen doorbell offers local storage. Some video doorbells have microSD card slots, while others record video to a hub device inside your home. You can expect to pay somewhere around $3 to $10 per month for 30 days of storage for a video doorbell.

Advanced features: The best doorbell cameras offer features like package detection and person recognition. These features can be handy for filtering alerts, so you only get useful notifications. Bear in mind that you may need a subscription to gain access to advanced features.

Security: A couple of things I recommend looking for are two-factor authentication (2FA) to ensure that someone with your username and password cannot log into your doorbell, and encryption to ensure that anyone accessing the manufacturer’s servers cannot see your Wi-Fi login details or watch uploaded videos.

Which Is Better, a Wired or Wireless Video Doorbell?

Smart doorbells require more power than traditional doorbells. If you opt for a wired video doorbell, you may need a new transformer, and you will likely want to hire an electrician for safe installation. The main advantages of wired doorbells are that you shouldn’t need to touch them again after installation, and they will ring your existing doorbell chime. Wired doorbells are usually a bit cheaper and slimmer than models with batteries, too.

Battery-powered smart doorbells are easy to install yourself and can be mounted wherever you like. The main downside is that you must remove and charge the battery every few weeks or months, which means some downtime unless you buy a spare battery to switch in. Remember also that your regular doorbell chime won’t work with a battery-powered smart doorbell, so you will probably need to buy a wireless chime device to plug in somewhere in your home, though you can also configure smart speakers to act as doorbell chimes.

Most battery-powered video doorbells can also be wired, which may be the best solution if you have concerns about power outages. Wired doorbells are generally faster to alert and more reliable than battery-powered doorbells.

How Well Do Video Doorbells Perform?

All smart doorbells need a strong Wi-Fi signal to perform well. Some come with hubs that double as Wi-Fi repeaters for a better connection. Remember that performance away from home when you access the video doorbell on your phone will be heavily impacted by the quality of your phone’s internet connection. Every video doorbell I've tested has a slight lag, but you should be able to see the live feed in close to real time and carry on a two-way conversation. While feeds should load within two to three seconds, occasional delays in loading the live feed are common, and I have yet to find a flawless doorbell. Video doorbells tend to load fastest in their native app.

What Is the Best Video Doorbell Brand?

While Google's Nest Doorbell is our top pick, it might not be the best video doorbell for you. If you already have a security camera system or plan on getting one, it makes a lot of sense to stick with the same brand for your doorbell. That way, you can access everything in the same app and get a single subscription if required. If you have a lot of smart home devices, check that the doorbell is compatible with your preferred ecosystem and voice assistant.

Why We Hesitate to Recommend Ring

Ring is reintroducing a policy to enable local law enforcement to request footage directly from Ring users, making its camera tough to recommend. We stopped recommending Ring a few years ago due to this policy, and that reasoning still stands. We also have concerns about its data collection (among other issues), so we have decided to stop testing Ring doorbells and cameras again.

How I Test Video Doorbells

I've been testing video doorbells for several years now. I install every video doorbell I test and use it for at least two weeks, but usually longer, as our main doorbell. I check the responsiveness when at home and away, test all the features in the app, and explore the smart home integration options. After the initial test, I install the doorbell alongside other doorbells (usually at least our top pick) and directly compare the response time and accuracy of alerts.
